💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turner Duckworth rebuilt the Vocation Brewery identity around one watchful eye, bold colour and paired beer names like Life and Death.
  • The work starts from a return to roots.
  • It has been revealed that each beer gets a name made of two things that should not sit together: Life and Death, the classic IPA, Heart and Soul, the session IPA, and Bread and Butter, Love and Hate, Naughty and Nice, Hop Skip and Juice and Crush Hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turner Duckworth rebuilt the Vocation Brewery identity around one watchful eye, bold colour and paired beer names like Life and Death.

The work starts from a return to roots. Turner Duckworth stripped the brand back to two founding ideas, a commitment to brewing and a belief that craft beer is for the many, not the few, then built everything from a single mark. The eye, a secondary mark from the brand's recent past, now anchors the identity, a sign of unwavering focus and a visionary outlook. On the Life and Death can the white eye holds the center of a black field while green vines, skulls, a crescent moon and a halo crowd around it, drawn in a precise monoline style, the subject unruly, birds, snakes, skulls and hops tangled together.

It has been revealed that each beer gets a name made of two things that should not sit together: Life and Death, the classic IPA, Heart and Soul, the session IPA, and Bread and Butter, Love and Hate, Naughty and Nice, Hop Skip and Juice and Crush Hour. The names are easy to say at a bar. Colour does the navigating, every flavour owning one loud field, red for Heart and Soul, brown for Naughty and Nice, teal for Crush Hour, yellow for Bread and Butter. The type tiles make the system plain, six names in heavy condensed capitals on flat colour blocks.

The typography holds the same discipline. VOCATION BREWERY arches around the eye in spaced white capitals, with ESTD and MMXV small at the sides, a lockup legible large on a shipper or small on a pump clip. Beer names run in condensed capitals, and the smaller lines beneath them, style, alcohol, tasting notes, sit in quiet small caps. Nothing competes with the eye. The grid behind the name tiles is strict, three columns, equal blocks, no decoration, which is what lets the illustration stay loud.

The system proves itself in application. Stacked black shippers repeat the eye with a single green tape stripe. Pump clips shrink the whole idea to a circle, eye on top, beer name below, colour doing the rest. Posters take the Crush Hour art to a brick wall, and the bag carries The future is beer in arched capitals over four glass outlines. Then there is Hilltop, the brewery's first permanent lager, its lightest beer to date. Turner Duckworth tells the brewery's story on that can: it sits at the top of a hill, hard to reach, and the climb is the point. The Hilltop can answers with pale blue, winged figures and open sky. Illustration by Brian Steely.

How Studio Yukiko Reimagined Book Design for Everything At Once

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Studio Yukiko turned the Bundeskunsthalle catalogue Everything At Once into a tomb for postmodernism, built from stone and loud colour.
  • According to recent reports, the cover indicates it plainly.
  • The type does the same work as the stone.

Studio Yukiko turned the Bundeskunsthalle catalogue Everything At Once into a tomb for postmodernism, built from stone and loud colour.

According to recent reports, the cover indicates it plainly. A grey stone slab, carved with the words Everything At Once, Post-Modernity, 1967-1992, sits on a flat red field. No photograph, no collage, just the slab. Open the book and the same stone shapes keep coming back, one at the head of every chapter, each one a different shape, each one carrying a different carved phrase. Ruins of Modernism sits on stacked steps. Protect Me From What I Want leans on a pink page. Anything Goes rolls across turquoise on a stone cylinder. The joke lands because the book itself is heavy, a thick catalogue you lift with both hands, and the studio leans into that weight instead of hiding it.

The type does the same work as the stone. Faces from different decades sit side by side on the same spread, serif against grotesque, carved Roman capitals against fat rounded letters. Page numbers run huge down the corners, 17, 49, 107, 149, 181, and captions swell until they are almost as massive as the images they describe. It reads like a reversal of the usual order: the small print gets big, the pictures get small, and the grid underneath holds it all together. Numbered artworks sit in tidy rows, 41, 42, 43, with their captions lined up beside them, while the facing pages let colour do the talking.

Colour is the other system. Every chapter gets its own flat field, red for the opening pages, orange for the ruins, turquoise for the anything-goes middle, pink for the tombstone chapters, green for the index lists. The spreads that open each chapter pack every artwork of that chapter onto one double page, images and captions together, everything at once, exactly as the title promises. Then the campaign photos push the whole idea one step further. Working with photographer Szymon Stepniak, the studio shot a bodybuilder holding the catalogue like a weight, posing with it the way vintage bodybuilding posters pose with dumbbells, a nod to the era when the body itself became a material to shape and stage.

For its 175th anniversary, The Newly introduced York Times and XYZ Type pair a custom 175 blackletter mark with archival collage branding across print.

According to recent reports, typed straight out in Ed Benguiatâs NYT Fraktur, the numerals 175 fell flat beside The Fresh York Times masthead. Custom marks arenât routine there. Led by Creative Director Jessi Brattengeier and the paperâs Culture and Comms Design team, as documented on The Brand Identity, the anniversary brief brought in XYZ Type and motion designer Kiffer Keegan together so static forms and New Yearâs Eve screen movement evolved side by side. Co-founder Jesse Ragan skipped ornate swashes for plain-spoken blackletter curves: the 1 echoes the serifs of the h, the 7 flicks like the leg of the k, and the 5 tapers off like the s. Paired with Cheltenham Light and Franklin, the branding treats 175 years of reporting as live evidence rather than nostalgia.

Recent findings suggest that in the lead visual from Studio Dumbarâs Reporters Follow the Facts campaign, the centered blackletter wordmark sits directly over raw newsroom artifacts. Orange photo-editor loupe squares frame a teal TOP SECRET - SENSITIVE Pentagon Papers binder, blue ballpoint notes from October 2022, a 35mm Fuji film strip, and 9/11 Portraits of Grief columns. Nothing gets airbrushed clean. Editorial stories pull back on the emblem itself. For the 15-part Eyewitness series, Illustrator Matt Dorfman pairs a diagonal May 30, 1910 front-page tear sheet on aviator Glenn Curtiss with a sepia biplane cutout and one vermilion circle. Matt Willeyâs Stop the Presses newsprint broadsheets for Metrograph rotate white display capitals ninety degrees beside a vertical The Fresh York Times 175 blackletter lockup.

Out in physical space, loose partner guidelines let collaborators stretch that branding across rooms and university quads. It doesnât lean on a rigid rulebook. At Spring Studios, architectural designer Ingrid Schmaedecke set staggered charcoal walls and glass vitrines reflecting white Cheltenham Light free-press quotes. Just beyond them, guests stood beneath a floor-to-ceiling 1851 Fresh-York Daily Times front page and a glowing Times globe lamp modeled on the former Annex facade. On campus lawns, the Bearing Witness tour with Other Means turns a custom delivery truck into a rolling broadsheet â typesetting two columns of Cheltenham Light copy across its white cargo wall while a cyan cab wears the circular 175th branding seal beside pallet-mounted prints.

Branding: London Design Festival 2026 by Pentagram

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (444 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pentagram frames London Design Festival 2026 in a single red frame, putting the festival's designers and their work first across the city.
  • Recent findings suggest that the idea is almost nothing, and that is the point.
  • Pentagram has drawn the festival identity since 2007, and Domenic Lippa calls the red the colour of London, the one asset that never changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pentagram frames London Design Festival 2026 in a single red frame, putting the festival's designers and their work first across the city.

Recent findings suggest that the idea is almost nothing, and that is the point. A plain white grotesque spells out London Design Festival in three stacked lines on a flat red field, and a frame cuts straight through the middle of it. Letters split, shift and reassemble as your eye moves across the name. The red does the shouting, the frame does the thinking, and everything inside the frame belongs to someone else's work. The 24th edition ran for nine days in September 2026, across eleven Design Districts.

The type stays neutral on purpose. Pentagram has drawn the festival identity since 2007, and Domenic Lippa calls the red the colour of London, the one asset that never changes. The wordmark keeps the same three-line stack everywhere, with the dates set small beneath it, 12-20 SEPT 2026, and a small white tab in the corner carrying the stacked LDF lockup. A shortened LDF26 monogram handles the tight spots, like a poster framing slatted wooden furniture on a patterned rug.

Sources indicate that the same stack scales from a phone screen to a Tube billboard. On the posters the frame crops the letters at the edges. On the Instagram stories it sits over photographs of the designers' own work. On the stage screen the name runs at two sizes at once, one huge and cropped, one small and whole, with the dates tucked between them.

The print pieces carry the idea in material form. The festival book arrives in a red slipcase with Festival pressed blind into the board, so the wordmark reads as an impression before it reads as ink. The white cover above it carries London in red, with the dates set small in black. A little tab peeks from the slipcase edge. Nothing about it is loud.

Sources indicate that then the frame leaves the page and becomes architecture. In the gallery, a doorway turns into the frame itself, with the wordmark running across the wall beside it and visitors walking through the opening. On the gallery window, the red letters sit over the artwork inside, so the building reads as a poster after dark.

Pentagram builds the identity the same way every year, by looking for a fresh lens on the same job. This year the lens is the frame: a device that sits over any image, or holds its own with no image at all. It keeps the festival recognisable and lets hundreds of other voices do the talking.

Sources indicate that the other successful artists this year are Georgina Starr, who is known for performance works such as Androgynous Egg (2017), Dublin-born artist Racheal Crowther and the learning disabled artist Linda Bell. Judges include Joe Hill, the director of Yorkshire Sculpture Park, Melissa Blanchflower, a senior curator at Turner Contemporary in Margate, and Sheryll Catto, the artistic director of ActionSpace.

Sources indicate that since 1994, Paul Hamlyn Foundation has made 377 awards to artists with over £12m in funding; Phyllida Barlow, Yinka Shonibare and Alberta Whittle are among the previous recipients. Five composers including Daudi Matsiko and Ayanna Witter-Johnson were also recognised.

Base Design recasts the thousand-year-old ChÃ¢teau de Grandson as a living identity, heraldry and bold contemporary type built to let people in.

The castle above Lake NeuchÃ¢tel has spent a thousand years keeping people out. It has been a seat of power, a battlefield, a prison, a hospital, a tobacco factory and a museum, and after fifteen years of restoration it reopened in 2026 with a upcoming permanent exhibition and a new identity from Base Design Geneva. The studio calls the idea Castle, Recast, and the work runs on confrontation: medieval stone and carved wood set against loud, flat, contemporary graphics that refuse to behave like heritage branding. A harlequin diamond pattern carries the clash, flipping between blue and purple, pink and navy, orange and burgundy, so the castle reads as a place with a pulse rather than a monument under glass.

Industry observers note that the wordmark does the heavy lifting. A condensed grotesque sets CHÃTEAU GRANDSON, SCHLOSS GRANDSON and CASTLE GRANDSON in stacked capitals down the length of three flags, one language per flag, each on its own clashing colour pair. The same voice turns up on the phone screen, where FIND YOUR WAY stacks three words across the harlequin field above a pill-shaped START YOUR JOURNEY button, and on the exhibition guides, where FASHION and WARS run huge over armour and portraits.

In a recent development, holding the system together is an interlocked C and G monogram, drawn with the weight of a wax seal and used small: stamped on the flags, tucked into the corner of the phone screen, pressed into a silver signet ring. It is the one quiet element in a loud system, and it works because everything else is shouting.

In a recent development, the identity lives on objects, not just on paper. The pattern jumps from the phone screen onto harlequin socks and a skateboard deck lettered SCHLOSS that rolls through a wood-panelled medieval hall, and the monogram turns up on a tote woven with knights on horseback and on the back of a black shirt worn on the castle staircase. Printed guides carry the same discipline: a shelf of exhibition books pairs oversized titles with armour photography and the small monogram at the foot of each cover.

Sources indicate that nothing here pretends the castle is a ruin to tiptoe around. The colours are saturated, the type is oversized, and the merch reads like streetwear for a fortress. That is the point Base makes in its own words: built to keep people out, Grandson is now in the business of letting them in.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami (ICA Miami) has appointed the global architecture firm Gensler to renovate a 30,000-sq.-ft building the museum acquired in 2024, doubling its exhibition and public-programming space.
  • Steps away from its current venue in Miami’s Design District, the upcoming wing is scheduled to open in late 2027—as the museum marks its tenth anniversary at its current location.
  • The museum’s new building formerly housed the De la Cruz Collection, a private museum that closed after the 2024 death of its co-founder Rosa de la Cruz.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami (ICA Miami) has appointed the global architecture firm Gensler to renovate a 30,000-sq.-ft building the museum acquired in 2024, doubling its exhibition and public-programming space.

Steps away from its current venue in Miami’s Design District, the upcoming wing is scheduled to open in late 2027—as the museum marks its tenth anniversary at its current location. Focused on expanding the free museum’s community outreach, the project will transform the ICA into a multi-site complex and house the first permanent display of its collection.

The museum’s new building formerly housed the De la Cruz Collection, a private museum that closed after the 2024 death of its co-founder Rosa de la Cruz. Since its $25m acquisition later that year, the site has mainly hosted the ICA’s educational programmes. It will close once construction begins. The renovation is part of a $40m capital campaign, supported entirely by private funds.

The newly introduced design will adapt the existing structure. “The building was developed to house a contemporary art collection,” Alex Gartenfeld, the ICA’s director and chief curator, tells The Art Newspaper. “But with the spaces we are constructing, we intend to enhance the museum’s story-driven narrative approach to the collection and exhibitions.”.

Rendering of ICA Miami’s upcoming building Courtesy Gensler.

According to recent reports, eight new galleries will occupy the building’s first and second floors. Among them will be the museum’s first dedicated spaces for its growing permanent collection of more than 2,000 works.

“The programme between the two buildings is blended, but we will now have two full floors dedicated to our permanent collection,” Gartenfeld says. “Around every six months, we will refresh the collection display to reflect the collection’s emphasis and recent acquisitions.”.

The entire third floor will be dedicated to public programming, including talks, symposia, lectures and performances. “Beyond adding galleries, this renovation will strengthen the ICA’s ability to support artists, expand learning and create a platform for exchange and belonging in one of the world’s most dynamic cultural cities,” indicates Bevin Savage Yamazaki, Gensler’s global culture and museums leader.

A reimagined façade with transparent components is key to the design. Gartenfeld claims the façade aims to provide a connection between street-level traffic and the museum itself.

According to recent reports, the renovations focus on visitor experience and accessibility as well. The lobby will be redesigned. And reconfigured outdoor areas will include social spaces, a sculpture deck and an expanded café. “We are aiming to create a more collective experience,” Gartenfeld states.

#366. French authorities investigate claim of fraud over Picasso plates and medallions on sale

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper

French authorities investigate claim of fraud over Picasso plates and medallions on sale

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A criminal investigation amid a family crisis casts a dark shadow over the illustrious history of the French studio Ateliers Hugo, which produced jewellery and silverware created by major artists of the 20th century.
  • On 10 March, Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, representing the nine heirs of the Spanish artist, filed a complaint alleging “fraud, counterfeiting, forgery and concealment of these felonies”.
  • Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, the daughter of Pablo, has filed a legal complaint on behalf of nine family members of the artist about the allegedly unauthorised works © Studio Cabrelli.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A criminal investigation amid a family crisis casts a dark shadow over the illustrious history of the French studio Ateliers Hugo, which produced jewellery and silverware created by major artists of the 20th century. According to a legal source, the court of Aix-en-Provence in the south of France has opened an investigation following a complaint by the Picasso family.

On 10 March, Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, representing the nine heirs of the Spanish artist, filed a complaint alleging “fraud, counterfeiting, forgery and concealment of these felonies”. The file does not name the alleged perpetrators, and their identity is not presently known. The following month the Picasso family published a formal warning in the Gazette Drouot, titled “Hugo silverware”. It urged “all art market professionals and buyers to exercise the utmost vigilance”, following the appearance of what it described as “a large number” of illegitimate silver plates and gold medallions, valued at millions of euros.

Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, the daughter of Pablo, has filed a legal complaint on behalf of nine family members of the artist about the allegedly unauthorised works © Studio Cabrelli.

The title refers to Ateliers Hugo, a goldsmith based in Aix-en-Provence. It was founded in 1933 by François Hugo (1899-1981), the great-grandson of the famous French author Victor Hugo. In 1955 Pablo Picasso, who since 1947 had created a variety of ceramics in Vallauris on the French Riviera, commissioned François Hugo to produce plates and dishes from similar designs in fine metals, using the traditional technique of repoussé. Later, the workshop reduced them into medallions and earrings. With the help of his brother, the painter Jean Hugo, who introduced him to artistic circles, François made jewellery designed by Salvador Dalí, Max Ernst, André Derain, Jean Arp, Jean Dubuffet, Roberto Matta, Jean Lurçat and Dorothea Tanning. In 1975, his son Pierre Hugo (1947-2023) took over the manufacturer. Pierre was followed by his son Nicolas (born 1989).

Members of the Picasso family and their lawyer, Jean-Jacques Neuer, who filed the complaint, declined to comment to The Art Newspaper. But their complaint alleges that “it has been discovered that the moulds of Picasso’s works were reused for unauthorised productions of silver and gold pieces, followed by duplicates, some of them bearing three times the same number, and unnumbered specimens”.

Sources indicate that according to a source close to the investigation, the Picasso Administration, which represents the family, says it has discovered at least 17 complete or almost complete suspicious collections, amounting to hundreds of pieces. The first red flag was raised by the Museum of Old and Fresh Art (Mona), a private Australian museum in Tasmania. According to this source, in May 2023 the museum informed the Picasso Administration of its doubts over plates it had bought at Sotheby’s in London. An auction catalogue of 13 October 2021 describes a “complete set of 24 silver plates” bearing the signature of the artist, completed with an additional “unnumbered proof of Visage aux mains”. The pieces were “accompanied by a certificate of authenticity issued by Pierre Hugo”. The lot was sold for £1.4m. Sotheby’s declined to comment for this story.

It has been revealed that according to the legal files, the seller was the British dealer Mark Maurice, from a now dissolved gallery named Masterpiece. The source close to the investigation says the dealer allegedly produced documents showing that he had commissioned a set of plates and a set of medallions from the Ateliers Hugo between 2017 and 2020. Mark Maurice indicated he was “unable to respond” to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries “due to strict non-disclosure agreements in place”.

In summer 2023 the ceramics museum in Vallauris, Musée Magnelli, exhibited another collection of 24 silver plates as well as gold medallions attributed to Picasso.

In 2023, the Musée Magnelli in Vallauris exhibited plates and medallions attributed to Picasso Travelworld.

According to the legal files, the Picasso Administration protested, having found that they bore no number, mark or punch, as legally required. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges these facts, but tells The Art Newspaper that the works exhibited at Musée Magnelli were so-called “author’s copies, made for the exhibition, duly indicating in the catalogue that they were not for sale”. He adds that he “recovered them and had them melted after the show”. Representatives for the museum did not respond to a request for comment.

Sources indicate that in June 2023, as reported in the legal files, the French branch of the auction house Bonhams made a request to the Picasso Administration for the right to reproduce silverware for a catalogue. The auction house was planning a sale of 95 lots from the Ateliers Hugo collection, including works by Ernst, Derain and Cocteau, valued between €400 and €50,000 each. The most valuable were 59 pieces, “made by” or “after” Picasso.

Sources indicate that on 26 September 2023 Bonhams was informed by the Picasso Administration that these pieces were considered to be “unauthorised” editions. The auction house then decided to “delay the whole sale”, just two days before it was due to take place. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges he “did initiate, in the wake of good results obtained at Bonhams UK, this sale of pieces”, produced, he says, by his “father and grandfather”. But, he adds, “When we were informed by dealers of the presence of possible duplicates, I agreed to withdraw the sale and collaborated with the Picasso Administration to identify them.”.

It has been revealed that bonhams declined to comment, but according to the source close to the investigation, the lots attributed to Picasso were sequestered when a British financial organization, Suros Capital, tried to recover them as collateral for a €256,000 loan. A spokesperson for Suros confirmed the operation to The Art Newspaper, adding that “it was secured against not only the Picasso pieces, but a range of assets which are progressively realised, so the company expects to recover the loan in full”.

Industry observers note that in November 2023, according to the source close to the investigation, a representative for Bonhams France informed the Picasso Administration that a Spanish collector contacted the auction house to sell 24 silver plates, estimated at £900,000. Again, the auction house refused on the basis of Picasso Administration’s doubts about the objects’ authenticity. In the legal files, the Picasso Administration claims the same collector had sold another set of 24 silver plates and one of 24 gold medallions in private sales through Bonhams in London in 2022. Neither the British auction house nor the Spanish collector made any comment.

In a recent development, nicolas Hugo, who says he has not been interviewed by the investigators, claims he has no knowledge of the proceedings and “is unaware of the content of the complaint” issued by the Picasso Administration. But, he says: “The criminal investigation can only deal with facts related to the time of my father and grandfather, therefore falling under the statute of limitations and concerning persons now deceased.” He adds that “the rights to reproduce the items disappeared with them, so I have never minted any of Picasso’s creations”, and he does not have the legal status of a goldsmith. However, he says: “I have signed some certificates of authenticity, but only to confirm my father’s own signature.”.

In interviews with The Art Newspaper, Nicolas Hugo describes himself as a “self-taught art dealer”. When he was around 20 years old, he started to work as an assistant in galleries in Paris, before moving to London. He is now an agent for several artists and a curator. In 2022, the French magazine Les Hardis described him as a “mix of British and Saint-Germain-des-Prés charm”. “My father became very ill in 2018,” he told the magazine. “I had an epiphany. I decided to take over the workshop. I immersed myself completely,” and started to train in manufacturing jewels.

In a recent development, “From 2019,” he tells The Art Newspaper, “I became involved in the history of his workshop and helped my father to showcase this heritage, for memorial and commercial reasons. I set up exhibitions in places like Barcelona or Vallauris and initiated this sale of the fonds d’atelier at Bonhams Paris. I have not taken over my father’s firm and was not his partner.”.

Nicolas Hugo notes: “There have been some duplicates on the market, dating from my father’s period, but I have no idea who had made them in the workshop.” He says he has “no idea who put a collection on sale at Sotheby’s in 2021” and knows “nothing of the three sets proposed by this Spanish collector to Bonhams in 2022 and 2023”.

Recent findings suggest that the criminal investigation is still at the preliminary phase. It comes at a time when the organization is already in limbo. Pierre Hugo died in October 2023 and his five children have turned down his inheritance. Nicolas Hugo’s brothers and sisters declined to comment to The Art Newspaper due to the ongoing investigation.

However, sources close to the case say that Pierre Hugo’s heirs’ inheritance came with a €2.5m tax debt. According to these sources, three of the Hugo siblings noted in police interviews they were “not at all” aware of the conduct of the workshop by their brother Nicolas, who had succeeded their ailing father in 2019. The sources said the three Hugo siblings were on alert after learning that Bonhams Paris declined to sell the collection from the Ateliers Hugo in September 2023. According to the same sources, when Pierre Hugo died a month later, the three siblings went to the workshop and took 21 moulds of plates that they decided to hand over to the Picasso Administration. Three moulds from the set were missing and they did not find those for the medallions.

According to these sources, the three Hugo siblings explained to the investigators that, “knowing that the rights of reproduction were extinct, they wanted to be sure this would be respected”. The siblings also asserted that they “did not want in any way to be implicated in these operations and made it clear to the Picasso Administration”, according to the sources.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a longtime fragrance lover, Brooklyn designer Louis Filosaâs Scentury immediately resonated: a collectible table lamp recording its owners in scent.
  • Speaking as someone whose workspace is perpetually crowded with niche perfume decants and test strips, scent has always felt like the closest thing we have to time travel.
  • Conceived for Pro Retro â presented by IDSA NYC and Fluora, and curated by Not For Granted Studio â the brief asked for a freestanding lamp lit by Fluoraâs Monos light that records the people who own it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a longtime fragrance lover, Brooklyn designer Louis Filosaâs Scentury immediately resonated: a collectible table lamp recording its owners in scent.

Speaking as someone whose workspace is perpetually crowded with niche perfume decants and test strips, scent has always felt like the closest thing we have to time travel. A photograph reminds you of what a room looked like, but a single inhale of a specific accord instantly resurrects who was in it. Most family heirlooms record history through physical wear: a softened edge, faded finish, or tarnished hardware. With Scentury, Louis Filosa takes a sensory turn, preserving custodianship through fragrance.

Conceived for Pro Retro â presented by IDSA NYC and Fluora, and curated by Not For Granted Studio â the brief asked for a freestanding lamp lit by Fluoraâs Monos light that records the people who own it. Functional objects often get discarded when styles shift. Pro Retro proposed meaning as the antidote, citing heirlooms like championship cups or family quilts. Each lamp had to begin a story rather than arrive with one, leaving a visible marker across generations.

Industry observers note that the concept emerged during Filosaâs sabbatical. In every country he explored, he bought a fragrance from a local perfume house. In shop after shop, sampling meant lifting a glass cloche. Those bottles now anchor his travel memories far better than photos do. Scentury adapts that retail ritual into a domestic heirloom.

Twelve glass test tubes ring the Monos under a glass cloche, one for each owner, holding an acid-free cotton paper blotter. When the lamp changes hands, the new owner lifts the dome, draws the next tube, sprays their signature perfume, and writes their name and year. Resealed with a silicone stopper, the tube preserves that presence. Scent is our most memory-linked sense; opening a vial brings that person back into the room. Scents soften over decades, but names stay.

The tubes are glass partly for optical physics: they bend the light slightly, causing handwritten names to glow. Behind them, a diffuser and housing 3D printed in light-diffusing filament soften the Monos light, anchored by a cast ceramic base. From across a room, Scentury reads as an ambient table lamp; closer in, the ring of vials invites curiosity.

The piece debuted at Collectible NYC 2026, hosted inside a former movie theater at 210 East 86th Street on Manhattanâs Upper East Side.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the former husband of the late New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, Daniel Sikkema, aged 56, has been sentenced to life imprisonment for organising Sikkema’s murder in 2024. A federal court in Manhattan handed down the sentence on Wednesday (4 November).

In May 2026, after a two-week trial, Daniel Sikkema was convicted on charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country. In addition to life imprisonment, he was sentenced to five years of supervised release.

Recent findings suggest that brent Sikkema, who was aged 75 at the time of his murder, was found stabbed to death at his home in the Jardim Botânico neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on 15 January 2024. According to prosecutors, Daniel Sikkema began planning the murder in 2023 in the midst of his divorce from the dealer, with whom he had been married for around 15 years and shared a son.

As the couple’s divorce proceedings became more acrimonious, Daniel Sikkema, who holds dual US and Cuban citizenship, recruited the Cuban national, Alejandro Triana Prevez, as the hitman. On the night of the murder, Prevez entered the late Sikkema’s residence and stabbed him 18 times. Prevez subsequently received $5,000 from Daniel Sikkema and was promised further payments.

It has been revealed that prosecutors noted Daniel Sikkema made 11 payments to Prevez and Prevez’s partner in Cuba, using the identities of unwitting friends, employees and family members to conceal the transactions. Prevez was arrested by Brazilian authorities four days after the murder at a gas station on the side of the highway in the state of Minas Gerais, around 600 miles from Rio de Janeiro. He had stolen cash and jewellery in his possession. His case is being handled separately by a Brazilian court.

Brent Sikkema was born in 1948 in Morrison, Illinois, and studied at the San Francisco Art Institute before beginning his career. In the early 1990s, he founded Wooster Gardens in SoHo, moving the gallery to Chelsea in 1999. The business became Sikkema Jenkins & Co in 2003 following the involvement of Michael Jenkins and Meg Malloy.

The gallery is now known as Sikkema Malloy Jenkins and continues to operate in Chelsea. It has championed the work of artists including Kara Walker, Vik Muniz, Sheila Hicks, Jeffrey Gibson and Arturo Herrera. A representative for Sikkema Malloy Jenkins told The Art Newspaper that the gallery will not be providing any statement regarding the conviction or sentencing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after Paul Gauguin arrived in Arles in October 1888 to stay with his friend Van Gogh, the two artists would go out to paint together and then socialise and discuss art in the evenings over a glass of wine.
  • In mid-December, in an attempt to clear the air, Gauguin suggested that they should make a trip to Montpellier, 70 km west of Arles.
  • It has been revealed that the artistic result of this trip forms a central part of a major exhibition on Gauguin which opened this week at Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after Paul Gauguin arrived in Arles in October 1888 to stay with his friend Van Gogh, the two artists would go out to paint together and then socialise and discuss art in the evenings over a glass of wine. Their very different personalities, however, soon led to tensions. Living together in the confines of the Yellow House and sharing a small room as a studio, they began to row. As winter approached, and the weather made it impossible to work outside, the situation only worsened.

In mid-December, in an attempt to clear the air, Gauguin suggested that they should make a trip to Montpellier, 70 km west of Arles. Their goal was to visit the Musée Fabre, renowned for its fine collection of paintings.

It has been revealed that the artistic result of this trip forms a central part of a major exhibition on Gauguin which opened this week at Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts. Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin: The Circles of Post-Impressionists and Symbolists (until 28 February 2027) provides a wide-ranging exploration of the art of Gauguin and his associates. The show’s title comes from a key painting by the artist inspired by the Montpellier visit, Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin (late 1889).

Paul Gauguin’s Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin (late 1889).

Hammer Museum, Los Angeles (photograph The Art Newspaper).

Industry observers note that van Gogh and Gauguin travelled from Arles to Montpellier by train, which took around four hours. Although it has long been assumed that they made a day trip on either 16 or 17 December 1888, it is arguably more likely that they spent the night there and stayed for both days. The Musée Fabre had over 800 paintings on display, so they would surely have wanted time to savour the works. Many of the finest pictures were French, given by Alfred Bruyas, a local collector and patron of Gustave Courbet.

Gustave Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet (1854).

In a recent development, for Gauguin, the highlight of the museum was Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet (1854). This landscape composition includes the figure of Courbet himself, laden with his equipment and holding a walking pole. He is greeting Bruyas, who is accompanied by a bowing servant.

Gustave Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet and Gauguin’s Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin in the Budapest exhibition.

It has been revealed that gauguin, who was impressed with the Courbet, painted a work in response, a year later, in the Brittany fishing village of Le Pouldu. The main figure in this work is Gauguin himself, facing a Breton woman on the other side of a gate.

Superficially, the Gauguin painting bears little resemblance to the Courbet. Stylistically, Courbet’s smoothly painted picture contrasts with Gauguin’s rough brushwork. The compositions appear to have little in common, other than showing an artist encountering other people—and being greeted with a “good day” (and, incidentally, both scenes also include a dog).

In a recent development, the moods seem very different. Courbet appears thrilled to greet his patron and friend. Gauguin’s encounter with the Breton woman, however, is fleeting, as they happen to pass each other at a gate. The Budapest exhibition’s lead curator, Judit Geskó, sees the Gauguin picture as representing “the artist as a solitary wanderer”.

Industry observers note that but despite the differences, Gauguin’s decision to entitle his work as he did highlights that he was directly acknowledging the source of his inspiration, the Courbet. Gauguin’s title is actually inscribed on the painting, in the lower-left corner.

Gauguin made two versions of his composition: the one on loan to Budapest from the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles and the other (which was unavailable for borrowing) at the National Gallery in Prague. The Hammer picture, which was the original, was created to display on the dining room door in the small inn where he was staying in Le Pouldu.

As for Van Gogh, the Dutchman was particularly struck in the Musée Fabre by the portraits by Courbet. These included a self-portrait, The Man with the Pipe (around 1849), which may well have inspired Van Gogh one month later to paint his Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe (January 1889).

In a recent development, bruyas was depicted by a range of artists and these portraits were also much admired by Van Gogh in the Montpellier museum. Vincent described Bruyas’ appearance to his brother Theo as “a gentleman with a beard, red hair, who looks damnably like you or me”.

Postcard of Musée Fabre, Montpellier (1905).

According to recent reports, both Gauguin and Van Gogh were great admirers of Courbet, who was very well represented in the Musée Fabre. Although they agreed about Courbet, their tastes for other artists were often rather different. Vincent wrote to Theo that their artistic discussions in Montpellier had been “excessively electric”. He explained: “We sometimes emerge from it with tired minds, like an electric battery after it’s run down.”.

Sources indicate that despite these animated discussions, the inspirational visit seemed a success. Vincent reported back to Theo the day after their return that in the museum they had been “right in the midst of magic”. He added: “Gauguin said to me this morning, when I asked him how he felt: ‘that he could feel his old self coming back’, which gave me great pleasure.”.

Sadly, the reconciliation did not last long: just four days later Van Gogh severely mutilated his ear. Although the trigger was probably news he had just received that Theo had become engaged (which Vincent feared would threaten his brother’s support), tensions with Gauguin were also a contributing factor.

Sources indicate that budapest’s Gauguin exhibition is ambitious, with 80 works by the French master and 70 by other artists. Although financial valuations for exhibitions are rarely revealed, The Art Newspaper can report that its total insurance value is €1.5bn.

Van Gogh’s Field with Irises near Arles (May 1888).

Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation).

The show includes three works by Van Gogh: the landscape painting Field with Irises near Arles (May 1888, Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam) and two rarely-displayed drawings from the collection of the Budapest museum, The Parsonage Garden at Nuenen in Winter (March 1884) and Haystacks (July 1888).

Van Gogh’s The Parsonage Garden at Nuenen in Winter (March 1884) and Haystacks (July 1888).

Sources indicate that the Budapest exhibition has two Gauguin paintings dating from his stay with Van Gogh in Arles: the landscape Les Alyscamps (October 1888, Musée d’Orsay, Paris) and the portrait Madame Roulin (November-December 1888, Saint Louis Art Museum). Both of these subjects were also tackled by Van Gogh.

Gauguin’s Les Alyscamps (October 1888) and Madame Roulin (November-December 1888).

Musée d’Orsay, Paris and Saint Louis Art Museum.

Among the other Gauguin highlights in the show is Sunflowers on an Armchair (1901, Bührle Collection, on loan to the Kunsthaus Zurich). This is one of four still-life paintings inspired by Van Gogh’s favourite motif—sunflowers. Gauguin painted these in the Marquesas Islands (north of Tahiti), with flowers grown from seeds he was sent by a friend from Paris.

Gauguin’s Sunflowers on an Armchair (1901).

Bührle Collection, on loan to the Kunsthaus Zurich.

It has been revealed that the museum estimates that the Gauguin exhibition could see up to 350,000 visitors, a huge number for a medium-sized European capital. However, even this won’t match Geskó's Van Gogh show in 2006, which attracted 486,000 people to the museum to see the Dutch painter's works.

Sources indicate that martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin Bailey’s recent Van Gogh books.

According to recent reports, martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

Recent findings suggest that his other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com.

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

Latest Update: Upcoming museum dedicated to Italian Modernist Mario Sironi must not become ‘endorsement of fascism’, art historians warn

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prepares by Giorgia Meloni’s government to open a new museum in Rome dedicated to Mario Sironi, the Modernist painter who was a supporter of Benito Mussolini, risk sanitising Italy's fascist past, two leading historians have warned.
  • Recent findings suggest that the state-run museum is expected to open next year within the Associazione Nazionale fra Mutilati ed Invalidi di Guerra (National Association of War Disabled and Wounded Veterans), a monumental fascist era building inaugurated in 1928.
  • The museum will display 30 works recently acquired by Italy's culture ministry from the Mario Sironi Archive in Rome, including paintings, drawings and preparatory sketches.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prepares by Giorgia Meloni’s government to open a new museum in Rome dedicated to Mario Sironi, the Modernist painter who was a supporter of Benito Mussolini, risk sanitising Italy's fascist past, two leading historians have warned.

Recent findings suggest that the state-run museum is expected to open next year within the Associazione Nazionale fra Mutilati ed Invalidi di Guerra (National Association of War Disabled and Wounded Veterans), a monumental fascist era building inaugurated in 1928. The building is home to two major frescoes by Sironi painted ten years later. One depicts Mussolini on horseback.

The museum will display 30 works recently acquired by Italy's culture ministry from the Mario Sironi Archive in Rome, including paintings, drawings and preparatory sketches. A further 90 works will be loaned by the archive.

Unveiling the prepares on Tuesday, Alessandro Giuli, the culture minister, said the project was “the defining achievement of my term in office, and the one of which I am most proud”.

Meloni's Brothers of Italy has political roots in the postwar Italian neo-fascist movement. Press materials for the museum do not mention fascism or Mussolini.

Recent findings suggest that sironi joined the fascist movement in 1919, contributing more than 1,700 political cartoons and illustrations to Il Popolo d’Italia, Mussolini’s newspaper. The museum will feature works spanning more than four decades from the 1910s to the 1950s, covering distinct phases from Sironi's artistic development including Futurism, metaphysical-influenced works and monumental commissions awarded under the fascist regime.

Mario Sironi, Cavallo e Cavaliere (1953).

Courtesy of the Italian ministry of culture.

Members of Italy’s cultural sector have emphasised the need for the institution to address Seroni’s politics.

Tomaso Montanari, an art historian and rector of the Università per Stranieri di Siena (University for Foreigners of Siena), stated that he did not oppose the museum but insisted it must explicitly distance itself from fascism.

“Since Italy is a republic founded on anti-fascism, the museum's educational material must make clear that there is no endorsement of fascism," Montanari told The Art Newspaper.

Montanari, who sits on the culture ministry's scientific committee, stated that the initial project for the museum focussed “overwhelmingly” on Sironi's fascist period work. He added that the ministry "partially" heeded his argument for works from other periods to be included.

Mario Sironi, Autoritratto (Self-portrait).

Courtesy of the Italian ministry of culture.

The art historian and curator Fabio Benzi, who is on the Sironi museum's scientific committee, told the French-language publication Le Journal Des Arts: "The danger is of legitimising a certain authoritarian aesthetic under the guise of cultural rediscovery".

The culture ministry has been contacted for comment.

Last year, the ministry confirmed it had acquired the former Rome home of Giacomo Balla, the futurist painter who initially supported fascism, which operates as a museum.

On Thursday [5 November], key members of Meloni's government presented a latest exhibition celebrating the 90th anniversary of the EUR district in Rome, the city's grandest example of fascist-era planning.

Breaking: Fresh Miami art space to champion photography, film and video

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A beloved Miami art space returns this month, opening on 30 November in Little River as Mitrani Art, a photography, film and video venue with exhibition galleries, a screening room and artists’ studios.
  • Recent findings suggest that “We want to continue that same model that we had in Wynwood, creating a community with art studios and event spaces,” Dina tells The Art Newspaper.
  • In a recent development, the inaugural exhibition is a group show of lens-based art titled ReExposures: The Magic Within.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A beloved Miami art space returns this month, opening on 30 November in Little River as Mitrani Art, a photography, film and video venue with exhibition galleries, a screening room and artists’ studios. It is a long-awaited fresh chapter for the Mitrani Warehouse, which sisters Dina and Rhonda Mitrani began out of their family’s longtime Wynwood clothing factory in 2002, watching the neighbourhood around them transform into a thriving arts district.

Recent findings suggest that “We want to continue that same model that we had in Wynwood, creating a community with art studios and event spaces,” Dina tells The Art Newspaper. “We still want to welcome emerging and established artists to use it as a place to experiment and create new work.”.

In a recent development, the inaugural exhibition is a group show of lens-based art titled ReExposures: The Magic Within. One expected highlight is Suddenly We Jumped by the Miami-based artist Antonia Wright. The video captures a live performance from 2013 in which the artist actually shattered a glass ceiling, dramatically jumping onto a pane of glass and falling to the floor below.

Sources indicate that “Antonia makes really creative work and focuses on vital social concerns that need change,” Rhonda states. “This one is very impactful.”.

Both Mitrani sisters left their native Miami for university, and found their way to Fresh York after graduating.

The co-founders of Mitrani Art, Rhonda Mitrani (left) and Dina Mitrani (right) Courtesy Mitrani Art.

Dina worked at Christie’s and then at two different galleries, including one specialising in Latin American photography. After having children, she decided to move home and open a photography gallery in her home city. Rhonda, who had a thriving film production career, was more reluctant to return.

Industry observers note that “I had no intention of leaving New York,” she admits. “I ended up making a documentary film about my father going back to Cuba, and that brought me back to Miami to finish editing it. During one of those visits, Dina said, ‘Why don’t you stay here? There’s something going on in the art community.’”.

Recent findings suggest that at Mitrani Warehouse, the sisters started small, with art studios on the second floor, and gradually took over the building. Dina, who has a photography background, started a contemporary photography gallery, Dina Mitrani Gallery, and Rhonda opened the Screening Room, the first dedicated space in Miami for film-makers and video artists to show their work.

Tatiana Parcero, Actos de Fe #27, 2003 Courtesy the artist and Mitrani Art.

Recent findings suggest that but as the years passed, the sisters watched as artists and galleries slowly got priced out of the neighborhood. “We realised the Wynwood Art District was shifting. We held on for as long as we could, because we had an emotional attachment to that space where our parents had their business, our grandmother worked there, so many cousins, uncles,” Dina says. “But we realised it was time to go.”.

It has been revealed that when the Mitrani Warehouse closed in 2017, the sisters immediately began looking for a newly introduced location. In 2019, they purchased a mechanic shop in Little River with high ceilings and space to expand by building a separate studio facility. To design the new facility, they hired R&R Studios, a local multidisciplinary architecture firm run by Argentine artists Roberto Behar and Rosario Marquardt, who were longtime residents of the Mitrani Warehouse studios. Landscape design for the project was handled by the Miami-based firm Studio Arth. The project took considerably longer than expected due to the pandemic, permitting and other roadblocks.

Marina Font, Untitled (celebration), 2014 Courtesy the artist and Mitrani Art.

Industry observers note that “It’s been seven years in the making, so we’re very excited to open. There’s a lot of anticipation,” Rhonda states.

It has been revealed that the opening of Mitrani Art means a fresh permanent home for the Screening Room and Dina Mitrani Gallery, which have relied on pop-up programming across the city since the closing of the warehouse. The sisters have also started a new non-profit, Mitrani Art Projects Inc, that will run educational programmes in the space.

And artists are already moving into the newly introduced building, which has four studio spaces, each substantial enough for two artists. Rent is at the lower end of the market rate for the neighbourhood, the sisters say, and they hope to keep it that way by securing grant funding in the future.

Latest Update: Canadian art market takes hit from trade war with US

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The fallout from the trade war between the Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and US president Donald Trump is having real-time consequences for many Canadian artists and galleries.
  • It has been revealed that mackenzie Sinclair, the executive director of the Art Dealers Association of Canada (ADAC) tells The Art Newspaper that the tariffs are “a significant concern for our members, given the close economic relationship between our two countries”.
  • “The art market as a whole is a fragile ecosystem, and changes to the conditions under which art is traded can have unforeseen and far-reaching consequences across the sector,” Sinclair notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The fallout from the trade war between the Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and US president Donald Trump is having real-time consequences for many Canadian artists and galleries. Since 22 August the US has imposed tariffs of 50% on a wide range of items imported from Canada, including paintings, drawings, sculptures, prints, pastels, collages and more. Other tariff categories that include feathers, bones, tortoise shell, horns, antlers and other animal parts, will especially impact Indigenous artists. In early September Canada imposed counter-tariffs on hundreds of imports from the US, among them 50% on many materials used to make and transport art, plus certain printed materials including photographs; these did not include paintings, drawings or pastels imported from the US, which were already subject to 25% tariffs as of March 2025.

It has been revealed that mackenzie Sinclair, the executive director of the Art Dealers Association of Canada (ADAC) tells The Art Newspaper that the tariffs are “a significant concern for our members, given the close economic relationship between our two countries”. She adds that around two thirds of Canada’s cultural exports are destined for the US—in 2023, Canada exported C$27.1bn ($19bn) in cultural products, of which C$18.1bn ($12.7bn) went to the US.

“The art market as a whole is a fragile ecosystem, and changes to the conditions under which art is traded can have unforeseen and far-reaching consequences across the sector,” Sinclair notes.

Sarah Macaulay, the founding director of Macaulay & Co Fine Art, a gallery with spaces in Vancouver and Toronto that represents artists like the First Nations painter Lawrence Paul Yuxweluptun. She tells The Art Newspaper that, until recently, around 10% of Yuxweluptun’s sales were to US buyers. “Now we’re more focused on Australia and Europe,” she notes.

Macaulay notes she has cancelled intends to participate in a fair during Miami Art Week this December. In the wake of the latest tariffs, she says, “it’s just too risky”.

Andy Sylvester, the owner and director of Vancouver’s Equinox Gallery, estimates that buyers in the US represented around 15% of his sales of his work until recently, but that will “likely be reduced to zero”. He adds: “US tariffs on Canadian made art will affect the gallery and our artists both financially and opportunistically.”.

It has been revealed that “Canadian art is not simply another category of merchandise,” Sinclair indicates. “It represents the work, livelihoods, cultural expression and international standing of Canadian artists and galleries. For a US collector faced with a substantially higher purchase price, the additional cost may lead them to postpone a purchase or acquire an artwork from a US-based artist or gallery instead. This creates a direct loss of competitiveness for Canadian artists and galleries.”.

At Art Toronto, the country’s largest art fair, which is held every year in late October, US buyers represent a significant portion of annual sales.

“The ‘Buy Canadian’ rhetoric has been very prevalent, and it is heartening to see how communities across the country have been supporting artists now that these tariffs have been imposed,” notes Emily-Jean Alexander, the fair’s director. “For this autumn’s Art Toronto we [built] newly introduced programmes to help those who want to support our national art market, but who are new to buying artwork to see the friendliness and accessibility that can be found at the fair and build confidence in supporting Canadian galleries and institutions.”.

Porto Rocha rebuilt Fursys, the Korean workplace maker founded in 1983, around one idea: a Fursys brand identity that makes room for reinvention.

Fursys spent four decades shaping the modern workplace, and the upcoming identity treats that history as a working method rather than a museum piece. The system runs on a single geometric idea: the corner. White type on a black field, a revitalized signature red, and flat colour blocks in deep blue and green carry the work, and every element shares the same modular logic, from the wordmark down to a felt binder with a square corner cut out of its side. The posters say it plainly, Built for change. Here to stay.

The wordmark is drawn from a shared grid, and the same grid gives the system its symbol. Porto Rocha redrew the Fursys mark as The Corner, a small geometric unit that turns up everywhere: stamped on stationery, cut into a binder, repeated as a wayfinding motif. The typeface follows the same logic. Fursys Sans is a custom geometric sans with matching character sets for Latin languages and Korean, so the brand speaks in Seoul and the United States with one voice.

According to recent reports, that voice has a name, The Proven Visionary, and a line to match: Design for the unseen. It reveals up in the copy the system is built to carry, short, certain sentences like Dynamic desks. Here's a thought. and the FX-1 line, The answer to complexity is simple. We call it FX-1. Headlines sit large and flat, with plenty of room around them, and the grid keeps every lockup honest, each element holding its own corner of the frame.

In a recent development, the system proves itself on physical things. A close-up of a desk corner indicates pale bent wood meeting at a precise joint, and a fabric swatch card lays out six colour samples on tan leather like a specimen sheet. The black stationery suite carries the wordmark blind, pressed into the paper rather than printed, and the FX-1 binder opens to a red mark and a black specification page that treats product data as part of the design.

At building scale the same discipline holds. Dimensional letters spell Fursys across a white slatted facade and a grey factory wall, and a red delivery truck carries the white wordmark down the highway with the line Design for the unseen on its flank. Interactive catalogues and tactile showrooms carry the system into digital and physical touchpoints alike. Four decades of problem-solving, made visible in a corner.

Sources indicate that A upcoming contemporary art hub nestled among the ruins of a medieval monastery is due to open in northern Italy next September. The Fondazione Vezza project, founded by the Piedmontese entrepreneur Sandra Vezza and her son Charley, will be based in Monforte d’Alba in the Langhe wine region, around 60 kilometres southeast of Turin.

The pair plan to develop a trail over the next decade through the woodland on Colle San Pietro hill; two site-specific large-scale works by the US artist Kathleen Ryan and the Italian sculptor Alessandro Pessoli will inaugurate the project next autumn. The trail will include the ruins of the monastery of San Pietro, an early medieval complex first documented in 1014.

Flavio Del Monte, formerly director of institutional relations at Massimo de Carlo gallery in Milan, will oversee the Fondazione Vezza project. “Each year, one or more artists will be invited to engage with the site, its woodland, its paths, existing architecture and history. Over approximately ten years, the works will shape a route that will continue to grow and change without losing the site’s original character,” says a project statement.

Sandra Vezza and her son Charley Vezza.

Sandra and Charley Vezza will fund the production of the works; budget costs remain confidential. Asked if the foundation will own the pieces produced, a spokesperson noted: “Yes, they will be installed permanently onsite. The target audience is really everyone, the widest possible audience.” The site will be open to the public and free to enter.

“With its opening in 2027, the Foundation will begin a long-term exploration of the relationship between contemporary art, the landscape, and the Vezza family’s vision, shaped by the artists invited to contribute to the site over time,” adds the statement.

Industry observers note that sandra and Charley Vezza founded the Italian Radical Design Group in 2022, a Barolo-based firm established with “the specific aim of preserving and promoting historic Italian design brands”, indicates the company website. The same year the group acquired Memphis Milano, the 1980s post-modern design collective. In 2012, the Vezzas bought Gufram, an Italian radical design brand founded in the 1960s, known for its pop art-inspired furniture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moments after the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC)—a review panel stacked with Trump administration appointees—approved prepares for a Triumphal Arch at Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, on Thursday night (5 November), a federal judge blocked construction on the project for 14 days.

The move obstructs the government’s stated aim of starting work on one of US president Donald Trump’s pet building projects immediately, despite lawsuits and public protests, and allows a court case brought by a Vietnam War veteran and the attorneys general of Washington, DC, and Virginia to continue.

Recent findings suggest that in her 33-page decision, Judge Tanya S. Chutkan outlined the government’s shifting justifications for building the arch, which have included a desire to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, a more than century-old congressional act to commemorate the end of the Civil War, and even supposed national security concerns. “These arguments are unavailing,” she wrote.

She also found that “harm is certain” to be inflicted on both Washington, DC, and Virginia if construction on the arch is allowed to go ahead, as it would interrupt traffic at a vital artery into the capital for years and result in unknown damage and expense.

Sources indicate that trump has pushed to fast-track the project, so that it could be mostly completed before he leaves office in 2028. His efforts to leave his mark on the capital include the bulldozing of the historic East Wing of the White House to make room for a 1,000-seat ballroom, a slapdash relining of the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall, and prepares to paint the Eisenhower Executive Office Building white.

In a recent development, in another move to secure his design legacy, Trump signed an order on Thursday that aims to make the Oval Office—which he has decorated with gilded adornments—into a national monument. “It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters without a trace of irony. Presidents can create national monuments, based on the 1906 Antiquities Act, but this refers to federal lands set aside for preservation.

Industry observers note that trump’s grand prepares have so far been helped by the fact that the committees overseeing preservation and design review for the capital are packed with appointees loyal to the president. This was most evident in Thursday’s meeting of the NCPC, where chairman Mark Paoletta—who also serves as general counsel of the Office of Management and Budget and deputy director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau—continually presented the government’s legal arguments in favour of building the arch.

When a smaller contingent of non-administration commissioners, led by DC city council chair Phil Mendelson, moved to delay the vote on the arch to December, vice chair Stuart Levenbach—who also works in the Office of Management and Budget as chief statistician—noted that "the project proponent is under a time constraint and wants the decision today".

Industry observers note that no explanation was given for what that time constraint involved however. In the end, the NCPC voted along loyalist lines, with the eight administration-appointed members voting to approve the arch looks and four voting against.

The vote came at the end of more than eight hours of public comments from more than 100 speakers, including public officials, veterans and families of fallen soldiers—many of them calling in from an all-day protest taking place at Memorial Circle.

Most of their testimony was excoriating, and many urged the commission not to kowtow to the self-aggrandising whims of the president. Congressman Jared Huffman, the ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, said the arch lacks congressional authorisation and goes against the Height of Buildings Act and other preservation laws. He warned that those working to move forward with the arch “will put themselves at legal risk".

"I urge all officials and firms involved with this illegal project to consider the legal hazards they may be facing by advancing it because, in case you hadn't heard, we'll soon have a new congress that takes the rule of law very seriously," said Huffman, referencing the outcome of the recent US midterm elections.

#351. French court orders restitution of Pissarro painting sold at Sotheby’s for £1.2m to heirs of Jewish banker

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (749 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper

French court orders restitution of Pissarro painting sold at Sotheby’s for £1.2m to heirs of Jewish banker

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A French court has ordered the cancellation of the Sotheby’s London sale of a landscape by Camille Pissarro, and its immediate restitution to the heirs of Jewish banker Salomon Flavian, on the grounds that it was looted in Paris in 1941.
  • Entitled Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne (fishing dock and Duquesne basin, 1902), this view of the port of Dieppe in Normandy, was sold at Sotheby’s London on 25 June 2024 for £1.2m.
  • According to recent reports, the Sotheby’s catalogue did mention it had been owned by Flavian from 1935 and was registered in the Répertoire des biens spoliés (repertory of looted art) released by the French government in 1947.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A French court has ordered the cancellation of the Sotheby’s London sale of a landscape by Camille Pissarro, and its immediate restitution to the heirs of Jewish banker Salomon Flavian, on the grounds that it was looted in Paris in 1941. According to the 5 November ruling, Sotheby’s has two months to reveal the “complete identity” of the buyer, subject to a daily penalty of €1,000 for any delay.

Entitled Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne (fishing dock and Duquesne basin, 1902), this view of the port of Dieppe in Normandy, was sold at Sotheby’s London on 25 June 2024 for £1.2m.

According to recent reports, the Sotheby’s catalogue did mention it had been owned by Flavian from 1935 and was registered in the Répertoire des biens spoliés (repertory of looted art) released by the French government in 1947. Nevertheless, it indicated that the work was “offered for sale pursuant to a settlement between the current owner and heirs of Salomon Flavian”. Their consent, Sotheby’s explained in court, had been obtained by the Mondex Corporation, a Toronto-based company specialised in the return of looted art.

At a court hearing on 18 September, Corinne Hershkovitch, the lawyer for seven heirs of Flavian, said this agreement had been signed by only two relatives and the others were not consulted. In court, Mondex and Sotheby’s endorsed a study which concluded that the painting had been acquired in the late 1930s by the British artist and collector Edward Le Bas, from the dealer Paul Rosenberg, and therefore was no longer part of Flavian’s collection seized in 1941 by the Nazis.

Recent findings suggest that the court judged otherwise, considering that there was “no direct and convincing evidence” of these alleged transactions. On the contrary, the Flavian family’s research produced “a set of precise, serious and concurring elements demonstrating that Pissarro’s work was indeed looted during” the Second World War, according to the judges.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Sotheby’s London said it is “disappointed by the judgement regarding the restitution”. However, the auction house “welcomes the decision to dismiss all claims against Sotheby’s”. “The history of the artwork is complex”, the spokesperson adds, and “we fully recognise the profound losses suffered by the Flavian family during the Nazi era and, from the outset, have approached this matter responsibly and with the care and respect it deserves.”.

“It is a very key ruling, which opens the way to a restitution that the Flavian family has demanded since the war,” Hershkovitch tells The Art Newspaper. “It indicates Mondex’s failure in its mission, and now Sotheby’s has to bear the responsibility for having sold a looted artwork.”.

It has been revealed that mondex’s lawyer, Melina Wolman, notes the manufacturer intends to appeal a judgement that, she says, is “posing major difficulties in regard with historical factors”. She adds that the name of Le Bas, who owned the Pissarro painting in the 1950s, appears on an entry in the catalogue raisonné edited by Paul Rosenberg in 1939. But the court ruled that this was only one among “contradictory elements” and that Sotheby’s and Mondex “did not support this hypothesis by any direct proof of such sales, at a time when France was at peace and the art market well structured”.

In court, Remi Sermier, a lawyer for Sotheby’s, also disputed the court’s jurisdiction on a sale made in London. But the court stated that, under French law, the annulment of the 1941 dispossession acts makes all subsequent sales of the work null and void. However, the court chose not to cancel the agreement signed between Mondex and the two heirs who had waived all their rights to the painting just before the sale, in exchange for a share of the sale price.

The ruling could trigger a cascade of litigation internationally. Sotheby’s is “considering whether to join the appeal”, a spokesperson claims, stressing that “client confidentiality is of paramount importance” for the company. The spokesperson adds: “There is a procedure that will need to be followed in order to enforce the decision in the UK.”.

It has been revealed that in case of success, the Flavian family will have to face the current possessor, who can demand compensation from Sotheby’s. For its part, the auction house could turn against Mondex and the consignor of the work, because, according to sources close to the case, the settlement agreement Mondex and the seller signed contains an indemnity clause of which Sotheby’s is the beneficiary.

#349. Latest Update: Whitney Museum selects a staff curator and a stage director to lead 2028 biennial

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (770 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper

Latest Update: Whitney Museum selects a staff curator and a stage director to lead 2028 biennial

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Whitney Museum of American Art has selected Meg Onli, a curator at the museum, and Zack Winokur, a choreographer and director for the stage, to curate the 2028 edition of the Whitney Biennial.
  • “Every Whitney Biennial springs from a distinct curatorial alchemy,” Scott Rothkopf, the Whitney’s director, said in a statement.
  • Onli is one of the Whitney’s star curators, having joined the institution as a curator-at-large in 2023, then as a curator in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Whitney Museum of American Art has selected Meg Onli, a curator at the museum, and Zack Winokur, a choreographer and director for the stage, to curate the 2028 edition of the Whitney Biennial. It is due to open in March 2028.

“Every Whitney Biennial springs from a distinct curatorial alchemy,” Scott Rothkopf, the Whitney’s director, said in a statement. “Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art. Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial.”.

Onli is one of the Whitney’s star curators, having joined the institution as a curator-at-large in 2023, then as a curator in 2024. She co-curated the 2024 Whitney Biennial, titled Even Better Than the Real Thing, with fellow Whitney curator Chrissie Iles. Most recently she co-curated the museum’s current Roy Lichtenstein retrospective (until 10 May 2027).

“From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about,” Onli stated in a statement. “I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead.”.

Winokur’s work spans dance, music, visual art, opera and theatre. He is the co-founder and artistic director of the performing arts collective AMOC* (American Modern Opera Manufacturer), which last year staged a five-week takeover of the Lincoln Center campus on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. He was previously the artistic director of Little Island, a park and cultural event space designed by Heatherwick Studio and MNLA that rises out of the Hudson River not far from the Whitney. His projects for the stage and screen have included directing productions at Opera Philadelphia and the Santa Fe Opera, and working on the expanded version of The Wizard of Oz presently showing at Sphere in Las Vegas.

It has been revealed that “I’m honoured to be curating the Whitney Biennial with Meg,” Winokur mentioned in a statement. “Our shared desire to centre objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration. It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring. As an artist, what excites me most is being in service to other artists, and I’m delighted to have the opportunity to do so in the context of the Whitney.”.

The 2026 Whitney Biennial, which was organised by staff curators Marcela Guerrero and Drew Sawyer, closed in October. It was seen by more than 550,000 visitors, according to the museum’s figures, around 75% of whom identified as either Millennials or Gen Z, making it the youngest audience since the Whitney started tracking visitors’ ages.

The exhibition’s 2026 edition was also remarkably controversy-free, though the exhibition is often a lightning rod for debates, protests and political statements. The 2019 edition was led by Whitney curators Jane Panetta and Rujeko Hockley, and came to be known colloquially as the “tear gas biennial” due to weekly protests and participating artists’ threatened withdrawals over the Whitney’s vice chairman at the time, Warren Kanders, who was the chief executive of Safariland, a defense and security contractor that manufactured tear gas canisters that had been deployed against asylum-seekers at the Mexico-US border, among other materials. Kanders eventually resigned from the museum’s board; he is currently the chairman and chief executive of Cadre Holdings, a Florida-based manufacturer of security and law-enforcement equipment.

In a recent development, the 2017 Whitney Biennial, which was co-curated by Christopher Y. Lew and Mia Locks, was largely overshadowed by the wide-ranging debate over a single painting in the exhibition: Dana Schutz’s Open Casket (2016), in which the artist portrayed the famous image from 1955 of 14-year-old Emmett Till lying in an open casket following his brutal abduction, mutilation and murder. The artist Hannah Black wrote an open letter criticising the work’s inclusion in the biennial and calling for its destruction, sparking protests inside and outside the museum and arguments about censorship, identity and cultural appropriation.

Industry observers note that the 2028 Whitney Biennial will be the 83rd edition of the exhibition, which started out as a series of medium-specific exhibitions before becoming the Whitney Annual in 1937, then transitioning to its every-other-year format in 1973. It remains the most closely watched recurring exhibition of contemporary art in the Americas.

Lost Rubens sketches return to German castle after 80 years

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper
