#326. Tate Britain spotlights Bloomsbury artists Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant for the first time since 1999

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (852 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper

Tate Britain spotlights Bloomsbury artists Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant for the first time since 1999

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Bloomsbury Group seems to have been ever-present in UK culture since its inception in the early 20th century, just before the First World War.
  • Sources indicate that the Bloomsbury Group has largely retained its high profile over the decades, with feature films on many of its protagonists and even a BBC mini-series in 2015 called Life in Squares, named for the supposed Dorothy Parker gag that the group “lived in squares, painted in circles and loved in triangles”.
  • But the Tate show marks the first Bloomsbury-focused show at the national home for British art for over a quarter of a century.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Bloomsbury Group seems to have been ever-present in UK culture since its inception in the early 20th century, just before the First World War. Lytton Strachey, John Maynard Keynes, Virginia Woolf, E.M. Forster, Vanessa Bell, Duncan Grant—their names are legion as representatives of a flowering of British intellectualism across the full spectrum of literary and artistic endeavours. While Roger Fry was arguably Bloomsbury’s most influential art-world voice, as the critic who essentially introduced European Post-Impressionism to Britain with a celebrated exhibition at the Grafton Galleries in 1910, Bell and Grant were the group’s most active and high-profile painters. The pair’s bracketing together for a latest Tate Britain exhibition is also a result, no doubt, of their 40-year open relationship that saw them live and paint together—and each other—over many decades.

Sources indicate that the Bloomsbury Group has largely retained its high profile over the decades, with feature films on many of its protagonists and even a BBC mini-series in 2015 called Life in Squares, named for the supposed Dorothy Parker gag that the group “lived in squares, painted in circles and loved in triangles”. Bell and Grant’s former home Charleston, near Lewes in East Sussex, has maintained a near-constant programme of exhibitions to keep the flame alive, the latest of which, Mad Bloomsbury (4 November-11 April 2027) examines the group’s engagement with mental health issues.

But the Tate show marks the first Bloomsbury-focused show at the national home for British art for over a quarter of a century. Thomas Kennedy, the curator of Modern British art at Tate Britain, thinks it is about time. “That means an entire generation of visitors have not seen an exhibition on Vanessa or Duncan’s work at Tate, and we felt that it was notable for us to revisit their practices again after so long,” Kennedy claims. “I don’t believe there’s ever been a major exhibition on Vanessa and Duncan together, and it’s so fascinating to see the ways they differ. We should recognise their individual accomplishments of course, but also the works they made together and how they influenced each other. We know about their relationship—she was married and he was gay—but this exhibition explores what that really meant in their artworks and in their life.”.

Looking back at that previous 1999 show, the cuttings files reveal that the turn of the millennium clearly marked a low point in critical opinion of the Bloomsbury artists; outright abuse might be the best description of some of the responses. The Guardian art critic Adrian Searle called them “a bit crap”, “lightweights” and “third rate”, while for the novelist Philip Hensher writing in The Independent, these “no-hopers” and their “rubbish” inspired simple “rage and loathing”.

Sources indicate that but Kennedy is not having it. Bell and Grant, he indicates, “started experimenting with art in unique ways that hadn’t really been seen in Britain before”. He adds: “They created some of the first abstract works in Britain, which is sometimes very much overlooked. And they were creating these works together, and talking about art all day, every day, breaking the distinction between fine and decorative art with the Omega Workshops. What they were doing was really special.”.

Bell, whose sister Virginia Woolf was even more celebrated in her field, is perhaps now the slightly more recognisable name of the two painters, though, as Kennedy points out, both Bell and Grant were considered leading figures during their lifetimes. Their close physical proximity, from when they moved to Charleston in 1918 to Bell’s death in 1961, meant their styles were often similarly adjacent, though Kennedy is clear on the differences. “Vanessa’s painting is more deliberate with very considered blocks of colour and very strong outlines, whereas Duncan’s is scratchier, more impulsive and it feels like he is experimenting more with more expressive techniques,” he states.

Kennedy adds: “However, later on, when they’re working on the Famous Women dinner service [a collection of 50 hand-painted plates], their styles are completely the same: the authorship has very much broken down and we can’t tell who did what. So much so that Roger Fry told them to paint in different studios to reassess their own way of making. It’s fascinating to see that push and pull between what they were taking from each other.”.

In the end, it might be that the very thing that seemed to diminish the Bloomsbury Group for previous generations—their complex, near-incestuous love lives—is what is powering their current revival: to contemporary perspectives they now look like pioneers of unrepentantly queer lifestyles. Bell married fellow painter Clive Bell in 1907, then had a long relationship with Fry and had a daughter, Angelica, with Grant in 1918. Grant, for his part, had a string of male lovers while maintaining his domestic relationship with Bell. “They were looking towards non-monogamous relationships and accepting queer relationships. The latter, as you know, was illegal in the UK at the time,” Kennedy notes. “Within the Bloomsbury Group they felt freedom—both artistically and the way they lived.”.

• Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, Tate Britain, London, 12 November-11 April 2027.

#324. What next for Shanghai? City’s art scene leans into an uncertain future

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1811 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper

What next for Shanghai? City’s art scene leans into an uncertain future

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Its impatient hustle may spare its art scene from the plateau of middle age as it navigates a crisis of transition after the Covid years derailed its late 2010s momentum.
  • Industry observers note that “Shanghai has so many galleries, so many museums, so many eccentric little spaces that you could come in the middle of summer and still see art non-stop,” says Lorenz Helbling, who founded ShanghArt in 1996.
  • The city’s two large-scale fairs, Art021 Shanghai (11-14 November) and West Bund Art & Design (10-15 November), established in 2013 and 2014 respectively, set the barometer and prime the mood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shanghai is a restless city. Its impatient hustle may spare its art scene from the plateau of middle age as it navigates a crisis of transition after the Covid years derailed its late 2010s momentum. Going into Shanghai’s annual art week (10-15 November), with two established fairs anchoring an explosion of art events across the city, its galleries, artists and institutions are assessing how the city’s art market can weather China’s economic slowdown and whether the cultural momentum of the past three decades can be sustained.

Industry observers note that “Shanghai has so many galleries, so many museums, so many eccentric little spaces that you could come in the middle of summer and still see art non-stop,” says Lorenz Helbling, who founded ShanghArt in 1996. One of the first contemporary art galleries in China, it now has locations in Shanghai, Beijing and Singapore. The Swiss transplant says the volume of artistic activity in the city of 25 million people can be compared to Upcoming York’s, though the scene can be harder to find. “You can make a lot of fun things here.”.

The city’s two large-scale fairs, Art021 Shanghai (11-14 November) and West Bund Art & Design (10-15 November), established in 2013 and 2014 respectively, set the barometer and prime the mood. So far, Shanghai’s core galleries have largely survived China’s property crash and deflationary economy, but they need young artists and upcoming collectors to continue buoying their businesses.

In a recent development, lise Li, who founded Shanghai’s Vanguard Gallery in 2004, indicates the city is “still in an upward phase, just growing much more slowly than before”. During art week, Li’s gallery will participate in the second iteration of the boutique fair Hangover Shanghai (11-15 November) and in Art021, while showing the artist Tang Chao in the gallery and collaborating on a group show at the artist-run 33ml Offspace. Several artists represented by Vanguard are having big moments nearby: Liao Fei will simultaneously be showing at Hangzhou’s Imagokinetics and the artist group known as Jiū Society has an exhibition at Nanjing’s Beiqiu Museum of Contemporary Art.

Established in 2013, Art021 Shanghai (pictured in 2025) is one of the most successful art fairs in the city Photo: Lisa Movius.

Though the buzz of the 2010s has quieted, Li states, “there are quite a few more art institutions, and more newcomers are getting involved. The number of young artists is increasing rapidly; we see a lot of fresh faces every year. But most exhibitions are relatively conservative, which is rather a pity.”.

In a recent development, the market has “changed considerably” compared to what now “might be called the ‘golden 15 years’ of China’s contemporary art market: the shift in the broader economic environment over the past few years has been impossible to ignore”, Otto Neu states. In 2022 he co-founded Nan Ke Gallery, which has a group show about art and literature on view during the fair week. “For artists and galleries alike, it is certainly a challenging moment. We probably have to work twice as hard as we did before simply to survive and keep things moving.”.

Industry observers note that change, Neu adds, does not have to be negative. He cites the Chinese expression “great waves wash away the sand and leave the gold behind”, adding that “difficult periods can force an industry to become more focused, more rigorous and perhaps more honest about what really matters. In that sense, this may also be an important stage of maturation for Shanghai’s art scene.”.

In addition to this month’s two international art fairs, Shanghai’s many resident artists—ranging from established figures like Ding Yi, Zhang Enli and Yang Fudong to mid-career and emerging talents—can rely on year-round programming at a healthy variety of homegrown and imported galleries. Western outfits like Almine Rech, Perrotin and Lisson maintain spaces in Shanghai, as do Asian powerhouses including Japan’s Ota Fine Arts and Korea’s Arario Gallery. ShanghArt has been joined by several influential local galleries, among them Antenna Space, Gallery Vacancy, Capsule Gallery and Don Gallery.

Major state-backed museums like the Power Station of Art, Museum of Art Pudong and West Bund Museum (which is partnered with the Centre Pompidou in Paris) have a complement of private museums that have proliferated since the 2010s. The Rockbund Art Museum, Long Museum and Yuz Museum are the best known, but smaller, newer, specialised or further-flung institutions like Fotografiska and the Museum of Glass, and non-profit spaces like Pond Society, Longlati and Prada Rong Zhai, have also enriched the Shanghai art ecosystem.

Vanguard Gallery’s Li credits Shanghai’s “open-city vibe” and its large base of collectors and visitors, along with the museums, galleries and artists, plus a citizenry curious “about fashion and new things, a strong history of business, and a diverse cultural structure. The main downside is that the cost of living is too high.” The lack of art information platforms, even in Chinese, is the other main challenge, she notes.

The sense of openness is what drew the collector Cherry Xu to open her art-meets-fashion space Cheruby in the city last year. With fresh initiatives, “the boundaries between artists, designers, musicians and people working in fashion are becoming increasingly blurred”, she states, opening the art world to new audiences. “This kind of natural crossover between different fields is something very particular to Shanghai,” Xu says. “Art here doesn’t operate as an isolated system; it is constantly in conversation with design, music, fashion, technology and a broader youth culture, with these different communities influencing one another.”.

Compared to Beijing’s art scene, Neu notes, Shanghai’s creative community maintains a “healthy sense of distance. There is a certain independence between galleries, institutions, artists and collectors, which has shaped a rather distinctive ecosystem here”, a happy, pragmatic chaos of sorts. Beijing’s art scene is built on personal connections, Neu says, while in Shanghai, “between institutions, between galleries and even between galleries and collectors, there is often an understanding that business is business, friendship is friendship, and collaboration does not necessarily require complicated personal obligations or relationships”.

However, Neu adds that those divisions could become vulnerabilities in the current economic upheaval. “Perhaps this is precisely the moment when Shanghai’s art community needs to become a little more connected and cohesive than it has been in the past—not by giving up its independence, but by finding better ways to support one another,” he notes.

According to recent reports, helbling notes that Beijing is “more split up into scenes which work on their own”, while Shanghai has various circles that interact and are more permeable. He likens the city’s art community to its fairly compact geography, with the art neighbourhoods all within comparably easy reach of each other.

Twenty years ago, Shanghai was the upstart artistic challenger to Beijing, the political capital home to China’s leading art academy. Hong Kong’s concurrent cultural rise proved complimentary to Shanghai’s, and many in Shanghai say the expanding art activity in Korea, Japan and Singapore—as well as in mainland Chinese cities like Chengdu, Shenzhen and nearby Nanjing, Hangzhou and Suzhou—have been net positives for the local scene.

It has been revealed that “This situation didn’t happen overnight; it’s the result of years of collaboration between Shanghai’s art institutions, galleries and fairs, as well as the collectors and artists living here,” Li notes. “It’s not simply due to fairs or art weeks alone. The rise of art in new Chinese cities has also become developed, likely influenced by Shanghai and Hong Kong.”.

Shanghai “was one of the earliest cities in China to develop a contemporary art market, and its relatively open culture and international outlook have given it a particular advantage”, Neu notes. “Whether we are talking about collecting, aesthetic awareness or public understanding of contemporary art, Shanghai has accumulated more than two decades of experience and audience development. That kind of cultural infrastructure takes time to build.”.

He adds that growing art scenes in other mainland cities represent “something very positive for Shanghai rather than a threat. A stronger regional art ecosystem ultimately creates more audiences, more conversations and more opportunities for everyone. Healthy competition and exchange between cities can only make the broader Chinese art scene more dynamic.”.

It has been revealed that regionally, Xu indicates, Shanghai “has a very distinct local culture, its own audiences and creative communities, [while] its relationship with other Asian cities is becoming much more direct. It feels increasingly natural for artists, curators and other creative practitioners to live and work across different cities in Asia, and for us to look to what is happening in Tokyo, Seoul, Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok and elsewhere in the region, rather than instinctively treating Europe and the US as the only points of reference.” For Shanghai’s art week, Cheruby is showing a solo exhibition by the multidisciplinary Thai artist Tanat Teeradakorn.

In a recent development, “Shanghai has an interesting place within this network,” Xu says. “It has a relatively mature art infrastructure, but also very strong fashion, design, commercial, technological and popular cultures, and these worlds exist very close to one another in everyday life. It also has a large and increasingly young audience, so when an artist comes to Shanghai, they are encountering more than an established ‘art world’; they are entering a complex and fast-moving urban environment that is constantly being reshaped by new forms of consumption, technology and youth culture. That complexity creates a lot of possibilities.”.

Zhang Ruyi, whose 2022 exhibition at Beijing’s UCCA Center for Contemporary Art is shown here, is among Shanghai’s mid-career artists to watch Photo: Sun Shi; courtesy UCCA Center for Contemporary Art.

After helping to build the careers of some of Asia’s biggest art stars, Helbling now focuses on cultivating rising talents through more group indicates and dialogue. “You always look at what artists are doing,” he notes. “Many of them now operate between here and the West—educated here and in the West”, with networks and roots in both cultures.

After suspended mobility during the Covid years, dual-culture artists in Shanghai and across Asia have resumed their frequent travels between regions. Often the children of artists or collectors, young Chinese artists are very well versed in both Western and Asian artistic traditions, giving them a sophisticated perspective. “They have an interesting job to do to figure out what kind of art makes sense today,” Helbling claims.

In a recent development, he recalls the “loneliness” of Shanghai’s 1990s avant-garde, now rendered “impossible” by contemporary art’s citywide popularity. Still, he views the 2000 internationalisation of the Shanghai Biennale, the first contemporary art fair SH Contemporary (2007-14), and the flowering of galleries and museums as all part of one era.

Industry observers note that “There was from the 1990s when Shanghai opened up until the Covid time, and there is after Covid time,” he claims. “The first 30 years, and now the second 30 years.”.

Peruvian senator calls for removal of large-scale replicas of Moche erotic sculptures from public park

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “What happens when children see these images?
  • The sculptures are located in Parque de la Fertilidad (Fertility Park), a public space where in 2021 then-mayor Arturo Fernández of the Moche district began installing giant fibreglass reproductions of ceramic depictions of sexual acts to promote tourism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A controversy over 3m-tall erotic sculptures in northern Peru reignited recently after a senator requested that the cultural ministry remove them from a public area. Located in a park outside the city of Trujillo, the sculptures are replicas of ceramics from the pre-Incan Moche civilisation.

“What happens when children see these images? Neurological and psychological factors are affected, because they see body dimensions that are completely different from how they see themselves,” Milagros Jáuregui, a conservative senator from the Renovación Popular party, said in a speech on 26 October.

The sculptures are located in Parque de la Fertilidad (Fertility Park), a public space where in 2021 then-mayor Arturo Fernández of the Moche district began installing giant fibreglass reproductions of ceramic depictions of sexual acts to promote tourism.

Industry observers note that known as huacos eróticos, the much smaller original ceramics date from the 3rd to 8th century AD. No more than 30cm in height, they were placed in tombs as burial offerings. But the debate about their much larger versions in the park goes beyond political prudishness.

Industry observers note that “It’s a complicated issue,” the Peruvian archaeologist Walter Alva tells The Art Newspaper. “There’s freedom to express or re-create themes from the past, but these ceramics were created to be placed as offerings to the dead, with a sense of revitalising life. They are associated with both fertility and an entire system of beliefs.”.

An original huaco erótico ceramic offering made by the Moche civilisation, Larco Museum, Lima Photo: László Varga, via Wikimedia Commons.

It has been revealed that the Moche civilisation covered 700km of the coast of what is now Peru, between the regions of Piura and Ancash, centuries before the Inca dominated the area. “Moche art is primarily ceramic, and these vessels depict erotic scenes or concepts of sexuality from that era,” Alva states. “The sculptures in the park were created outside of their historical context.”.

One of the greatest archaeological discoveries from the Moche civilisation was that of the Lord of Sipán near the city of Chiclayo—a discovery Alva made in 1987. A 3rd-century monarch, the Lord of Sipán’s body was found covered with gold along with eight other people, a dog and two llamas and nearly 500 objects including ceramic vessels, ornaments and textiles.

It has been revealed that the Moche have the largest number of erotic representations among pre-Hispanic civilisations. The most complete collection of its ceramics is in Lima, at the Larco Museum of pre-Columbian art, which celebrated its centennial in July. Before the 1960s, children were forbidden from entering the room that housed the huacos. Today, minors must be accompanied by an adult. The institution’s Erotic Gallery is one of its most popular attractions.

Recent findings suggest that jáuregui, an evangelical pastor as well as a senator, believes these Moche sculptures should only be in closed spaces. “Displaying these types of images in public is harmful to children,” she told congress. “We should have them in museums, where high-school students can observe a part of our culture that is a national treasure with the help of teachers or some kind of tutor.”.

Latest Update: Collector Elie Khouri to create physical home for his private foundation in Dubai

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Dubai-based art collector Elie Khouri is building a space in the city for his eponymous foundation.
  • Sources indicate that khouri is one of the Unite Arab Emirates (UAE)’s biggest and best-known collectors.
  • Sources indicate that he began making looks for the foundation around five years ago, as one of the London-based Deflina Foundation’s collectors-in-residence, a programme rolled out in 2017 that considers collecting as a practice and seeks to support more ambitious implementation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Dubai-based art collector Elie Khouri is building a space in the city for his eponymous foundation. The Elie Khouri Art Foundation (Ekaf) will be located in the coastal district of Jumeirah 1, in a villa renovated and redesigned by Counterspace, a firm led by the architect Sumayya Vally. The space, expected to open in 2028, will host public exhibitions and educational programmes.

Sources indicate that khouri is one of the Unite Arab Emirates (UAE)’s biggest and best-known collectors. Originally from Lebanon, he made his name as the chief executive officer of Omnicom Media in the Middle East and North Africa, and has been based in Dubai since the 1990s.

Sources indicate that he began making looks for the foundation around five years ago, as one of the London-based Deflina Foundation’s collectors-in-residence, a programme rolled out in 2017 that considers collecting as a practice and seeks to support more ambitious implementation. With them he conducted feasibility studies to better understand what Dubai needs.

“The whole idea is to give back and foster exchange of ideas, challenge thinking and bring new perspectives,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “Dubai is about entrepreneurship. They support people like me, people coming to fulfil their ambitions. And what Dubai needs is private institutions, because that's how they will build their own version of culture.”.

Despite Dubai’s large number of artists and galleries, it has never had a major museum, and private foundations have become a significant part of its infrastructure. The Jameel Arts Centre and Alserkal Avenue, each backed by individuals, are the two pillars of the art scene, in addition to smaller foundations such as Ishara, which focuses on art from South Asia.

Ekaf has an emphasis on global contemporary art, though one in which art from the Middle East will play an important role.

“We are here to support talent internationally,” notes Khouri. “We're not about the region, but since we are in the Middle East, we also look at the best talent here. We have a responsibility to the ecosystem and the galleries.”.

Ekaf will take Khouri’s collection, comprising works by more than 300 artists, as its starting point, drawing from it for initial exhibitions. Later highlights will increasingly involve loans and collaborations. Ultimately, Khouri intends to establish an Ekaf collection that is separate to his personal holdings.

The veteran art strategist Caroline Louca, who was formerly at Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism and Christie’s Middle East, has been appointed as the director of the foundation. Louca and Khouri are looking to hire a curatorial team closer to the completion date for the museum.

Louca underlines that community engagement will be a major part of the foundation, with plans for talks, lectures and education streams. The foundation’s location, in Jumeirah 1, is a bonus in this respect. Jumeirah 1 is one of the oldest neighbourhoods in Dubai, where many affluent long-time residents live. Ekaf’s villa was home to an Emirati family in the 1980s, and Vally’s designs retain the elements of old-school Gulf architecture that is a source of nostalgia for many in the UAE.

In a recent development, "We are focusing on how we can make a place become part of the community—and not just focus on what we’re showing,” says Louca. “You can see beautiful artworks everywhere, but we want people to be a bit daring. We want them to walk in and ask questions—and not be embarrassed to ask questions—and then come back and ask more. If we can achieve that, it will be our barometer of success.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Ghanaian-French artist Kwama Frigaux and the Senegalese Fatoumata Sy have been announced as the joint winners of the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize.
  • The prize is named after the former Ashanti queen mother, renowned for her anti-colonial resistance when Ghana was under British rule.
  • Installation view of The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, Gallery 1957's show by Theresah Ankomah, who won the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Prize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Ghanaian-French artist Kwama Frigaux and the Senegalese Fatoumata Sy have been announced as the joint winners of the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize. The prize, founded by the London and Accra-based Gallery 1957 in 2021 to support women artists in Ghana and its diaspora, has this year expanded to include artists from Senegal, in partnership with Institut Français du Sénégal. Frigaux and Fatoumata have been awarded $5,000 each, as well as a three-month residency (in Senegal for the Ghanaian and in Ghana for the Senegalese), and solo exhibitions.

The prize is named after the former Ashanti queen mother, renowned for her anti-colonial resistance when Ghana was under British rule. The call for applications for this year’s edition opened in June and ran until September, and was open to Ghanaian and Senegalese women artists aged 18 or older, based either in their home countries or in the diaspora. The winners were announced during Accra Cultural Week (29 October-2 November), which is organised by Gallery 1957. On view there until 5 December is The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, a solo show by Theresah Ankomah, the winner of the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize.

Installation view of The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, Gallery 1957's show by Theresah Ankomah, who won the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Prize.

Frigaux and Sy were selected by a jury comprising Touria El Glaoui, the founder of the 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair; the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey; Marie Hélène Pereira, a senior curator at Berlin’s Haus der Kulturen der Welt; Jeanne Barral, a curator at the Fondation Cartier; the collector Alexa Waley-Cohen; and Dominique Heyse-Moore, the senior curator of contemporary British art at Tate Britain.

Industry observers note that runners up participate in a mentorship programme, which provides support on topics such as grant applications and entrepreneurship. Mentors this year include the Nigerian artist Modupeola Fadugba and Aisha Ayensu, the founder of the Ghanaian luxury fashion brand Christie Brown.

"I think [it's] an incredible programme that helps drive the longevity of [the prize's] impact,” Leila Zakhem, the director of the prize, tells The Art Newspaper. “And it really creates a beautiful community.”.

Zakhem explains that her team considered several countries for the expansion, including Nigeria. A key part of this search was finding a "very good implementing partner". The Institut Français du Sénégal, which is a non-commercial space, has a lot of credibility, she adds, “and they were very excited to partner with us on the prize”. Zakhem says that she hopes the expansion will help develop and create a bridge between art communities in English- and French-speaking West Africa.

The planned next steps are to expand further into West Africa, and then potentially beyond, with winners selected from different regions of the continent. “The goal is eventually to be the leading Pan-African female art prize on the continent,” Zakhem claims.

#318. Five examples of Mesoamerican modern architecture

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (832 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen

Five examples of Mesoamerican modern architecture

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that mexican architects have been combining principles from ancient architecture with modern techniques.
  • Wu’s book, Mesoamerican Modern: Ancient Ideas in Contemporary Mexican Homes, details projects that illustrate this trend, from the 1970s to today, with a focus on residential architecture.
  • Recent findings suggest that “These homes reflect the complex aesthetic cultures of Mesoamerica,” Wu told Dezeen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Luis Garvan.

Recent findings suggest that mexican architects have been combining principles from ancient architecture with modern techniques. Curator and writer Su Wu picks five examples of this phenomenon from her Mesoamerican Modern book.

Wu’s book, Mesoamerican Modern: Ancient Ideas in Contemporary Mexican Homes, details projects that illustrate this trend, from the 1970s to today, with a focus on residential architecture.

Recent findings suggest that “These homes reflect the complex aesthetic cultures of Mesoamerica,” Wu told Dezeen. She chose the phrase that titles the book over “pre-Columbian” because she wanted to demonstrate that the monumentalism and logic of pre-Columbian Mexican architecture did not end with colonisation.

“I think these homes show instead that rather than being relegated to the past, these Mesoamerican materials, techniques, typologies, and forms are alive in the present and also perhaps inspiration or guides for the future.”.

Each shows aspects of monumentalism that recall the stone architecture of the wider Mesoamerican culture, while acknowledging the diversity.

The book tries to depart from projects that just use symbols and focus on the logic of the buildings, noting specific characteristics such as patios as intrinsic the the design.

“For me, the most defining characteristics of Mesoamerican architecture are the ones that reflect underlying principles, rather than the disjunction when symbols become separated from their meaning,” Wu mentioned.

“So throughout the book I wanted to highlight forms that arise from ideas such as the use of light or shadow as a physical object, or how homes are aligned to natural features, or the everyday presence of craft and the handmade, with an expanded sense of beauty as an attenuating consequence.”.

Read on for five examples of the Mesoamerican modern style in Mexico with commentary by Wu.

Casa Amalia, Agustín Hernández, 1973.

“This 1973 home is one of a few 20th-century homes in Mesoamerican Modern, built by architect Agustín Hernández for his sister Amalia, the founder of Mexico City’s Ballet Folklorico.

“A poet as well as an architect, Hernández is celebrated for injecting ‘Mesoamerican semantics into the brute vocabulary of modernism’, but  wrote most of all about the geometric and cosmic principles at the heart of Mesoamerican architecture, and the ‘mathematical, almost symphonic rhythm’ of Mesoamerican structures and cities.

According to recent reports, “His sister Amalia’s home was inspired by the convex forms of seashells as well as by the prominent ocular motifs in Mesoamerican imagery. “.

Casa Mobius by Ernesto Gómez Gallardo, 1974.

“Built by the architect for his own family in 1974, this house in Mexico City’s San Jeronimo neighborhood is today the studio and home of ceramicist Perla Valtierra.

“Shaped loosely like a mobius strip, with a triangular lattice allowing spaces to fold in upon themselves and a cantilevered living room, the home reconsiders both volumes and typologies, in rooms that are anything but square.

“The house is furnished with an eclectic mix of iconic Japanese, Brasilian and Mexican furniture, including a chair originally designed for the Museo Experimental El Eco in Mexico City by its founder Matthias Goeritz, a close friend and frequent collaborator of Luis Barragan.”.

Casa Terreno by Fernanda Canales, 2018.

“Architect Teodoro González de León once described the patio as a defining characteristic of a Mesoamerican home, a space that is at once enclosed and exterior, and open to the elements.

“In this house in Estado de Mexico, Mexico City-based architect Fernanda Canales reclaimed land that had been devastated by cattle overgrazing, creating an interlocking series of patios that, in their deliberately undefined sense of function, create more space without having to build more of it.

“Each room in the home, which is approached through a pyramidal foyer with an opening to the sky, looks out onto courtyards or landscape, replete again with plants of the Americas.”.

Casa Cometa by Taller Mauricio Rocha + Gabriela Carrillo, 2019.

“In this home inspired by the spatial organization of ceremonial Mesoamerican sites, communal areas extend horizontally, while private spaces descend and rise vertically, like a dramatic bedroom tower with a daily view of both the sunrise and the sunset over the Pacific.

“With its overlapping platforms and passageways, the space designed by Gabriela Carrillo and Mauricio Rocha reflects the multiple planes of existence in Mesoamerican cosmology.

“In this house, a walkway weaves under the swimming pool, which itself slips under a long orthogonal platform, cut through with a descending staircase.”.

It has been revealed that “Casa Monte is a one-bedroom house with no exterior doors. Instead, the house deliberately discourages approach by appearing like a fortress over the tree line, and by its placement on a stepped platform, which creates a sense of separation from the jungle floor below.

“The open space with a pool cutting across the interior suggests the idea that architecture exists foremost as a way to engage with nature.

“Cast by Matos himself in earth-tinted cement on the beach where the house now sits, the home’s hundreds of individual forms were fitted together on-site.”.

Photography by Luis Garvan.

#317. As war continues, local people mobilise to salvage southern Lebanon’s history

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2122 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper

As war continues, local people mobilise to salvage southern Lebanon’s history

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Can you hear the bombing?” Riad Al-Assaad asks The Art Newspaper, speaking from his village of Zrariyeh in southern Lebanon.
  • It has been revealed that the south has lived with Israeli invasion and occupation for nearly half a century.
  • Sources indicate that the present conflict began on 8 October 2023, the day after the Hamas attacks on Israel, with exchanges of fire between Hezbollah and Israel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “Wow. Can you hear the bombing?” Riad Al-Assaad asks The Art Newspaper, speaking from his village of Zrariyeh in southern Lebanon. An Israeli strike on a nearby village cuts short a conversation about his efforts to save what remains of the heritage in the country’s south: scanning its old buildings, recording its oral history and now rescuing its libraries. Despite a ceasefire, south Lebanon remains under Israeli occupation and at war, and its people say their history is being erased.

It has been revealed that the south has lived with Israeli invasion and occupation for nearly half a century. Israel invaded in 1978 and pushed north to Beirut in 1982, the year Hezbollah formed to fight it, and it did not withdraw from the south until 2000. In 2006, the two fought a month-long war after Hezbollah captured two Israeli soldiers in a cross-border raid.

Sources indicate that the present conflict began on 8 October 2023, the day after the Hamas attacks on Israel, with exchanges of fire between Hezbollah and Israel. It escalated in September 2024 into full-scale war, with an Israeli ground invasion and strikes on Beirut, before a ceasefire that November. Fighting resumed in March 2026, when Hezbollah fired on Israel after the US and Israel attacked Iran; a ceasefire agreement reached in US-led talks in June has not ended it. Strikes continue daily, and Israeli forces occupy around 600 sq. km of the south, reaching up to 10km into Lebanon, behind what the army calls the Yellow Line.

Zrariyeh has around 2,000 houses, Al-Assaad estimates. By his count, 65 have been destroyed in this war and more than 100 damaged. His father’s house, in the middle of the village, was hit twice: first by shrapnel, then by blasts that “levelled” neighbouring buildings and blew out its windows and doors. Like others who have repaired their homes “once, twice, three times”, he now covers the openings with plastic. “We are living in the nylon era,” Al-Assaad states. But what is at stake, he adds, is “our historical existence”.

According to recent reports, the most visible part of that history is the south’s ancient monuments, and international protection has not kept them safe from the war. Since 2024, Unesco has granted 73 sites across Lebanon enhanced protection, which prohibits targeting them or using them for military purposes. In July, it inscribed the five castles of Mount Amel, all of them granted enhanced protection, on its World Heritage List and its list of sites in danger. Three of the castles, Beaufort, Dubieh and Chama’, are under Israeli occupation. Days after the inscription, the Israeli military detonated 700 tonnes of explosives about 800m from Beaufort, claiming it was destroying Hezbollah tunnels. In Tyre, a World Heritage Site since 1984, strikes have damaged columns, mosaics and the site’s offices and stores.

Sources indicate that ali Badawi, the ministry of culture’s regional director for south Lebanon, claims his teams cannot reach the occupied sites and rely on low-resolution satellite images and footage released by the Israeli army. One broadcast showed Israeli soldiers in Beaufort’s historical halls watching the Fifa World Cup on televisions he believes were taken from the castle’s information centre. Unesco has allocated some funding for the restoration of Tyre, but elsewhere donors are holding back while the war continues. “We cannot do anything at the moment,” Badawi says. “We have to wait.”.

Badawi lives in a village south of Tyre, close to Al Mansouri, an area that he indicates Israeli forces strike daily. “Sometimes at night we don’t sleep, because it is just explosion after explosion,” he says.

His colleague, Mohana Chahine, who manages the artefact stores at Tyre’s Al-Bass site, was seriously injured in an Israeli drone strike on 14 August 2024, weeks before the war escalated. She was driving home with her husband when a missile was fired at a motorcycle behind them, shattering the car’s windows and leaving her unable to move. Her husband pulled her from the car, and a second strike threw them both clear of it. After a month in hospital and further treatment in France, Chahine has completed her PhD and returned to work. “I go to work actively, but I am constantly afraid, unsettled and distracted,” she says. “I am constantly anxious about another war or being injured again.”.

According to recent reports, beyond Tyre and the castles lies heritage that appears on no Unesco list: the old houses, mosques, churches and cemeteries of southern Lebanon’s villages. Joanne Farchakh Bajjaly, an archaeologist and former journalist, is the founder of Biladi, a heritage organisation that has monitored the south since October 2023. In 2025 it recorded 389 historical buildings in five villages—according to Biladi, 85% of them are now destroyed. It was preparing to publish a report last March, but the return of war halted that project and Biladi widened its survey instead. With architecture students from the Lebanese University, the organisation logged around 850 sites across 105 villages, occupied or under threat, from archaeological ruins to houses built before 1950. The full findings are being held for its delayed report, but Biladi shared some of them with The Art Newspaper. Among them: the loss of the area’s Shia religious sites—mosques, shrines, mausoleums or husseiniyas (halls for religious gatherings)—stands at around 98%.

The 18th-century St George’s Melkite Catholic church in Dardghaya in the Tyre district was severely damaged in Israeli attacks in October 2024 Photo: courtesy Biladi.

It has been revealed that in July Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, stated the army had completely destroyed 24 villages that were “hundreds of years old”, totalling 15,000 to 20,000 homes, by his estimate. Lebanese counts are higher.

“We have 38 villages that have been bulldozed to the ground. Nothing remains,” Bajjaly says, adding that villages still under attack, such as Al Mansouri, have not yet been assessed and the figure could rise. Badawi puts the total number of villages destroyed at around 50. Each village has an ancient centre built over older remains, he notes, some of them Byzantine, Roman or Phoenician, so the loss cannot be counted in homes alone. “It is not just a matter of number of houses. The historical fabric itself is destroyed.”.

It has been revealed that according to both Badawi and Bajjaly, historic cemeteries across southern Lebanon have also been bulldozed by Israeli forces. At shrines, Bajjaly says, the earth has been turned over and the dead dug up. “This is total desacralisation, and these are well-calculated gestures,” she says.

Olive trees have been destroyed, too. After seeing images of trees being uprooted, Badawi went to Naqoura in early 2025 and found a field stripped of its old trees. In September a French Lebanese businessman filed a lawsuit in France accusing the Israeli military of war crimes, alleging that 600 trees his family had cultivated for 250 years were uprooted and taken to Israel. “When they remove 500-year-old olive trees, this is not anymore an concern of security,” Al-Assaad states.

The aim, Bajjaly believes, is “to kill the relationship between the people and their land and their history, and therefore to make it clear for them that there’s no return”.

The artist Oussama Baalbaki knows all too well what that means. His late father, the renowned painter Abdel Hamid Baalbaki, began building the family’s house in their ancestral village of Odaisseh, close to the border, in 1984, two years after Israel’s invasion of Beirut displaced them. With the village under occupation, his parents built it “over a very long period, with limited financial means and amid occupation, recurring war and displacement”.

His father, an amateur collector, hoped the home would become “something like a museum, or a cultural centre for literature and poetry”, and filled it with manuscripts, rare books, sculptures, paintings and antiquities. “Most key of all, the house shelters, beneath the trees of its garden, the tomb of my mother and father,” Baalbaki says.

The artist Oussama Baalbaki’s family home in Odaisseh was destroyed in 2024.

Industry observers note that in October 2024 the house was “rigged with explosives, along with every neighbourhood of the village, in a systematic, annihilating manner”, Baalbaki notes of the detonation, which was captured on video. His siblings visited the ruins in February 2025 to salvage what they could, but the village is now occupied and out of reach. “We lost our connection to the land of our ancestors,” he says, “and were left wandering in a torn space of imagination and time.”.

It has been revealed that the house had looked out over a valley towards a bare plateau, a view that shaped two generations of paintings. “This natural horizon imprinted itself on my father’s paintings and, in time, passed into my own,” Baalbaki claims.

A 2017 painting by Oussama Baalbaki of his village of Odaisseh and family home Courtesy the artist.

In Al Qantara, the family village of the artist and film-maker Ahmad Ghossein, the landscape itself has gone. His father returned there when the Israeli occupation ended in 2000, built a house and retired among his olive trees and chickens. When fighting began in 2023, he refused to leave, answering his son’s pleas from Beirut with photographs and videos.

In a recent development, “He was sending me all the time images of the sunrise, every morning, to say, ‘I’m fine’,” Ghossein says. He held out until September 2024, and even then went back whenever a ceasefire allowed. This March, Ghossein says, the village was blown up by Israeli forces and the hill it stood on levelled. “It’s not that you don’t find your house, you don’t find the land. It became white sand.”.

Ghossein has made his father’s daily photographs, videos and WhatsApp voice notes into a four-screen video installation, The Sound of Silence. It was shown at the Beirut Art Center and at Frieze London in October, and is due to be shown at Art Jameel in Jeddah. The footage is as his father shot it: the garden, the chickens, the road to the village, never the war. The question behind the piece, Ghossein indicates, is: “Can you do something about a place that doesn’t exist anymore?” His father, who now lives in Beirut, is “lost, more or less”, facing the reality that he may not go back for a long time.

Installtion view of Ahmad Ghossein , The Sound of Silence.

© Ahmad Ghossein. Courtesy: Beirut Art Centre.

In a recent development, but Ghossein refuses to be cast as a victim. “Yes, it’s horrible. Yes, it’s a disaster. Yes, they are erasing,” he says. “But I’m just continuing. This is a resistance by itself.”.

In a recent development, al-Assaad’s answer is to save what can still be carried or recorded. He owns a construction tech giant, which in wartime becomes “like a civil defence company”, handing out food, medicine and fuel. Working with the culture ministry, he supplies architectural scans of old mosques and houses in the border villages. “We can’t remove them. We can’t sandbag them,” he says, but they can be documented for future generations.

In a recent development, with Biladi he is now also rescuing private libraries: family collections handed down through generations. In Zibqin, known as the village of poets, they have found around 20. The two largest were lost under rubble; one of them, with around 6,000 books, was burned by an incendiary bomb, he claims. From another damaged home the team is recovering up to 2,000 volumes, many of them handwritten. Each book is cleaned, photographed, catalogued and moved to safe storage until its owner can reclaim it. He is appealing to anyone in the south with a library at risk to get in touch. “We don’t have the luxury of time,” he says. “We don’t have the luxury of doubt.”.

A destroyed home with a private library, containing manuscripts and historic books, in Zibqin, known as the village of poets © Riad Al Assaad.

Recent findings suggest that bajjaly fears what happens to a people’s past when nothing physical is left to hold it. “Is the history of south Lebanon going to turn into a myth? ‘We had a house here. We had a mosque here’,” she states. Documentation is her answer, a way “to give back to the population a proof of their own existence”. Biladi’s survey will go to the ministry of culture, which she says is pressing for heritage to be part of any rebuilding. “Any plan of reconstruction for south Lebanon that does not include heritage would be a continuity of the destruction,” she says.

Baalbaki says the uprooting will be temporary. “We will return to our land. But with what imagination will we return, and to what landscape?”.

#316. Fala Atelier embeds trio of playful volumes into Portuguese hillside for Cookie Cutter Retreat

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (400 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen

Fala Atelier embeds trio of playful volumes into Portuguese hillside for Cookie Cutter Retreat

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (400 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Francisco Ascensão (unless stated otherwise).
  • Three semicircular volumes of different scales make up this retreat for digital nomads in Portugal, completed by Porto architecture studio Fala Atelier.
  • The three volumes are nearly identical, emerging from the site with blocky, blue chimneys and topped with grass roofs, which Fala Atelier remarked “almost disappear” into the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Francisco Ascensão (unless stated otherwise).

Three semicircular volumes of different scales make up this retreat for digital nomads in Portugal, completed by Porto architecture studio Fala Atelier.

The three volumes are nearly identical, emerging from the site with blocky, blue chimneys and topped with grass roofs, which Fala Atelier remarked “almost disappear” into the landscape.

“The three buildings enjoy considerable freedom in their relationships with the site, the slope and one another, sharing a geometric vocabulary without submitting to a rigid overall composition,” the studio told Dezeen.

“From a distance, they almost disappear, leaving the windows and bright blue chimneys to announce their presence,” it added.

“Their placement makes the landscape a fluid game.”.

Industry observers note that the retreat’s three buildings were scaled as small, medium and large versions of the same semicircular volume. and built with the same materials and dimension ratios.

Sources indicate that each one is composed of a concrete frame, which is embedded into the landscape and incorporates round columns. These are adorned with glazed fronts and tilted metal canopies.

Diagonal walls slice through each of the volumes to distinguish the public and private areas, behind which are spaces that draw on houses by architects Frank Gehry, Toyo Ito and Alvaro Siza, according to Fala Atelier.

“Each [volume] is divided by a diagonal wall, placing a dense collection of small rooms beside an expansive, almost empty space,” the studio remarked.

“We treated fragments of [Gehry, Ito and Siza’s] looks as objets trouvés, borrowing their internal formal relationships almost verbatim.”.

The hall, which is the largest of the three spaces, was designed by Fala Atelier to “host almost any activity”.

Its front portion is open proposal, while private spaces sit behind, finished with a combination of white-painted and tile-clad walls contrasted by blue and fluorescent-yellow details.

This same materiality and colour palette is repeated throughout the retreat’s private and shared dwellings to create a consistent visual language across the site.

  • The PharmaPrinter Aurum was born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent – nearly a third – of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.
  • This compounding, when you combine different ingredients to make tailored medication, is usually done by pharmacists using traditional methods such as a pestle and mortar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by CurifyLabs.

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs have created a pharmaceutical compounding system, designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine.

The PharmaPrinter Aurum was born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent – nearly a third – of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

This compounding, when you combine different ingredients to make tailored medication, is usually done by pharmacists using traditional methods such as a pestle and mortar.

CurifyLabs and Studio Aslak Siimes wanted to create a machine to automate part of this process and enable pharmacists to achieve “system-guaranteed” dosage consistency while eliminating friction in the process.

“To put it simply, the main concept behind Aurum was to reduce the possibility of human error from the compounding workflow and empower the pharmacists to bring high-quality compounded medication to their patients with ease,” Siimes told Dezeen.

The Aurum design is part of a wider ecosystem of products from CurifyLabs, a health tech organization that Studio Aslak Siimes has worked together with for two years.

The machine comes in after a doctor’s prescription arrives and a compounding pharmacist picks the accurate recipe for the prescription, known as a blueprint.

“[The] active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) and excipient base are carefully weighed, mixed and put into a syringe, which is then installed to Aurum’s heating jacket and inserted into the machine,” Siimes remarked.

Recent findings suggest that “We have a patented syringe plunger attachment called gripper, where you simply squeeze a lever and move the gripper against the syringe plunger manually and then release it. It attaches tightly and works as the movement to control the dispensing from the syringe.”.

Blisters for the medication, which are also designed by the studio, are then placed on top of the scale in a dedicated blister holder.

Sources indicate that “The scale handles weight-based quality control,” Siimes explained. “Then you start the print, and it dispenses fully accurate compounded medication in exact dosage quantity and weight.”.

“The print is fast, and a few moments later the ready blisters are removed, sealed and labelled with dosage-specific labelling, and then it is ready for distribution to the patients,” he continued.

“I guess in short: put medication into syringe, put syringe into Aurum, press play and you have ready meds.”.

The machine also has interchangeable modules to let pharmacists create different dosage forms, including tablets, films, suppositories and troches within one system.

Siimes believes that his design is the “only fully working semi-automated compounding ecosystem in the world”, and the product is already on the market and used by compounding pharmacies and hospitals around Europe and North America.

“The technology is already present in 30 states in the USA, and the reception has been highly positive,” Siimes noted.

“From the client base, we hear that we are truly making a difference, and can help them to deliver better products to patients with a system that really works and is easy to operate,” he continued.

“It has been such a lovely thing to notice that all the hard work put into it really translates into positive outcomes.”.

Other healthcare products recently covered on Dezeen include a wearable patch that detects heat exposure and a meter for at-home hormone level readings.

Photography by CurifyLabs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A month after closing its Berlin exhibition space, the Julia Stoschek Foundation, a nonprofit arts organisation set up by the German collector and businesswoman Julia Stoschek, announced it will reopen its Düsseldorf headquarters in April 2027.

The Düsseldorf space closed for renovation in 2025. The inaugural exhibition in the newly revamped space, called Selfish in Bed, is curated by Krist Gruijthuijsen, formerly the director of the KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin will feature works by 43 artists from the foundation’s collection. The foundation’s more than 1,000-piece collection is focused primarily on time-based art—including video, film, moving-image installations, multimedia work, performance, sound work and virtual reality work.

“Seeing the collection continue to grow and welcoming new audiences two decades on brings me enormous joy,” Stoschek remarked in a statement. “And I can think of no better home for it than Düsseldorf, a city where art has been part of everyday life for generations.”.

Stoschek’s Berlin space operated for ten years from June 2016 to October 2026. It hosted 22 exhibitions and drew 500,000 visitors. In April, the foundation said the closure was the result of a “strategic realignment” and that it would “now focus on international projects in order to make the collection accessible to a global audience.”.

The Düsseldorf reopening marks the foundation’s 20th anniversary.

Recent findings suggest that selfish in Bed (10 April 2027-19 December 2027) takes its name from a 2000 self-portrait by Sarah Lucas. Other artists who will feature in the exhibition include Wolfgang Tillmans, Bill Viola, Simon Fujiwara, Rosemarie Trockel and Tracey Emin.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Visitors to the Victoria and Albert Museum in London vacuumed digital dust from an overheating data server in game installation The Server by art and design duo Playfool.
  • Handling a decommissioned data-centre vacuum formerly used in a data centre, players were tasked with vacuuming as much ‘dust’ as possible within 60 seconds from a replica data server.
  • The installation was designed to emulate the unseen physical labour tied to the technological infrastructure underpinning the AI boom, and to evoke the gamified optimisation strategies employed in Amazon fulfilment centres.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography and video by Nico Lejtreger.

Visitors to the Victoria and Albert Museum in London vacuumed digital dust from an overheating data server in game installation The Server by art and design duo Playfool.

Handling a decommissioned data-centre vacuum formerly used in a data centre, players were tasked with vacuuming as much ‘dust’ as possible within 60 seconds from a replica data server.

The installation was designed to emulate the unseen physical labour tied to the technological infrastructure underpinning the AI boom, and to evoke the gamified optimisation strategies employed in Amazon fulfilment centres.

During their visit to one, the design duo “discovered the unique internal video games workers can play to gamify their tasks, displaying real-time performance rankings among peers”.

The Server game emerged as a means of surfacing the often overlooked physical labour that goes into maintaining the ever-expanding material infrastructure fuelled by the rapid growth of AI.

“We often overlook the fact that technologies are based on a material foundation, subject to the forces of an ever-changing environment, and thus requiring constant upkeep after being brought into existence”, Playfool’s Daniel Coppen and Saki Maruyama told Dezeen.

Their installation consists of a replica of technology brand Nvidia’s latest AI server and a vacuum module featuring a set of screens that visualise clouds of digital particulates and rank players’ performance metrics.

It was intended to show that our relationship to the digital world is less frictionless than we might think.

“Behind the frictionless, smooth interfaces on our screens is a messy entanglement with the material world”, the designers added.

Situated amid the priceless antiquities of the V&A, the installation draws a parallel between the hidden human labour that sustains the availability of both a museum’s collections and the digital infrastructure we are increasingly dependent upon.

In this way, the game “serves as a reminder that all creation comes with an infinite responsibility of maintenance”, the designers stated.

“AI has been especially prone to this blind spot, due to both the black box nature of how it works and of the infrastructure behind it, from undersea fibre-optic cables to data centres”, Coppen and Maruyama explained.

With the US set to double its data centre building to keep pace with the boom in AI, and spending on data centre infrastructure projected to top $800 billion per year globally in 2026, the designers hope The Server will help interrogate the responsibilities of care generated by the contemporary AI boom.

Commissioned by the V&A Museum’s Emerging Designer scheme, Playfool intended for The Server installation to help create discussions around AI and digital caregiving such as cleaning and maintenance.

“We believe games are a powerful medium to provoke conversation about these complex topics, crystallising experiences and ideas through introducing latest forms of agency”, Playfool noted.

For more stories related to AI data centres, see this toy from Basrua that emits an “ear piercing hum” when squeezed, this 60-building data centre by Gensler and this East London data centre approved as part of Truman Brewery masterplan.

Sources indicate that the Server exhibition took place from 12 to 18 September at The V&A. For more events in architecture and design, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

Photography and video by Nico Lejtreger.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese electronics company Sony has leaned into 1980s nostalgia with its remake of the original Walkman headphones, complete with colourful, interchangeable foam pads.

The MDR-3R, with its slim headband and sliding metal arms, looks almost exactly like the model that debuted with the first portable Walkman cassette player in 1979.

But the design now comes with a USB-C connector that works with most modern devices, feeding into the growing return to wired headphones.

The original MDR-3s pioneered the idea of modern portable headphones and have inspired a host of copycats – both then and now, as retro on-ear headphones have staged a comeback in recent years.

“The value of wired headphones is being rediscovered for their simplicity, ease of use, and freedom from charging or pairing,” Sony remarked.

The company went back to its archives and stuck close to the lightweight, open-ear design, adding interchangeable blue and orange foam pads and details in recycled plastic.

Sony even replicated the 1979 packaging and reengineered the headphones with the same 23-millimetre driver units to stay true to the original sound – although subtle refinements were apparently made to suit “modern listening preferences”.

On top of the USB-C connector, the product has been updated with a built-in microphone and an inline remote for controlling audio and calls.

Sony has also released a limited-edition version of the MDR-3R with red foam pads and a black headband in collaboration with Netflix‘s Stranger Things, celebrating their “shared 1980s inspiration”.

Retro gadgets have grown increasingly popular in recent years, as Gen Z has rediscovered gadgets such as cassette players, digicams and Tamagotchis.

The trend seems to have grown hand-in-hand with the rise of calm technology, as consumers have grown weary of modern tech.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Tolu Sanusi / Oshinówò Studio unless stated.

The Commonwealth War Graves Commission has unveiled a memorial to the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps in Freetown, Sierra Leone.

Officially opened this weekend, the memorial designed by Oshinówò Studio sits on top of a war memorial designed by British architect Edwin Lutyens in 1931.

While the original memorial honoured soldiers who died in the first world war, it did not include the names of the 946 members of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps – men enlisted to transport supplies and materials – who also died in the war.

Oshinówò Studio extended the Lutyens-designed, stone memorial by adding a structural glass pyramid etched with the names of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps men.

“The Freetown Memorial is conceived through a material symbolism that allows it to resonate across cultures and contexts,” noted Oshinówò Studio founder Tosin Oshinówò.

“The structure we designed is, in effect, an extension of Sir Edwin Lutyens’ existing monument. By following its tapering geometry, the new monument rises higher, elevating the immense volume of names etched into glass. “.

According to Oshinówò, placing the names of the carrier corps men higher than the soldiers was also a symbolic move.

“In this gesture, the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps are symbolically carried by their comrades, reversing the relationship between those who served and those who were served,” she remarked.

“There is a profound irony in this act: it becomes a fitting expression of gratitude to men whose sacrifice was fundamental to shaping the world we inhabit today.”.

Sources indicate that along with the glass pyramid, the memorial also includes a laser beacon that will be illuminated on significant days of remembrance. According to the team, this column of light will be visible from up to five kilometres.

As part of the project, the 1930s memorial was also full restored by stonemasons and bronze specialists from the Commonwealth War Graves Commission.

Recent memorials featured on Dezeen include a “serene and contemplative” memorial to Queen Elizabeth II designed by Foster + Partners and a park in Ethiopia dedicated to the 157 victims of the Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crash.

Industry News: EBBA Architects transforms former agricultural barn in Cornwall into a "calm sanctuary"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Rikard Kahn and Benni Allan.
  • London studio EBBA Architects has updated and extended a house within a converted barn in Cornwall, stripping away previous alterations to create open, pared-back interiors.
  • Topped by a distinctive gambrel roof, the former agricultural barn had already been converted into a dwelling, but also undergone years of incremental, ill-suited adaptations and extensions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Rikard Kahn and Benni Allan.

London studio EBBA Architects has updated and extended a house within a converted barn in Cornwall, stripping away previous alterations to create open, pared-back interiors.

Topped by a distinctive gambrel roof, the former agricultural barn had already been converted into a dwelling, but also undergone years of incremental, ill-suited adaptations and extensions.

EBBA Architects looked to restore the Dutch barn‘s original, open spatial character, expanding its area by almost a third with the addition of a pavilion-like extension that is framed by columns of white stone.

“The overall concept was about finding clarity in the form of the building and finding ways to add in a way that didn’t take away from the original character,” EBBA’s founding director, Benni Allan told Dezeen.

Industry observers note that “Over the years the barn had gathered a series of piecemeal alterations that took away from the original simplicity. Our process involved removing later additions and then adding where felt most appropriate,” he added.

“The house is a place that will act as a place to enjoy the vast contrast of weather throughout the year, while also providing a calm sanctuary and background for family life.”.

The ground-floor plan of Dutch Barn is based on the central position of an existing stair, around which a bathroom and storage core has been built to separate the more open kitchen and living spaces.

A row of full-height openings links the existing barn to its extension, where a long, uninterrupted space containing a skylit dining area and lounge opens out onto a covered colonnade via sliding doors.

“The intention is for the house to be used by the large family, and for there to be a blend between spaces,” Allan explained.

“We are always interested in making flexible arrangements in planform, to accommodate different ways of living.”.

The home’s interior finishes were also guided by ideas of simplification, with plaster walls, concrete floors and gridded white-painted timber ceilings.

EBBA Architects wanted to emphasise material junctions, as seen in a newly introduced oak column in the kitchen, which has been rotated to highlight where it meets the flitch plates that connect it to the exposed ceiling beams.

Externally, this theme was extended into the design of the extension’s roof, which stops short of the edge of the stone columns to emphasise the point where the two meet.

The existing barn was clad in reused cedar shingles that were replaced where necessary, while the extension was built using white stone masonry that references the walls on the adjacent street.

“At first glance the house presents itself as a simple barn, but we like that a series of quite serious architectural moves have been complemented with some playful elements, such as the exaggeration of the junctions and the contrast between textured columns and clear, almost gallery-like floors,” explained Allan.

“We wanted the projecting roof and latest columns to read as an independent object that reaches out into the garden and takes up the change in level, rather than as a continuation of the barn,” he added.

EBBA Architects has previously completed a cafe in Marylebone with clay plaster walls and an illuminated glass ceiling, and an apartment in London for its founder that is lined with Douglas fir.

Photography by Rikard Kahn and Benni Allan.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (776 w)

Venice exhibition tells the story of the man who brought together contemporary artists and Murano’s master glassblowers

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1952, Egidio Costantini, an entrepreneur based in Venice, had a brainwave: to take the designs of contemporary artists and, with the collaboration of master glassblowers on the island of Murano, to make artistic sculptures in glass.
  • It has been revealed that three years later, Costantini established the Fucina degli Angeli gallery to exhibit the results of his experiment.
  • Recent findings suggest that an exhibition opening at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice this month, curated by the art historian Cristina Beltrami, will tell the Fucina’s story from the 1950s to the 1980s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1952, Egidio Costantini, an entrepreneur based in Venice, had a brainwave: to take the designs of contemporary artists and, with the collaboration of master glassblowers on the island of Murano, to make artistic sculptures in glass. This was a different approach from that adopted by traditional furnaces like Venini in their decorative glassware, which, although it increasingly involved international designers, was often produced in large, commercially dictated series.

It has been revealed that three years later, Costantini established the Fucina degli Angeli gallery to exhibit the results of his experiment. From then until the 1970s, when other glassmaking companies began to compete, Costantini played a pioneering role in the evolution of glass in Venice, acting as interpreter for more than 100 international artists to Murano’s master glassblowers.

Recent findings suggest that an exhibition opening at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice this month, curated by the art historian Cristina Beltrami, will tell the Fucina’s story from the 1950s to the 1980s. It will also examine the little-documented but vital role played behind the scenes by Peggy Guggenheim herself, whose purchase of many items helped sustain the gallery financially and whose connections enabled Costantini to exhibit his glass across Europe and even in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. (As it happens, the collector is also the focus of an exhibition opening this month at the Royal Academy of Arts in London, about her Mayfair gallery of the late 1930s—Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector, 21 November-14 March 2027.).

Industry observers note that more than 100 works, including glass, painting and sculpture, will be on display in Venice, as well as material from the Fucina’s archives, which have never before been studied in depth. These will be exhibited in 11 rooms organised by artist and theme, and will include glass translations of works by many luminaries of the period, from Max Ernst and Oskar Kokoschka to Lucio Fontana and Paul Jenkins.

Peggy Guggenheim among her glass artworks and guests at Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, Venice, in 1964 © Getty Images, by SIAE 2026.

In a recent development, born in Brindisi in the south of Italy in 1912, Costantini established himself permanently in Venice, where he had been raised and educated, at the beginning of the 1950s. There he became a commercial agent for several of Murano’s glassworks. It was the time of Italy’s post-war economic boom and the city was teeming with creative energy. Costantini seems to have found no difficulty in assembling a group of Venetian artists to form the Study Centre for Painters in the Art of Glass, a collective that exhibited its work at the furnace of Ferro & Lazzarini in 1953.

Recent findings suggest that the next step was to involve international artists of even greater stature. Acting on his own initiative, Costantini had glass versions made of some ceramic sculptures by Pablo Picasso and then travelled to Picasso’s house in Vallauris, near Cannes, to show him the results. In return, Picasso gave Costantini a copy of the book Faunes et Nymphes de Pablo Picasso (1952). This survives in the archives with markings on the images of ceramic figures that were later reinterpreted as glass sculptures at the Fucina. But who made the markings remains a mystery.

The name “Fucina degli Angeli” (smithy of the angels) was proposed by the French writer and artist Jean Cocteau, a long-term friend and collaborator, apparently in reference to Costantini’s large family. The Austrian Expressionist artist Kokoschka contributed an emblematic sketch of two angels holding up an anvil, which he dedicated to the gallery and its founder, “who first succeeded in making me fascinated with the glass of Murano”.

Max Ernst’s King (Re) and Queen (Regina), both from 1964 © Max Ernst, by SIAE 2026.

Cocteau enjoyed designing extravagant mythological heads for the Fucina, as well as visiting the furnaces and discussing his ideas with the maestri. Both he and Jean Arp, the German sculptor and painter whose work also features in the exhibition, were “seduced by the colour” of glass and its richness, Beltrami says.

Sources indicate that the results, though, may not have pleased everyone. The Swiss artist Walter Bodmer allowed his sketch Asymmetric Cat (1955) to be transformed into an oversimplified glass vessel. But after this, for reasons unknown, he never participated again.

The exhibition looks set to offer a fascinating insight into a very personal approach to collaborations between artist and craftsman, as well as an evocative record of an under-appreciated chapter in Venetian history.

• Fucina degli Angeli: Peggy Guggenheim and 20th-Century Artistic Glass, Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Venice, 14 November-29 March 2027.
