Recent findings suggest that sneaks is often the highlight of Adobe MAX, giving the brand an opportunity to share the exciting innovations it's working on. Among the wild Adobe Sneaks announced today, one tool in particular could be game-changing for a whole host of creatives, from illustrators to concept artists, marking an exciting upcoming era for the brand.

Sources indicate that project Link Up is set to revolutionise vector design, turning the simple dragging function into context-aware fusion that automatically matches a scene's perspective. (TLDR: constantly redrawing objects at newly introduced viewing angles could soon be a thing of the past).

To understand more about Project Link Up, I caught up with Hailin Jin, senior principal scientist and research lead for imaging and design at Adobe, to get his behind-the-scenes insight into the work.

Sources indicate that mohit and the team started with an observation about an everyday gesture: dragging an object. Design tools usually interpret that as an instruction about placement, but there’s much more intent in what a designer moves, where they move it and how they move it.Placing an illustrated car into a parking space, for example, can involve separately adjusting its perspective, scale and style. The team asked whether the gesture itself could communicate more of that creative direction and help adapt the object to its surroundings, while keeping the result editable.

Yes. In our current prototype, a creativity slider lets the designer guide how subtle or expressive the adaptation should be, from preserving more of the original form to exploring a more dramatic transformation.The goal is to combine the ease of a gesture with explicit creative control. The resulting vector artwork remains editable, so designers can continue refining it.

In a recent development, two contrasting styles don’t necessarily need to become one. The key is understanding the creator’s intent: should the object match the scene, retain its own personality, or create a deliberate contrast?Project Link Up explores combining the drag gesture and scene context with creative controls and prompt guidance. A designer could specify “match the scene’s illustration style” or “keep this character’s style, but adapt its perspective and lighting.”The aim is to help designers steer the relationship between elements, while keeping the resulting vector artwork editable.

The philosophy is to make creative exploration more immediate. When combining two elements requires substantial adjustment before you can judge whether an idea works, that effort can interrupt the process of discovery.Link Up explores how a familiar gesture could let designers try different relationships between objects, see what happens and develop the ideas they find interesting. Keeping the result editable as vector artwork matters: a promising combination becomes something the designer can continue shaping.

A strong example is manually reworking an asset to fit a new scene, particularly redrawing it from a different perspective. The team is exploring how that adaptation could happen as the designer places the object. That could reduce the preparation needed to evaluate a composition and give designers more time to refine the creative decisions that make it work.

In a recent development, A major direction in our research is helping tools understand creative content and the relationships within it. That understanding can make interactions more meaningful: moving an object into a scene could communicate an intention about perspective or composition, rather than simply a newly introduced position.For experienced designers, the opportunity is to express their judgment more directly and retain precise control over the result. Link Up explores one part of that future. We want to learn what creators expect a gesture to mean and how tools can respond in ways that feel useful and predictable.

ZAV Architects extends house in Iran with ombre "architectural limbs"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Parham Taghioff unless otherwise stated.
  • A series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue on this home extension on the outskirts of Tehran, designed by Iranian studio ZAV Architects.
  • Named Golmorad, the colourful extension transforms the residence from a weekend villa, originally designed by Iranian studio Firouz Firouz, into a permanent home in the town of Kouhsar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Parham Taghioff unless otherwise stated.

A series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue on this home extension on the outskirts of Tehran, designed by Iranian studio ZAV Architects.

Named Golmorad, the colourful extension transforms the residence from a weekend villa, originally designed by Iranian studio Firouz Firouz, into a permanent home in the town of Kouhsar.

ZAV Architects‘ intervention extends both ends of the home into three adjacent orchard plots acquired by the client.

Constructed from masonry, the extension is coated in plaster to blend in with the earthen exterior of the original home, while its curved geometries set it apart from its predecessor.

Aiming to appear as if organically growing from the home, Golmorad emerges as a series of overlapping arched roofs.

At one end, the vaulted extension branches into two curved forms that gradually decrease in height – one wing containing a bedroom and ensuite, and the other an open-plan kitchen, living and dining room that opens onto an outdoor pool.

Openings between the overlapping roof planes let light into the home’s interior.

“Rather than approaching the extension as either a replication of the original structure or a distinctly separate addition, the project explores a third possibility: an architecture that emerges from within the existing building itself,” ZAV Architects told Dezeen.

“This intervention can be understood as a process of grafting, in which latest needs and aspirations are grafted onto the existing body of the villa, giving rise to new architectural limbs that branch out and grow from it,” it continued.

“It is as though the original building, while retaining its underlying architectural logic rooted in thick-earth construction, has developed newly introduced and distinct organs of its own.”.

ZAV Architects created a gradient effect across the building with terracotta tones fading into blue, intending to strengthen the appearance of the extension growing from the home.

“The uniform colour of the original villa develops into a chromatic spectrum that radiates outward from the existing core towards the newly formed branches,” the studio stated.

“This transition makes the process of transformation visible, with each segmented shell expressing a distinct stage in the building’s evolution.”.

Golmorad is shortlisted in the house extension category of this year’s Dezeen Awards. It recently won the awards’ public vote alongside a playground also designed by ZAV Architects.

Last year, ZAV Architects was among the winners of the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the Majara Residence and Community Redevelopment, a colourful domed cultural retreat on the Iranian island of Hormuz.

Photography by Parham Taghioff unless otherwise stated.

#254. How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

📅 2026-08-07 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Recent findings suggest that most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again. It does its job, the tests pass, and we move on. But the web platform keeps moving too, and a surprising number of the libraries sitting in your package.json today are now built into the browser.

Recent findings suggest that in a typical mid-sized JavaScript app, you can often find somewhere between 60KB and 90KB (minified and gzipped) of dependencies that the platform can now handle on its own. Date and number formatting, HTTP requests, modals, tooltips, deep cloning, grouping arrays: these were all real gaps a few years ago. A lot of them aren’t gaps anymore.

The reason those libraries stick around isn’t laziness. It’s that most teams don’t re-audit their dependencies on a Baseline cadence, or are simply not aware of how fast browsers are shipping these days. You check npm audit for security, but is this library still doing something the browser can’t? is a question that rarely gets asked. So the libraries stay.

Sources indicate that in this article, we’ll run that audit together. Instead of going through dependencies one by one, we’ll work in clusters, because the wins tend to come in groups. We’ll do the bundle math, build a small decision framework you can reuse, and stay honest about the cases where the platform still falls short. By the end, you’ll have a repeatable process you can run on your own package.json.

Before we start deleting things, let’s promptly recap what Baseline is. Feel free to skip this section if you’re already familiar.

Baseline is a project from the WebDX Community Group that tells you, in plain terms, how safe a web feature is to use across the major browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari). A feature can be in one of three states:.

Sources indicate that that 30-month gap between “Newly” and “Widely” matters a lot for this audit. A feature that’s Widely available is something you can usually drop a library for today. A feature that’s only Newly available is something you can drop a library for if you check your audience first, or if you’re comfortable with a small feature check. We’ll treat those two cases differently throughout.

Sources indicate that you can look any feature up on webstatus.dev, on MDN (every reference page reveals a Baseline badge near the top), or programmatically with the web-features npm package. We’ll use all three later when we run the audit on a real project.

In a recent development, it’s tempting to read “the browser does this now” and start ripping libraries out. Let’s not do that. A swap that looks free on paper can quietly break things for a chunk of your owners, or cost you a feature you were relying on without realizing it.

According to recent reports, so before dropping any library, ask three questions. We’ll reuse these in every cluster below.

Sources indicate that 1. Is the replacement Baseline-safe for my audience?

Not “is it Baseline” in the abstract, but “is it safe for the people who actually use my app.” If the native feature is Widely available, this is usually a yes. If it’s only Newly available, check your analytics or your browserslist config and see what share of your owners would miss out. A B2B dashboard where everyone’s on the latest browser is a very different situation from a public-facing site with a long tail of old Android devices.

2. What does the swap actually cost?

Dropping a library isn’t always free. Sometimes the native feature isn’t supported widely enough yet, so you’d reach for a polyfill. If that polyfill is heavier than the library you’re removing, you’ve made your bundle bigger, unless you load it conditionally. We’ll see exactly this with Temporal later.

It has been revealed that 3. Does the platform feature cover my real use case?

Libraries often do more than the platform feature they resemble. axios isn’t just fetch with automatic JSON parsing; it has interceptors, request cancellation, and retries. If you’re using those, a straight swap to fetch will leave you reimplementing them. Check what you actually use before assuming it’s a drop-in replacement.

Sources indicate that keep these three in mind. Every cluster below is really just these questions applied to a different corner of your dependencies.

This is the cluster where you’ll usually find the most KBs sitting on top of features that are already Widely available. The browser ships a whole family of formatting tools under the Intl namespace, and a lot of small, popular libraries became unnecessary.

Here are the usual suspects and what replaces them:.

Let’s walk through some of them.

It has been revealed that timeago.js exists to turn a timestamp into “3 hours ago”. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat does the same thing, and it’s Baseline Widely available.

The numeric: "auto" option is the nice touch here: it gives you “yesterday” instead of “1 day ago” where the language has a word for it. You pass a number and a unit, and you get a localized string back.

You may be wondering about the one thing timeago.js does that this snippet doesn’t: it picks the unit for you. Given a date, timeago.js decides whether to say “seconds” or “days.” Intl.RelativeTimeFormat expects you to do that part. It’s a few lines of arithmetic (work out the difference, find the largest unit that fits), and once you’ve written that helper, you don’t need the library anymore.

Intl.NumberFormat covers most of what number-formatting libraries do: thousands separators, currency, percentages, and compact notation.

And Intl.ListFormat, Widely available, handles the “join an array into a sentence” problem, including the Oxford comma, which is the kind of thing people write fiddly helper functions for:.

In a recent development, humanize-duration turns a number of milliseconds into “1 hour, 30 minutes”. The platform equivalent is Intl.DurationFormat:.

Recent findings suggest that one thing to keep in mind is that Intl.DurationFormat is Baseline Newly available at the time of writing, not Widely available. It landed in all the major engines in March 2025, and it’s on track to become Widely available in 2027. So this one fails question 1 for broad-audience apps unless you check your traffic first or add a fallback. For an internal tool on modern browsers, it’s fine today. For a public site with old devices, give it another year or guard it with a feature check.

According to recent reports, if your app uses the full set (humanize-duration, timeago.js, pluralize, numeral), that’s roughly 14 KB gzipped of dependencies, most of it replaceable right now with Widely available APIs. The internationalization cluster is usually the easiest win in the whole audit.

This cluster is more nuanced, so it’s a good one to slow down on.

The browser HTTP libraries people reach for are axios (17 KB gz) and superagent (19 KB gz). For most requests, fetch plus AbortController covers what you need, and both are Widely available.

In a recent development, the one extra line (res.json()) is fetch being explicit where axios was implicit. That’s the pattern across this whole cluster: fetch does less for you by default, and you decide whether you want the things it leaves out.

Industry observers note that axios has a timeout option. fetch has AbortSignal.timeout():.

This is where question 3 does most of the work, so let’s be specific about the gaps:.

In a recent development, I personally heavily rely on interceptors in my interactive online courses, such as Learn JavaScript, and I have solved that for years using a custom class on top of fetch. I’ve shipped this to millions of customers and have seen lots of success with it.

Industry observers note that none of these are hard to rebuild, and most apps only use one or two of them. But this is exactly the kind of cluster where you shouldn’t do a blind find-and-replace. Look at how you actually use your HTTP client first. If it’s plain GETs and POSTs, dropping axios for a thin fetch wrapper saves you about 17 KB gzipped.

This cluster has some of the most satisfying swaps, because the platform features don’t just match the libraries, they’re often more accessible than what teams ship by hand.

The libraries here are modal dialogs (something like a11y-dialog, 1.8 KB gz), tooltip and popover libraries (tippy.js, 14 KB gz, which bundles Popper for positioning), focus-trap (6.6 KB gz), and body-scroll-lock (1.3 KB gz). They get replaced by three platform features: the element, the Popover API, and CSS anchor positioning.

A huge amount of modal-related code exists to solve accessibility problems: trapping focus inside the modal, closing on Escape, restoring focus to the previous element when the dialog is closed, and rendering above everything else. The element, Widely available, does all of that for you.

According to recent reports, calling showModal() does the work that focus-trap was installed for: focus moves into the dialog, the rest of the page becomes inert so you can’t tab out of it, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the element that opened it. The dialog renders in the browser’s Top layer, so you don’t fight z-index. You also get a ::backdrop pseudo-element to style the overlay.

That single element can replace your modal library and focus-trap. The one piece it doesn’t handle on its own is locking the background from scrolling, which is what body-scroll-lock was for. That’s now one line of CSS:.

Sources indicate that if you’re wondering why we’re using dialog:modal instead of dialog[open], it’s because the open attribute is set as soon as you call show(), but the dialog isn’t actually modal so you don’t want to lock scrolling yet. The :modal pseudo-class is only true when the dialog is actually modal, which is the case when you call showModal().

So three libraries collapse into one element and one CSS rule.

For things that aren’t full modals (dropdown menus, tooltips, the small floating panels that tippy.js handles), the Popover API gives you light-dismiss behavior, top-layer rendering, and Escape-to-close with no JavaScript at all:.

It has been revealed that clicking the button toggles the popover. Clicking outside it closes it. It’s Baseline Newly available (since January 2025).

The other half of what a tooltip library does is positioning: keeping the floating element pinned to its trigger and flipping it when it would overflow the viewport. That’s what Popper (bundled inside tippy.js) handles, and it’s now a CSS feature called anchor positioning. Here it pins the same #menu popover directly under its trigger button:.

Anchor positioning is the newest feature in this article. It became Baseline Newly available in January 2026, when Firefox 147 shipped it (Chrome had it since version 125, and Safari since version 26). Because it’s this fresh, it’s squarely a question-1 feature: great for modern audiences, but check your traffic, and note that some of the more advanced parts (like position-try fallbacks) have uneven support across versions. Keep a sensible fallback for older browsers.

Between , the Popover API, and anchor positioning, the UI primitives cluster (tooltip library, modal library, focus-trap, body-scroll-lock) adds up to roughly 24 KB gzipped, and you come out the other side with better accessibility defaults than most hand-rolled solutions.

Sources indicate that lodash is rarely imported whole anymore, but its individual functions show up everywhere, either as the full lodash package (25 KB gz) or as standalone installs like lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby. Several of the most common ones now have direct platform equivalents.

According to recent reports, lodash.groupby reorganizes an array into an object keyed by some property. Object.groupBy does exactly that:.

There’s also Map.groupBy for when you want a Map instead of a plain object (handy if your keys aren’t strings). Both are Baseline Newly available, since March 2024, and on track to become Widely available in late 2026.

Industry observers note that lodash.clonedeep makes a deep copy of an object. structuredClone is the platform version, and it’s Widely available:.

structuredClone handles the tricky cases that trip up JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...)): it clones Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, and circular references correctly. The limit to know about (question 3 again) is that it can’t clone functions, DOM nodes, or class instances; it throws on functions and drops the prototype on class instances. For plain data, which is what most people deep-clone, it’s a clean replacement.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever pulled in a Lodash helper for union, intersection, or difference, the Set object now has these built in. They’re Baseline Newly available, since June 2024:.

The full set of methods is union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, and isDisjointFrom.

Sources indicate that not all of Lodash has moved into the platform. debounce and throttle still have no native equivalent, and they’re genuinely useful, so cherry-picking lodash.debounce is reasonable. The point of this cluster isn’t “delete Lodash,” it’s “stop shipping the parts the browser already has.” Dropping lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby alone is about 8 KB gzipped, and if you were importing the full lodash for a handful of functions, replacing the platform-covered ones can let you drop it entirely.

Every cluster so far has ended in “go ahead, drop it.” This one is the opposite, and that’s why it’s worth including: it demonstrates the framework telling you to wait.

Temporal is the long-awaited replacement for JavaScript’s Date, and it’s a genuinely better API: immutable objects, sane time zone handling, and no more month indexes starting at zero. It reached TC39 Stage 4 in March 2026 and is part of the ES2026 specification. Firefox shipped it in version 139 (in 2025), and Chrome shipped it in version 144 (January 2026). Safari hasn’t shipped it in a stable release yet; it’s in Safari Technology Preview, with stable support expected later in 2026.

If Temporal is news to you, check out the Temporal Cheatsheet for a quick overview of the API and a comparison to Date.

However, Temporal is not Baseline. It’s still in limited availability, because Safari people don’t have it. To use it across all browsers today, you need a polyfill, and this is where the math turns against you.

Recent findings suggest that the official @js-temporal/polyfill is about 44 KB gzipped. There’s a smaller polyfill that internally does not depend on BigInt and it weighs 19 KB gzipped. A lightweight date library like dayjs is about 3 KB gzipped. So if you swap dayjs for Temporal plus its polyfill right now, you’re not saving 3 KB, you’re adding roughly 41 KB to your bundle, unless you are able to load the polyfill conditionally.

Industry observers note that the verdict is generally clear: keep dayjs (or date-fns) for now. The moment to revisit is when Safari ships Temporal in a stable release and it reaches Baseline. At that point you can use Temporal natively and conditionally load the polyfill for people on older browsers. This is a feature to write down and check again in a few months, not one to act on today.

Recent findings suggest that the clusters above are a starting map, but your dependencies are your own. Here’s a repeatable process you can run this quarter.

Start by listing what actually ships to owners:.

For a quick per-package number, Bundlephobia gives you the minified and gzipped size of any npm package. For the real picture (what each dependency costs in your actual bundle, after tree-shaking and deduplication), run a bundle analyzer against your build. npx source-map-explorer works on most bundles, and npx vite-bundle-visualizer works for Vite projects.

In a recent development, for each candidate, find the platform feature that would replace it and check its Baseline status. The quickest way is webstatus.dev or the Baseline badge on the feature’s MDN page.

According to recent reports, for each library with a platform replacement, go back to the framework: Is it Baseline-safe for your audience? What does the swap cost? Does the feature cover how you actually use the library? Most of your decisions will fall out of question 1 (check the feature’s status against your browserslist) and question 3 (check your own usage).

Recent findings suggest that for Widely available features, swap and move on. For Newly available ones, either confirm your audience is on modern browsers or guard the fresh code with a quick feature check and keep a fallback:.

That way you ship less code to the people who can run it, without breaking the ones who can’t.

In a recent development, add the clusters up, and the picture is concrete. The internationalization cluster is around 14 KB gzipped, HTTP is around 17 KB, the UI primitives are around 24 KB, and the Lodash utilities are 8 KB or more depending on how much of the library you were shipping. For a typical mid-sized app, that’s somewhere between 60 KB and 90 KB gzipped of dependencies you can hand back to the platform, and more if you were shipping the full lodash or several of these libraries at once. (The uncompressed numbers are two to three times larger, which is what you’ll see in a bundle analyzer before gzip.).

Recent findings suggest that I’ve chosen relatively lean packages for most of these features, but some individual packages could still be heavy. Your dialog package, for instance, could alone weigh as much as 50KB gzipped depending on what you’re using.

A few features are worth keeping an eye on over the next year, because they’ll open up further swaps:.

In a recent development, none of this is a one-time cleanup. The platform ships new features constantly, and the gap between “you need a library for this” and “the browser does this” keeps closing. The habit worth building is small: once a quarter, run the audit. List your dependencies, check what’s now Baseline, and hand back what you can.

Pick one cluster from this article, open your package.json, and see how much of it the browser already does for you.

Bát Tràng Museum

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Bát Tràng Museum stands as the first private museum authorized by the government within Bát Tràng Village, founded by National Artist Vũ Đức Thắng.
  • Sources indicate that we carefully researched and studied to include his unique artistic techniques and style in creating a fresh look for the museum.
  • The brand’s visual system was created to resonate with the beauty of the various unique artworks while systematizing them into an archive through a fresh, clean photography style.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Bát Tràng Museum stands as the first private museum authorized by the government within Bát Tràng Village, founded by National Artist Vũ Đức Thắng. Originally named “Hồn Đất Việt” — translated as “Viet’s Ceramic Soul” — this museum embodies his remarkable legacy. Vũ Đức Thắng gained widespread recognition for his spectacular creation of 12 remarkably genuine pottery boots, earning the Guinness Record in 2013. His artistic skills include a collection of modern artworks highlighted by two unique techniques: color-changing ceramic glaze and intricate three-dimensional sculpting. These methods display his mastery and creativity in ceramic art.

Sources indicate that we carefully researched and studied to include his unique artistic techniques and style in creating a fresh look for the museum. This involved giving the museum a new name and creating a unique custom typeface MN Vũ Thắng with “pottery-shoes-soul” inktrap touches. We wanted to echo his process and masterpieces into the content system.

The brand’s visual system was created to resonate with the beauty of the various unique artworks while systematizing them into an archive through a fresh, clean photography style. A deliberate pottery silhouette canvas was employed for buttons and patterns across different applications, maintaining a unique and relative aesthetic. This design approach bonded to a grid system inspired by the 3-parts floor blueprint layout of the museum, ensuring consistency and structure throughout the brand’s visual elements.

In a recent development, we simplified the color palette, emphasizing the vividness and authenticity of the artwork, especially the rich colors and textures of the ceramic glaze. This focused approach highlights the authentic essence of each piece, elevating their visual impact while preserving their nature.

Collaboratively, we aimed to assemble the Bát Tràng Museum towards a more contemporary style while preserving its rich heritage.

When front-end developers and UX engineers are tasked with building a web interface that feels tactile, bouncy, or destructive, the industry instinct is almost always the same: reach for a physics engine. Frameworks like Matter.js, Cannon.js, or custom WebGL solutions have become the gold standard for creating immersive, gamified websites.

When our team at Isadora Agency set out to build Stress Release, a digital stress-relief squeeze toy designed to let burnt-out creatives smash, stretch, and distort animated UI characters, we initially explored that route. The goal was to build a highly tactile experience where every click yielded a satisfying, squishy reaction.

But as we began prototyping, we realized something crucial: Physics engines produce plausible motion, but in our case, the animators produced intentional motion.

We didn’t need our characters to act like realistic rubber balls bouncing uncontrollably around a canvas. We needed them to react in very specific, highly designed ways. So, we scrapped the physics engine entirely.

In this article, we’ll break down how we built a real-time stress-relief squeeze toy without a single line of WebGL or Matter.js, relying entirely on programmatic Lottie state controls, DOM manipulation, and distance-based math.

Recent findings suggest that our core requirement for Stress Release was absolute deterministic control. Our animators had crafted bespoke .json Lottie files that required exact, frame-by-frame sequencing.

It has been revealed that for instance, our ‘mega squeeze’ reaction required a precise 181-frame build-up followed by a specific release sequence. To honor this design, we needed an architecture that wouldn’t overwrite the animators’ crafted keyframes with algorithmic approximations.

It has been revealed that the tighter the click-feedback loop (click → squish → score), the more you need deterministic frame control. By choosing programmatic state control using Lottie’s native API, we ensured that the interaction layer acted as a flawless trigger for the animation layer.

Because our architecture relied on Lottie and the standard DOM, rendering is handled directly by the Lottie runtime, which plays the JSON-based vector animations as SVGs internally. We selected elements directly by ID and CSS class, driving their behavior using a combination of Lottie animation segments, CSS transforms, and click-event math.

It has been revealed that to achieve a deeply satisfying “tactile feel” upon hitting a character, we used radial input mapping. The first step was converting the click from page coordinates into the character’s local coordinate space.

Every click was measured against the character’s center point, then translated into score, feedback intensity, and explosion placement:.

Then we calculate the straight-line distance from the center of the click using the Pythagorean theorem:.

That single number drives everything: the score, the feedback intensity, and where the explosion animation appears:.

The result is a concentric zone system — a perfect circle of scoring rings around the character’s center, similar to a dartboard. The visual complexity of the Lottie SVG is completely irrelevant to hit detection; the hitbox is always a clean circle. Critically, the explosion Lottie animation is repositioned to (a, b) — the same vector used for scoring, so it always appears exactly where the player clicked. This spatial accuracy creates the tactile “I hit that” sensation entirely through math and DOM positioning.

According to recent reports, because the experience used DOM-managed SVG elements, desktop clicks and mobile taps could be handled directly through native event listeners. This avoided extra raycasting or coordinate remapping layers, while keeping the interaction model aligned with how the animations were rendered.

Recent findings suggest that since the game requires a visual reaction at a specific point, Lottie handles all the squish and bounce feelings internally through its animation curves. Each character has a defined set of animation sections (idle loops, reaction frames, and end states) stored as frame ranges. When a click lands, we jump directly to the exact segment that matches the current game state:.

On every click, we advance through the play order and fire the next segment:.

When the segment completes, control returns to the idle loop:.

And for the mega squeeze build-up, the bar loops on a specific frame range until triggered:.

According to recent reports, another major factor in our architectural decision was responsive behavior. Because we built Stress Release in the DOM, we bypassed the complexities of scaling bounding boxes and collision vectors across different devices.

We handled responsive resizing entirely through CSS variables. By recalculating CSS custom properties on every resize, the layout simply reacts to the updated variables, and the Lottie SVGs scale naturally inside their containers without losing their state:.

While this architecture gave us total control over the art direction, it introduced a different challenge: file size.

Industry observers note that lottie JSON files can be heavy. We had 21 different character animations, plus multiple explosion variants that all needed to load. To ensure the experience remained fluid — especially on mobile devices — we implemented a few aggressive optimization strategies:.

When determining the stack for a gamified web experience, it is critical to let the design requirements dictate the technology.

It has been revealed that because our interactions required bespoke, highly controlled visual reactions, we opted for programmatic state control over emergent simulation. This decision empowered the animators to dictate the exact feel of the experience, leaving the code to do what it does best: listen, calculate, and trigger.

By mapping Lottie’s native timeline capabilities to the DOM, you can deliver incredibly rich, tactile user experiences while maintaining absolute control over the art direction.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Under the curator Ekow Eshun, the upcoming 13th edition of the Site Santa Fe International Biennial, There Are Other Worlds (11 June 2027-10 January 2028), will aim to reflect how artists open up new ways of understanding the world, potentially inspiring connection and kinship amid the complexity of our times. The exhibition’s citywide programming will span more than six venues, bringing together more than 40 artists from over 15 countries. The biennial is due to include new commissions by the US artists Cauleen Smith, Sanford Biggers and Edgar Arceneaux, the New Mexico-based Diné artist Raven Chacon and the Canadian artist Lotus Kang.

Founded in 1995, Site Santa Fe is one of the US’s key contemporary art events, showcasing international artists while building on Fresh Mexico’s history and social fabric. Eshun—who chairs the Fourth Plinth in London’s Trafalgar Square and is the curator of the touring British Art Show 10: A Chorus of Strangers (touring the UK until June 2028)—is drawing inspiration from the region.

“New Mexico has a layered history, including colonial settlements, but also in the 20th century it had artistic communities that found something here that allowed them to think with expansiveness,” Eshun tells The Art Newspaper. “It is the site of settlement, world-making and self-discovery.”.

Site Santa Fe, Marlene Nathan Meyerson Auditorium entrance Photo: Shayla Blatchford, 2024; courtesy Site Santa Fe.

It has been revealed that beyond Newly introduced Mexico, Eshun’s vision explores how artists challenge, interpret and shape reality. “We live in a time of divisiveness, uncertainty, inequality and environmental crisis,” he says. “I am inspired by how, in contrast, artists hold complexity and contradictions, inviting us to look beyond binary positions and consider other ways of seeing the world.” These might include imaginative, psychological, emotional and sensory worlds.

The sprawling exhibition is structured into three sections, the curator explains, conceived as “interlocking territories”. The first, “Worlds Beyond”, explores sensory and psychological perception, drawing on the legacy of the Transcendental Painting Group that was active in Fresh Mexico in the 1930s and 40s. “I am interested in how artists look beyond the physical world and can be inspired to think metaphysically, psychologically and emotionally,” Eshun states. He cites the participating Danish Icelandic artist Olafur Eliasson, who thinks with scientific precision while creating works that have both sensorial and emotional impacts.

The exhibition’s second section,“Worlds in Common”, draws on Fresh Mexico’s history of utopian settlements to explore “how artworks may enable us to move beyond hierarchies of power or status and conjure connection or kinship, finding imaginative ways in which we can relate to each other”, Eshun says. He cites the work of Chacon as an example, which uncovers histories of displacement in the Americas, but also turns to connection and memory as routes to reimagining assertions of place.

Tavares Strachan's Black Madonna (Louise Little and Malcolm X) (2022) Courtesy the artist and Perrotin. Photo: Claire Dorn; courtesy Site Santa Fe.

The exhibition’s third section,“Worlds Alive”, will focus on interactions with nature, considering “the planet as a living territory where all the creatures may have a say in how we live collectively”, Eshun claims. He is particularly interested in artists who imagine a relationship with the planet beyond extractivism and grounded in connection across organisms. The participating Colombian artist Delcy Morelos, for instance, reflects on the earth as a physical and ethical territory and a space for aesthetic adventure.

The line-up of participating artists, spanning generations and geographies, reflects the curator’s intention to create a locally rooted biennial with an international scope. “The biennial exists in conversation, not isolation,” Eshun says, adding that community programming will be key. Nearly half the artists are from the US, including Arthur Jafa and Nan Goldin, while five, such as the Indigenous artists Rose B. Simpson and Cannupa Hanska Luger, are based in New Mexico. The exhibition will also include a large contingent of international participants, such as Louise Giovanelli (UK), John Akomfrah (Ghana/UK), Sandra Vásquez de la Horra (Chile), Shilpa Gupta (India) and Tavares Strachan (Bahamas), among others.

In a recent development, while touching on pressing complications, Eshun hopes the biennial will also carry a sense of possibility, empathy and even optimism. Artists, he says, “offer no answers but may open new ways to see, imagine and engage with the present”.

Breaking: Newly introduced EU Guidelines For AI Labelling

📅 2026-08-13 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • It has been revealed that there’s been a lot of confusion and panic this week about “huge fines”, “drastic measures” and “sweeping new AI rules” in the EU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that there’s been a lot of confusion and panic this week about “huge fines”, “drastic measures” and “sweeping new AI rules” in the EU. In reality, it’s a lot more narrow — and a lot more sensible. And mostly it’s about making AI more obvious when it actually needs to be obvious — especially for AI-generated content.

Starting from Aug 2, 2026, AI labelling is a legal requirement for any manufacturer that serves EU citizens. And similar to European Accessibility Act, it’s not limited to EU companies. It affects any company worldwide with EU operations as long as their AI output is used by people in the EU. Let’s see what exactly it means for us.

The goal of AI labelling is to help everyone exposed to AI content to recognize, in a clear and distinguishable way, that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

According to Article 50(4) of the AI Act, AI labelling applies to:.

It has been revealed that both providers (who build or supply the AI system) and deployers (who use it) carry legal obligations. Similar to GDPR and EAA, a company doesn’t escape Article 50 just because it licensed an external AI tool from a third party.

However, it doesn’t mean that all AI-generated content must be explicitly labelled.

Recent findings suggest that beyond the use cases above, pretty much everything else — the vast majority of AI-assisted work — simply isn’t covered by new transparency rules. Most notably, the disclosure obligation does not apply where the AI-generated text has been reviewed and edited by a human, with a named person or entity taking editorial responsibility for it.

Industry observers note that some confusion circles around what exactly “public interest” means, where it starts and where it ends. On its own, it refers to health, safety, environment, economy, finances, politics, science, or culture. If AI-generated product claims touch upon them, the disclosure rule applies.

Sources indicate that some law firms recommend labelling realistic AI-generated illustrations or photos as a precaution for advertising, marketing and other commercial content. AI-generated product illustrations, photos, or posters do need a disclosure, as long as they resemble a real person, place, object, or event.

Industry observers note that but at which point does edited AI content stop being AI content? When a form is pre-filled with AI, but then a user edits it, is it still AI? EU Commission’s guidance is a little fuzzy. Small assistive edits — spellcheck, grammar, formatting, cropping, colour correction, and AI-generated translation — don’t count as AI generation.

Sources indicate that AI-generated summaries, composite imagery, substantive rewrites, or adding and removing elements from a photo are considered AI generation. In practice, fine-tuning a sentence a person wrote is fine, but generating the sentence on its own requires a disclosure.

“A human skimmed it before publishing” doesn’t qualify as editorial review. The Commission is explicit that it needs to be substantive, with a named person responsible for the editorial control.

According to recent reports, in other words, the fine line lies between intentional manual intervention and automated generation. The latter always has to be disclosed (exception: closed B2B environments).

As part of the Code of Practice, the European Commission has published an EU AI icon set. It’s a specific “AI” mark (similar to the AI label in Carbon Design System) — not the generic ✨ sparkle that many products use to signal AI. The signal must be “clear and distinguishable”.

The sparkle might be too ambiguous to signal AI clearly. Mostly because it’s often used to mean “AI-powered feature”, rather than “this specific content was generated by AI”. That’s the kind of signal EU guidelines are trying to rule out.

The Commission is explicit: using an icon “does not establish legal compliance by itself.” A barely visible icon, a note buried in the footer, or a label that flashes for a second are all not compliant.

In a recent development, the icon should be clearly visible, with a plain language label and accessible to assistive technologies. A safe bet is to pair any icon with plain text (“AI-generated”) — and it needs to persist when being reshared or downloaded.

In fact, the EU Commission also published Code of Practice on marking and labelling of AI content.

It might feel like a yet another regulation coming from the EU, but in reality there are plenty of other similar regulations that emerged recently worldwide:.

All of these are signs of upcoming AI regulation that looks more like a pattern, rather than a coincidence. So if you’re shipping anything AI this year, it’s probably a good idea to have a conversation about what exactly is going to be AI-labelled, and what not.

One final note is that newly introduced EU AI transparency rules are much broader than US laws on AI disclosure, where certain state laws require disclosures for synthetic human performers, political advertising or specific AI applications.

It has been revealed that none of this really deserves panic or confusion. It’s about a fairly simple idea that has been emerging worldwide at almost the same time:.

If anything, it will help people distinguish between AI slop and not AI — and everybody can only benefit from that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pact's Anagram brand identity starts from a single square and rearranges it into a kaleidoscopic system of glyphs, grids and 8-bit color.

Sources indicate that anagram is a venture capital firm backing builders of decentralized networks, with a mission to bring the ownership economy to the masses. Pact's answer is a concept called Reorder the world: an identity that never settles into one fixed shape. The space it lives in speaks two dialects, cold institutional finance or loud speculative hype, and Anagram is neither. Pact describes the personality as pioneering, based, optimistic and fun, so the system is friendlier, stranger and more open than either dialect allows.

Everything starts from one square, the genesis block. From it the system grows into shapes, networks, letters and characters, every element sitting on the same grid. Monospaced type and rudimentary graphics keep something complex feeling approachable, and the posters carry the same discipline: dates set large, 07.11, 01.12 and 05.19, a 3.0 mark, network diagrams drawn as constellations of colored dots.

The logo itself is modular. It opens up to reveal different worlds, and inside its A's sits the A-man, a small 8-bit figure who stands in for every individual building the decentralized ecosystem. He comes in 8 colors and 8 expressions, and the A-men combine with the logo and the portals to bring more personality wherever they land.

The system holds its language at every scale. A black blade sign runs ANAGRAM down a stone facade in white capitals, a pink billboard carries the slash and square glyphs over a city street, and a glowing cube hangs over a doorway with a different glyph on each face: two dots, two asterisks, two tildes. Blue garage doors take the same glyphs at architectural scale.

Smaller things carry it too. The website runs on black screens with a timer, a network diagram and a team page that reads Reorder the world. An arcade card deals nine pixel game tiles, ARCADE 00 to 08, and the swag, tote bags, stickers and a deck all stay on the same grid, so the identity flexes from poster to digital surface without losing its common language.

We know that everything on the web is a box by default, but you’ll find many animated s pretending to be circles. But if you’ve ever met a real , you’ll know that they’ve got a lot more going for them. Dressed in SVG, they fit into a wider range of crowds than a humble wearing HTML/CSS can. has a strict no .html policy.

Sources indicate that the tag is not as static as its name suggests. Any embedded JavaScript unfortunately won’t run if you load an SVG file with an tag, but CSS animations work perfectly fine. Many of the SVG attributes do have CSS property counterparts, and the geometry properties have been supported across the major browsers since 2024. Some attributes that you might want to animate, like viewBox, don’t have equivalents yet.

Besides JavaScript and CSS, there’s another way to animate SVGs: Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language (SMIL). Despite its quirks, it’s still worth learning. Like CSS animations, SMIL animations also work in tags and can fully animate everything in an SVG, without JavaScript.

According to recent reports, if you’ve never heard of SMIL or need a refresher, check out Andy Clarke’s well-named article. Then we’ll look at a way to initiative an animation and make SMIL markup more manageable.

Recent findings suggest that SMIL has a problem: it gets bloated swiftly. Unlike CSS and JavaScript, where you can list multiple properties in each keyframe and easily reuse animations, each SMIL tag can only target one element and only one property of that element at a time. A property can be animated through a list of values. But it is still one tag, one element, one property. The shortest way you can write a color and opacity change that will run is the following:.

According to recent reports, that’s not bad, but consider that it needs to be repeated for every element included in the animation. A SMIL animation can rapidly get longer than its CSS equivalent.

To make things easier when starting a new animation, let’s initiative all of the elements and properties we want to animate, and create a list of descriptive IDs for each tag.

According to recent reports, I like to initiative my animations using what’s called a timing chart. A timing chart is effectively a line segment; some choose horizontal lines, others prefer vertical, which is a great analogy for animation as a whole because line segments can run parallel, overlap, and follow each other with or without a gap. Just like animations.

It has been revealed that for now, we’re only interested in when animations start and stop. When drawing our charts, we’ll forget about the in-between lines and instead draw a line for each component animation, marking the beginning and end. I like to annotate timing with a circle and a bar. You can draw your chart using whatever, and it doesn’t have to be exactly to scale, as long as the relative timing between all the little animations that make up the whole is clear. Besides, adding labels for the durations is an easy cheat to get around drawing to scale.

Here is a demo of how I typically set up a timing chart with more than one animation:.

See the Pen [colorAndOpacityChange [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016dc-399c-7652-b172-4cd4663746b9) by Johan Grobler.

It has been revealed that the notable thing to note is that the timing chart lines are arranged according to how the animations are arranged in time. One piece of the animation follows the next piece, which is followed by a subsequent piece, and so forth. It visualizes how the animation’s parts run together and cascade over time.

According to recent reports, A significant part of SMIL is synchronization. It’s even in the name, after all. And there are multiple ways to specify when an animation should start (here’s a test case to check what your browser supports). One of the most useful ways is with a syncbase value, which is a SMIL tag’s ID followed by either .begin or .end, with an optional positive or negative offset.

Let’s piggyback off the previous animation example that includes changes in color and opacity. If we want the opacity animation to start 300 milliseconds before the color animation finishes, we could do arithmetic. Alternatively, the second animation can use the syncbase value colorChange.end - 300ms. This way, the relative timing between the two animations becomes explicit.

Using syncbase values, the beginning of an animation is positioned in time relative to the .begin or .end of some other animation. A positive offset moves the start to the right (forwards in time), and a negative offset to the left (backwards in time).

See the Pen [syncbase.end [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/emgwwGJ) by Johan Grobler.

Something with negative offsets is that they can specify a time before the document has loaded or when a click happens. Computers can’t predict the future (at least not yet). The best they can do is jump the animation to where it would have been had the computer peeked into the future to preemptively start the animation. The second animation only runs from start to finish if there is enough room, so to speak.

See the Pen [syncbase.begin [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/xbgooXq) by Johan Grobler.

It has been revealed that syncbase values don’t only allow you to connect animations from .end to .begin. Elect a primary animation; the animation that first comes to mind is usually the best representation of the group. All secondary animations can be set with begin="primary.begin". I’ve only used the ID #primary for emphasis. That way, all the other animations begin relative to that starting point. Stacking animations like this reduces maintenance if, say, we later want the whole group to start at a different time.

Let’s put the idea to work and build a loading indicator (or spinner). Then we’re going to explore how changing the relative timing between the parts changes the effect of the whole animation:.

According to recent reports, browsers have wide support for the prefers-reduced-motion media feature and Val Head explains this in depth in another article. We definitely want to respect this user preference as we consider moving things around. In fact, consider it non-negotiable.

There are various approaches to adhering to a user’s prefers-reduced-motion setting when it comes to SMIL. Each with its pros and cons. Evaluating early on what’s going to work best for your use case could save you a partial rewrite down the line.

For example, we could consider using a element instead of a plain because supports multiple elements that can be used as fallbacks in a media attribute for reduced motion preferences.

Or one SVG file with an inline CSS @media query that uses display: none to swap between versions. That remarked, it’s an approach that might cause trouble in various environments. But browsers are continuously changing, and this might not be an issue in the future.

You might also consider a CSS background-image instead because we can wrap that style in a media query — @media (prefers-reduced-motion) — that sets a static image as the fallback for reduced motion preferences.

According to recent reports, there are even more options we can turn to! For example, SVG’s element can also be used to swap things out for motion preferences.

Or, if we prefer everything bundled together, we can use JavaScript .matchMedia() and the handy SMIL DOM interface to control which animations start instead of completely switching out files.

For this, I’m avoiding any motion and sticking to opacity animations, which tend to cause less trouble. For a non-interactive animation like this, we can load it in an tag. When we add motion, we can go the route to show the most appropriate version of our animation.

Once again, Andy Clarke has a great article about his process for optimizing and structuring his own drawings.

Note: There’s a gotcha with Inkscape. Setting what you would expect to be an element’s ID via the Layers window actually sets the value of a metadata attribute used internally by Inkscape. Use Inkscape’s object properties or XML editor window to set the true element’s ID. Your mileage may vary with a different editor. Also, in Inkscape, remember to save the file as optimized SVG when the drawing is done to strip away unneeded metadata.

As you iterate on your animation, timing charts are a great way to keep track of your work, and they make visual comparison between versions possible. And by drawing a timing chart, you might even see a pattern in the timing between the parts of the animations that you might otherwise have missed.

In a recent development, as you animate more elements and properties, it gets harder to keep track of what starts when. To see how timing charts can help you make sense of things, let’s build on the basic spinner:.

You’ll need to take into account which tags can animate and set which data types if you do decide to animate the transform attribute instead of translating the rectangles with the y attribute.

Recent findings suggest that the fade-outs still use the normal opacity property, so both the fill and stroke fade out together. Because this arrangement is set up to use a group fade-out at the end, there are a few places the markup could be optimized. One of them is dropping the fill="freeze" to automatically reset the dot’s opacity back to its starting value once the tag finishes running:.

That’s just one of the possible timing variations, and most of what you’ll need to try some of the others, as we did with the basic spinner, is already in place. You might want to have a try at coming up with a couple of your own alternate timings.

To sum things up, we know that balancing the different stages of an animation can be difficult at best, and untenable at worst. Any time we get into multi-step animations that exceed one or two steps, it’s a form of orchestration. You’re almost building a Rube Goldberg machine of markup. And using a timing chart is a strategy I use that I hope will help you in your projects as well. They are outlines of what to expect and when, allowing you to map things out in a way that not only helps strategy your code, but also makes future updates and maintenance a lot more bearable than going into it without a plan.

Industry observers note that while a timing chart can’t reduce the complexity of the markup, it can give a good overview of what should happen when. Timing charts are definitely not limited to SMIL animations. Unfortunately, syncbase values are, and they can still help even if you’re going to use a different approach to implementing your animation.

In a recent development, I highly recommend checking out Andy’s other articles on Smashing Magazine. There’s even more stuff on combining CSS and SVG.

Yosra Emad wrote a great article on creating animations with multiple steps in CSS, and you might want to try drawing a few timing charts as you read through it.

When you’re ready to start adding those in-between lines to your timing chart, Nash Vail’s article on easing dives deep into the details of easing curves.

You might also be interested in tests for your browser’s SVG implementation to see what is supported.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Product: Logitech MX Master 4 (Special Edition).

Sensor & Tracking: Darkfield high precision, 200-8000 DPI.

Scroll: MagSpeed electromagnetic wheel plus thumb wheel.

Connectivity: Bluetooth and Logi Bolt receiver.

Battery: up to 70 days per charge, USB-C.

Software: Logitech Options+ (Windows and macOS).

Best for: creatives, office workers and anyone with long desk sessions.

The MX Master 4 Special Edition takes Logitech's excellent black mouse and spruces it up with a new white colourway and red-and-grey accents. Inside, it's the same MX Master 4, and like the 2025 version, it has a tough act to follow. Its predecessor, the MX Master 3S, is already one of the best productivity mice you can buy, so Logitech never intended to reinvent the wheel. Instead, we get more customisation, haptic feedback, and a handful of design tweaks, and in this Special Edition, a more personalised colour choice.

These are all the developments I’d expect from a follow-up to the excellent MX Master 3S, one of the best mice you can buy, but they make this a nicer-looking version of a mouse that was a smart evolution rather than a must-have upgrade, unless, I'd argue, you're a creative; then the Actions Ring becomes a bigger thing than you may expect and is new to MX Master 4, Special Edition or not.

The shape is the same as the MX Master 3S, with its sculpted ergonomic design, deep thumb rest, and plenty of controls to keep your hands off the keyboard. It’s comfortable for long workdays, and the weight is spot on. It has enough heft to feel planted on the desk without feeling clumsy. It’s big, though, and it won’t suit everyone. This is a mouse for your desk, not your laptop bag.

• For more control consider one of the best drawing tablets.

Industry observers note that the MagSpeed wheel is as good as ever. Flick it, and it free-spins through a long spreadsheet or a 40-page document, then ratchets back to click-by-click scrolling when you need precision. Switching between the two is automatic, which is why it’s so easy to take for granted.

It has been revealed that the finish is where things have changed. This is the Special Edition of last year’s MX Master 4 release, so the design changes over the MX Master 3S remain. Logitech has swapped the soft, rubberised coating of older models for something harder, but it’s not slick or glassy. The cover has a nice bit of tooth, and different areas have subtly different textures, so your fingers always know where they are without you looking. It feels different from the old MX Masters. A colleague wasn’t keen on it when they tried [2025’s MX Master 4], but I got used to it swiftly, so your mileage may vary, and existing owners may need a few days to adjust.

Those alterations aside, the Special Edition replaces flat blacks with a soft grey-white colour and red accents. The dark grey Actions Ring thumb rest pops in this colourway, and I far prefer it to the faceless black PC-mouse aesthetic of the base model. There’s no price difference between black and Special Edition.

The thumb rest gets the biggest rethink. It’s usually the most wasted area of a mouse, a bit of plastic to rest your thumb on. Here, it’s the way into the fresh virtual dial, called the Actions Ring, which makes it feel like part of the design rather than an afterthought.

The haptics are a lovely touch. They kick in when you make a selection and when you open and cycle through the Actions Ring, so I can keep my eyes on the screen, click and scroll, and still feel a little resistance and feedback. This also helps with gesture control, too, if you go as far as needing that kind of input. It’s subtle, but it makes the mouse feel more connected to what you’re doing.

Recent findings suggest that as you may have guessed, the Actions Ring is the real star of the upcoming features. It’s an on-screen dial that expands what the mouse can do, making it easy to open folders or switch between apps without dropping into the Windows menus. You can tailor the ring to the job, from something as basic as Google to Photoshop or DaVinci Resolve. Support isn’t universal, though. The best digital art and design apps like Krita, Affinity Photo and CorelDRAW are covered, but smaller apps like Escape Motions Rebelle aren’t a default option, so you’ll need a workaround: assign function keys in Options+, then match them to the app’s own shortcuts for undo, clear layer or brush toggles. It works, but you need to know your keys or set them up ahead of time.

This also means getting to grips with Options+ and its app features, which is a lot of learning for a mouse. I’d like it to work more without that software running in the background. But if you persevere, it adds real depth and makes the mouse faster to use and more flexible. Once it’s set up, you’ll love it. You can tweak everything from haptic strength to scroll speed, and I’d probably be moaning if I couldn’t fiddle.

The haptics, gestures, and Actions Ring are a step beyond the MX Master 3S, and creatives who map shortcuts to the ring will get the most from this mouse.

So, should you buy the MX Master 4 Special Edition? If you’re coming from a basic mouse, absolutely. The ergonomics, scrolling and customisation make it a brilliant tool for anyone who works at a computer all day, whether in creative apps or simply navigating menus and Google.

Recent findings suggest that if you already own an MX Master 3S, it comes down to how you work. The haptics and Actions Ring are genuinely useful and, for creative apps, a fresh, easier way to work, so it’s worth it if you’ll map shortcuts to the ring or, like me, hate sorting through Windows menus and would rather one-click into the regular apps and files. For everyone else, they’re not enough to make a perfectly good mouse obsolete.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian introduced Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that family-owned flooring manufacturer Mannington Commercial aims to solve problems for interior designers and their clients.
  • “An entryway has different demands than a lobby, patient room, corridor, or collaborative area, but those spaces still need to feel connected.
  • Rather than creating matching sets, Mannington Commercial establishes a design language that allows products to complement one another and carry a design concept throughout a project.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that family-owned flooring manufacturer Mannington Commercial aims to solve problems for interior designers and their clients. That’s why the manufacturer focuses on giving designers more freedom and flexibility with product, as discussed in The Art of Versatility last year. Building on that concept, Mannington Commercial designs products in families so individual flooring collections work together across an entire project.

“An entryway has different demands than a lobby, patient room, corridor, or collaborative area, but those spaces still need to feel connected. If every collection lives on its own island, then the designer has to create all of those relationships,” notes Stacey Gerbman, Mannington Commercial Director of Design. “The shift is from thinking only about individual launches to thinking about the life of the entire portfolio.”.

Rather than creating matching sets, Mannington Commercial establishes a design language that allows products to complement one another and carry a design concept throughout a project. Each latest product should be distinct yet work with existing and future collections, simplifying specification for interior designers.

According to recent reports, stepping Stones. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

It has been revealed that mannington Commercial’s design team looks ahead to ensure new collections pair naturally with existing lines. “Before a collection is fully developed, we look at the portfolio as a whole: where there are gaps, which colors and undertones are vital, what scales are missing, and which materials the new collection is likely to sit beside,” says Gerbman. The team considers how a collection might work with carpet, LVT, sheet, rubber, or an entryway product, as well as how scale and color should transition between materials.

Sources indicate that for Mannington Commercial, the key to connecting carpet with LVT and other materials is its yarn system, which Gerbman describes as “color architecture.” A core palette of solids and twists provides a foundation that carries across collections while allowing for different effects. “We do not look at carpet in isolation,” Gerbman notes. “We place the poms and tufted trials next to LVT, sheet, rubber, and other materials and study undertone, value, temperature, and contrast.” Rather than seeking exact color matches, the goal is a “believable relationship.” Gerbman adds, “The hard surface may provide clarity and structure, while the carpet adds softness, depth, and variation. When the yarn bank is built thoughtfully, those materials can play different roles and still feel as if they belong in the same environment.”.

Curated Underfoot. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

In a recent development, curated Underfoot puts this approach into practice with Mannington Commercial’s first system of carpet and LVT for commercial interiors. Five neutral tones carry across the LVT and five carpet patterns, creating a shared color foundation. “But each surface and pattern brings a different level of texture and movement,” Gerbman explains. “A designer can stay tonal or create contrast through pattern and scale, and the result still feels connected without looking overly matched. It supports the system while leaving room for the designer’s own authorship.”.

“Curated Underfoot reflects the way designers think about a space as a complete environment rather than a series of individual flooring decisions,” states Whitney LeGate, Senior Vice President, Commercial Product. “By bringing carpet and LVT together through one synchronized collection, we’re making it easier to create interiors that are visually cohesive and built to perform.”.

Atto, a terrazzo-inspired LVT, anchors the system with bold pattern, layered movement and contemporary color that translates to carpet for a seamless transition between hard- and soft-surface flooring.

According to recent reports, stepping Stones. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

Industry observers note that another product family, Stepping Stones, combines performance and aesthetics in an LVT collection for healthcare settings. Six curated palettes pair complementary colors and textures across wood, stone, and other material expressions, with tonal terrazzo anchoring each palette. Patterns inspired by nature take on softer, warmer qualities to promote a serene, restorative environment. The palettes simplify specification and help designers maintain visual continuity throughout a healthcare facility, where arrival, waiting, treatment and recovery areas require different flooring but should still feel connected.

Sources indicate that bioSpec. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

Mannington Commercial also makes BioSpec, a line of homogeneous sheet vinyl designed for high-use commercial and healthcare spaces. Mannington Commercial is the only manufacturer producing homogeneous resilient sheet vinyl in the United States. And it’s the only one making heterogeneous sheet vinyl in 6-foot, 9-foot, and 12-foot widths for easier installation, fewer seams, and less waste. Similar to the relationships in other product families, this line includes three variations tailored to specific needs: BioSpec Armor for demanding, high-traffic environments; BioSpec SR for enhanced slip resistance; and BioSpec MD for superior abrasion resistance and an extensive color selection. The products work together and pair with other Mannington Commercial resilient flooring and carpet.

It has been revealed that layeredLogic. Photo courtesy of Mannington Commercial.

It has been revealed that continuing this systems-based approach in 2027, Mannington Commercial is launching LayeredLogic, a heterogeneous sheet collection for healthcare interiors. Its three patterns share a visual language, allowing them to be layered, as the prints progress from subtle texture to more expressive designs. Created for acute care facilities, LayeredLogic gives designers a way to define spaces and create rhythm through an intentional palette designed to last and work with current and future Mannington Commercial LVT and carpet collections. By designing individual products to work together as part of a larger system, Mannington Commercial takes an approach that feels familiar and fitting for a family-owned company.

#239. Why Your Website Should Never Stop Changing

📅 2026-08-25 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1493 w)
