Why Your Website Should Never Stop Changing

📅 2026-08-25 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pierre Burgy is the co-founder and CEO of Strapi, the leading open-source headless CMS, and co-founder of Fimo, a product incubated at Strapi that keeps … More about Pierre ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Recent findings suggest that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Fimo, the infrastructure that keeps a website improving after launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pierre Burgy is the co-founder and CEO of Strapi, the leading open-source headless CMS, and co-founder of Fimo, a product incubated at Strapi that keeps … More about Pierre ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Fimo, the infrastructure that keeps a website improving after launch. It runs over your real code, lets your team edit anything visually, and puts agents to work on content, accessibility, and the maintenance you never get to. Incubated at Strapi. Thank you!

In a recent development, every website is at its best the day it ships. The final branch merges, the site goes live exactly as designed, and it is briefly perfect. It will never be this good again.

Not because anything breaks. The site keeps working. But the market moves, the messaging shifts, a competitor debuts something, and the careful thing you built slowly stops matching the firm it represents. A year later, it is a period piece. Not broken, just behind. Every team knows this decay, and almost everyone treats it as a law of nature.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn’t have to be that way. A website could keep improving after launch instead of drifting away from its best day, quietly optimizing itself while the team that built it works on something else.

Recent findings suggest that picture it working: while you sleep, an agent catches that last week’s design-system change never propagated to the pricing page, and fixes it. Another finds a set of images shipped uncompressed in a rushed release and optimizes them. A third flags an accessibility regression a new component introduced, and either fixes it or leaves it for you to check. You wake up to a site that is measurably better than the one you left, and a short list of the few decisions the agents wanted your eyes on. That is the version worth wanting.

And the moment you take that promise seriously, you run into a problem that has nothing to do with the technology:.

The obvious move, once you have capable agents, is to hand them the whole site. Let them write, edit, optimize, and publish, and get out of the way. It sounds like the natural endpoint, and it is the first thing most people picture when they hear “autonomous website.”.

It is also the thing almost nobody wants once it is real in front of them.

We learned this the way you learn most things worth knowing: by building the opposite first. Building Fimo, an autonomous website platform, we set out to make websites fully autonomous, assumed that was the goal, and then watched what people actually did with it. What they did was hesitate. Not because they distrusted the agents, but because a website has no single owner. Different parts belong to different people, and each one wants a different amount of autonomy. So the question was never whether to trust the agents. It was where to draw the line, and for whom.

Once you ask it that way, the work splits cleanly into three kinds.

Start with the largest pile, because it is bigger than people expect. Most of what keeps a website healthy is rule-bound, repetitive, and completely joyless. Keeping accessibility compliant as pages change. Propagating a design-system upgrade once a token moves. Catching a broken meta tag, an unoptimized image, a link that rotted when a URL changed three sprints ago.

None of this is where anyone’s talent lives. Nobody was hired because of their gift for spotting a missing alt attribute. This is the work you are actively relieved to hand off, and it is the work agents are best at, because it is defined by rules rather than taste. An agent that quietly keeps this layer correct across a whole site, unattended, is not a threat to anyone’s job. It is the tedious eighty percent finally taken care of.

Naming how much of the maintenance load actually lives in this pile is what makes the whole idea of an autonomous site feel less like a leap. You are not handing over judgment. You are handing over chores.

At the other end sits the work you would not delegate at any price. It is a small pile, but it is the reason you exist.

An agent can check a fresh page against every rule you have given it. It can confirm the contrast passes, the heading order is right, the tokens are correct, the copy matches the style guide. What it cannot do is decide what the page should feel like, or whether the thing you are shipping is, in the taste sense, good. That judgment is exactly what you were hired for, and no amount of capability moves it off your desk.

This is the part people reach for first when they resist autonomy, and they are right to protect it. The mistake is thinking the whole site is made of this kind of work. Almost none of it is. But that small part matters more than all the rest, which is why automating everything feels so wrong.

Between the chores and the untouchable sits the part no product can settle for you, because the line runs through different places for different people.

It has been revealed that notice what is happening there. It isn’t that one of them is cautious and the other reckless. It is that the same task carries different amounts of judgment for each of them. For one person it is a decision; for the other it is a chore. There is no default a product could ship that would be right for both, because “right” is a function of where your value sits, not of the task itself.

Sources indicate that this is why the control has to be per-task and per-person, and why we stopped trying to find the setting that would work for everyone. There isn’t one. There is only the line each person draws, and the tools to draw it precisely.

Once you accept that the line is personal, a toggle between “approve” and “delegate” stops being enough. Where the line sits depends on what the agent is actually doing, so the real unit of control is the agent itself.

This is where it stopped being a settings problem, and it is the shape Fimo took. You don’t pick from a fixed menu of behaviors. You compose the agents, deciding what each one is even allowed to touch. You can build one from scratch, or take one close to your needs and shape it to your own line: an accessibility agent you trust to run unattended, a content agent you keep close to anything brand-facing.

It has been revealed that and they don’t stay fixed. They learn from their tasks and from what you teach them, so the boundary you set last month isn’t the one you’re stuck with. What you had to approve then, you can delegate now, not because you lowered your guard but because the agent earned it. The line is not a setting you configure once. It moves as trust is earned, in the direction of less work for you.

Sources indicate that none of this means flipping a site to autonomous on day one. In practice it goes the other way. You delegate a little, watch how it does, and loosen.

And you can actually watch. Every agent’s runs, its history, its logs, and a before-and-after of what it changed are there to inspect. Trust doesn’t grow because you got used to the idea; it grows because you can see what happened and compare. The first time an agent quietly fixes something you would have missed, and you can see exactly what it did, the next delegation gets easier.

Deadlines keep you from becoming the bottleneck on what you have already handed over. If you don’t weigh in, the agent proceeds. You set the terms once, and you stop being the thing the whole site waits on.

The worry people voice first is that an agent will change something on their site without them. Turn it around: the real risk is a site that never changes at all. A frozen site doesn’t stay safe. It just falls behind, slowly, in a way nobody notices until it represents a firm that no longer exists.

It has been revealed that the point of autonomy was never to remove you from your website. It was to remove the decay.

The point of autonomy is to keep the launch-day version from being the best version, and to let you spend your judgment on the handful of things that actually deserve it, while the rest takes care of itself. Draw the line where your value is. Let the agents hold everything on the other side of it. And let the line move as they prove they can.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the morning of 4 December 2024, the Los Angeles-based artist Stanya Kahn opened X (formerly Twitter) to get her daily news digest, when she, like many Americans, was inundated with a mass chorus of tweets—ranging from celebratory snark to unbridled vitriol—about the assassination of United HealthCare’s chief executive Brian Thompson.

“The compression of anger and joy that I was seeing people write that day was astonishing,” Kahn tells The Art Newspaper; she immediately felt compelled to capture the torrent of reactions. “At first I was bookmarking them, and then [screenshotting] them, and fairly quickly my thought was to gather these up because the algorithm might start shutting them down.”.

Fairly swiftly, the Trump administration confirmed that any celebration of the killing could be criminalised. But with an ever-growing archive and a long-held practice as a time-based media artist, Kahn decided to create a film that chronologically presented the public’s rapidly unfolding response to this now-infamous event.

Flyer for Deny, Defend, Depose (2026) Courtesy of Stanya Kahn.

Industry observers note that titled Deny Defend Depose (2026)—a play on the words scrawled on three shell casings from bullets fired in the shooting, and the strategy invoked by major healthcare providers to reduce payouts and increase profits—Kahn’s film is now screening across the country at artist-run-spaces, cinemas and galleries. The Upcoming York non-profit space Participant Inc will screen it on 13 November, with more showings to come.

Originally, Kahn planned to release the film in the lead-up to 9 September, when the state trial of Luigi Mangione was due to take place in New York. Now that Mangione’s 14 August guilty plea—an attempt to avoid double jeopardy—has postponed the state hearing until 10 December, with a federal hearing to follow on 18 December, Kahn looks to continue updating the film with more responses from the public as the saga continues.

Sources indicate that when it all began, she had considered turning the project into a coffee-table book, which would afford a funny inversion of X’s quippy, short-form format. But switching to a film, her primary medium, afforded an opportunity for in-person film screenings, which enabled the originally solitary experience of watching the commentary unfold online to be transformed into a collective viewing experience.

Stanya Kahn, Deny, Defend, Depose (2026, still), 30:28 min Courtesy of the artist.

Sources indicate that set to a dramatic soundtrack of acid and jungle, the 30-minute film takes viewers on an emotional rollercoaster. Watching the tweets unfold in sequence together, the audience collectively holds its breadth as anticipation builds to the moment the suspect is revealed as Mangione, laughs as tweets comment on his attractiveness or the Monopoly money found in his backpack, and sighs at the devastating state of healthcare in the United States when statistics regarding industry salaries and investment patterns, or personal anecdotes about life-threatening denials, are shared.

Industry observers note that just like Kahn was glued to X that morning in late 2024, viewers of her film are often transfixed as they relive their reactions to the still-unfolding story at top speed.“The poignancy of such a broad spectrum of the American public responding in kind to what was basically a public political assassination felt like a rupture, especially in party-based politics,” Kahn says. “It cut across the entire political spectrum and the common ground that suddenly emerged in this flashpoint seemed like a latest beacon for potential mass movement, because it was a unity that emerged spontaneously and instantaneously, it wasn’t something that got hammered out in time.”.

According to recent reports, the outpouring of affection for Mangione has been staggering, Kahn states. “Without blinking,” she adds, “people were in full-throat applause of [an alleged] murderer.”.

Stanya Kahn, Deny, Defend, Depose (2026, still), 30:28 min Courtesy of the artist.

Attention from the media and public has remained steady since the early days of the manhunt, Mangione’s arrest and the trial, with comparisons to Robin Hood, lookalike contests and wanted posters for other healthcare manufacturer executives. While the extent of the public’s celebration of Thompson’s killing took many by surprise, Kahn sees this reaction as evidence of just “how deep the pain and anger and frustration is in this country about the evilness of the healthcare system and its inaccessibility”. (Per capita spending on healthcare in the US is double the average of other wealthy countries, and has been increasing faster than inflation for decades.).

Thompson’s killing and its aftermath are hardly a black-and-white tale of righteous moral vengeance. Though some originally attempted to paint Mangione as disaffected and radicalised, his Ivy League education and privileged upbringing told a different story. And the responses to the event “weren’t just coming from more radical spaces”, Kahn notes. While capturing their reactions in real time and reviewing the posters’ profiles, she found, “it was literally just ‘every man’—people with five followers and five million. It was regular people because they were pissed.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Claudio Parada Nunes.

Ring of Bjólfur is a mountain viewpoint in Iceland, designed by local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking.

Located in Seyðisfjörður, a fjord in eastern Iceland, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture‘s design draws on the legend of Bjólfur, an Icelandic Viking settler believed to have claimed this landscape and been laid to rest on the mountain.

According to recent reports, local lore notes Bjólfur was buried on the mountain with his most precious belongings, though they have never been found. The viewpoint, therefore, evokes a ring that has been left for him.

“The medieval Book of Settlements, or Landnámabók, tells of Bjólfur, the settler who first claimed land in Seyðisfjörður and gave the mountain its name,” Arkibygg Architects told Dezeen.

“The book says little about him, but local tales tell that he was laid to rest in a burial mound high up on the mountain,” it continued.

Industry observers note that “By ancient custom, chieftains were often buried with their treasures, silver and jewellery. Bjólfur’s grave goods have never been found, but we let our imagination run free and left him a great silver ring.”.

Industry observers note that arkibygg Arkitektar and Esja Architecture won a competition to design Ring of Bjólfur in 2021. The project was shortlisted in the small projects category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and also won the public vote for the same category.

Ring of Bjólfur takes the form of a perfect circle, measuring 32 metres in diameter. While emulating a ring, this was also designed to “work with views in every direction”.

Industry observers note that positioned on a mountain ridge 650 metres above sea level, the structure was built from post-tensioned concrete with stainless steel railings, chosen for durability and for colours that emulate silver. It partially cantilevers on one side.

“The ring can be used in many ways, and the view changes depending on where you are in the circle – and whether you are standing or sitting,” remarked Arkibygg Arkitektar.

“The choice of materials grew from the idea of creating a silver ring, while also having to withstand wind and weather at 650 metres, with the structure being submerged in snow for parts of the year,” stated the studio.

A major focus for the studios was ensuring accessibility, creating “an experience that everyone can enjoy, including wheelchair users”.

Industry observers note that to achieve this, they designed accessible parking next to the ring as part of the project. Further general parking is located further downhill to encourage people who are physically able to walk to the platform.

“The project has been very well received, not only by visitors but just as much by local residents,” it continued.

“The ring is already strengthening tourism in the town, and it has also become part of residents’ daily lives, widely used for outdoor recreation. People walk, cycle or even ski up there to take in the view.”.

The landscape surrounding the viewpoint was preserved as much as possible, with any boulders that needed to be temporarily removed lifted back into place upon completion.

Industry observers note that “The immediate surroundings – the soil and the rocks – matter a great deal. The aim was to disturb the ground as little as possible and to repair what was disturbed.

Recent findings suggest that “Other areas affected by the works were restored with native vegetation. Having one clear destination also keeps visitors from wandering across the fragile ridge.”.

Other viewpoints recently featured on Dezeen include an arrow-shaped structure in Denmark by Arup and the Lech Mountain Mirror by Snøhetta in Austria.

  • In a recent development, dispatch was made in Unreal Engine and stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as former hero Robert Robertson, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast.
  • I asked co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO and both co-creative directors, what survived the jump from live-action series to animated game, and what had to change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A year ago, Dispatch released a game that surprised many people, including me. It's a superhero game about managing reformed villains from behind a desk, introduced on PC and PlayStation 5. It has since garnered over five million players, and a mobile version arrives on iOS and Android on 9 December, following October's Dispatch anniversary Deluxe Edition.

In a recent development, dispatch was made in Unreal Engine and stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as former hero Robert Robertson, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast. It's an animated, episodic workplace comedy that plays like a TV series, but it wasn't always a game, and that's perhaps why it feels so unique. AdHoc was founded in Los Angeles in 2018 by Telltale Games alumni who planned to make interactive experiences with real actors on screen, and Dispatch began that way.

I asked co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO and both co-creative directors, what survived the jump from live-action series to animated game, and what had to change.

One piece of the original script made it through every draft: the doughnut shop scene in episode two. Lenart notes it was "one of the pieces from the early script that just kind of kept hanging around through every draft all the way from live action into the animated game".

The set-up was different back then. You watched a camera feed as the hero Invisigal dealt with a thief, and your job was to feed her the information she needed to succeed. In the live-action version, that meant switching cameras and pulling information from what each camera highlighted. Herman says the scene was "purely built around the technology" AdHoc was using to create its interactive live action. It ran in a browser and had hard limits, including, as Herman recalls, “I think it was like four simultaneous tracks of video”.

Sources indicate that the team turned that restriction into a mechanic. Watch the alley behind the shop, and you couldn't see what was happening inside the front. "By choosing where you were going to give your attention, the game would adjust, and you'd learn different things based on where you were looking," indicates Herman, calling it the perfect place to test the idea.

In a recent development, because they'd spent so long on it, they carried it forward. In the game, Lenart states, they wove in mechanics from the final design, such as hacking, "to make it feel a little bit more like Robert was helping out Invisigal".

According to recent reports, the original story was a mentorship, centred on the one-on-one relationship between Robert and Invisigal. Pivoting it into a game changed that. AdHoc wanted a dispatch mechanic, with the player sending heroes out on calls, and that needs a roster. "So the Z-Team was created to support the gameplay," Lenart indicates, "which then informed the story, and then changed the overall arc of the season, which brought a whole team into it as opposed to just a one-on-one mentorship with Invisigal.".

It's a neat illustration of how the studio works. "Everything at AdHoc starts with story," says Herman, contrasting that with studios that pick a genre first, polish the mechanics and the game-feel, and only later ask what the story is. AdHoc begins with the world, the characters and who the player is, then asks what that means for gameplay. "Oh, well, you're a superhero dispatcher, so maybe we should have some sort of dispatching mechanic, right?".

Sources indicate that once there's a script, it moves on to storyboards, animatics and animation. That storyboard stage is now part of the product: the anniversary Deluxe Edition update adds Storyboard Mode, which plays the whole game through its original animatics. It's a newly introduced mode that offers genuine insight into how a scene was planned, scripted and animated.

According to recent reports, the move to animation was driven by budget constraints, to an extent, because they could do more with a little extra, and it also changed the game's scale, given Dispatch's live-action origins; Lenart claims the team knew they were "severely limited from a budget standpoint compared to big-budget superhero tentpole movies". For budgetary reasons, the story was largely set in an office with a small cast.

Animation flipped that constraint and aligned with trends like Mixtape's hand-made animation, giving the team room to grow and aim higher within the fresh art form. "We're able to have a giant action scene because it doesn't cost that much more than having a bunch of characters walking around talking," Lenart explains. That let AdHoc expand the moments that deserved spectacle: "Let's really go all out and try to compete with some of the other best-in-class versions of these scenes in animation.".

Sources indicate that ask whether players have done anything that made AdHoc rethink how interactive stories should work, and Herman is refreshingly honest. “I don’t know that there have been any major epiphanies,” he states, before steering to a different answer: launching Dispatch “was a labour of love”, the culmination of a lot of work distilled into one experience the team felt was exciting and high quality.

Recent findings suggest that he adds: "The success of the game has just really injected a lot of confidence into us and other developers making similar types of games. For a long time, there hadn't been a really clear or recent example of something like this reaching a level of success that a developer could go out and raise funding for.".

He's proud of who found it, too. Dispatch "was able to pierce a fresh audience who perhaps thought gaming wasn't for them". Lenart agrees, saying the success feels like "motivation to keep making these types of games and expand our possibilities even more".

The Dispatch Deluxe Edition is out now on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch / Switch 2, and $10.99 digital upgrade path for existing owners.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

Monopoly and Scrabble Get a Scandinavian Modern Redesign

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, monopoly and Scrabble have been fixtures of family game nights for generations, but their colorful boards and familiar pieces rarely stay out once the competition ends.
  • According to recent reports, the newly introduced Nordic Collection gives the two classic board games a Scandinavian-inspired redesign, replacing conventional folding boards and cardboard boxes with warm wood, understated graphics, and carefully considered details.
  • “The Nordic Collection was inspired by the rich design history of Scandinavian modern design,” explains Kerry Addis, co-owner and COO of WS Game Firm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, monopoly and Scrabble have been fixtures of family game nights for generations, but their colorful boards and familiar pieces rarely stay out once the competition ends. When the last property has been traded or the final word spelled, everything usually disappears back into a cabinet. WS Game Company is rethinking that relationship between play and display.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced Nordic Collection gives the two classic board games a Scandinavian-inspired redesign, replacing conventional folding boards and cardboard boxes with warm wood, understated graphics, and carefully considered details. Rolled out last month, the collection draws on the principles of Scandinavian modernism to create games that feel as much like design objects as they do as games.

Photography courtesy of WS Game Company.

“The Nordic Collection was inspired by the rich design history of Scandinavian modern design,” explains Kerry Addis, co-owner and COO of WS Game Firm. She points to designers such as Hans Wegner and Arne Jacobsen, who combined natural materials and traditional craftsmanship with modern production techniques to create objects that were both innovative and inviting. For the Nordic Collection, the goal was to bring that same balance of familiarity and innovation to the games’ form, construction, and functionality.

Photography courtesy of WS Game Firm.

The goal was to create something that could fit comfortably into an existing interior while offering meaningful innovations in form, construction, and practicality.

Recent findings suggest that the most immediately noticeable change is the material palette. Both Monopoly Nordic and Scrabble Nordic feature wooden game boards made from individual panels that connect through concealed magnets. Instead of unfolding a conventional board, players snap the pieces together, creating a sturdy playing surface that breaks down for compact storage.

Photography courtesy of WS Game Company.

Sources indicate that the assembly itself was designed to be as satisfying as the finished product. “The intuitive magnetic connections allow the user to snap the panels easily together, creating a solution that is as elegant and functional as it is satisfying to use,” explains James Fuschetti, WS Game Organization’s senior industrial designer. Cork backing adds warmth while helping prevent the boards from sliding during a game.

Working with manufacturing partners, the designers selected woods and stains that would produce a warm tone with a subtle luster. Generously rounded corners on the storage boxes and other components soften their appearance while making them more comfortable to handle.

It has been revealed that the result is a collection designed to complement a range of interiors rather than compete with them. Each game comes in a coordinating beechwood box that can sit comfortably on a shelf or coffee table, with the components stored neatly inside.

Each game comes in a coordinating beechwood box that keeps the components neatly organized while allowing the games to remain on display between uses.

Photography courtesy of WS Game Firm.

Beyond the wooden construction, smaller details reveal how WS Game Company balanced Scandinavian influences with the visual identities of two instantly recognizable games.

Industry observers note that in Monopoly Nordic, the traditional houses have become miniature pine trees. Instead of placing four houses side by side on a property, players stack them vertically to create increasingly tall conifers. As the game progresses, the board begins to resemble a Scandinavian forest.

Photography courtesy of WS Game Company.

The graphic design draws on the region’s history, too. Monopoly’s Chance and Community Chest cards have been recolored light blue and red, a subtle nod to early Swedish editions of the game. The railroad icon has been reimagined as an electric trolley, while the custom money takes cues from modernist Scandinavian banknotes, pairing crisp graphics with patterns inspired by traditional folk art.

Sources indicate that despite these updates, the game retains its recognizable corner-square icons, Chance question mark, and classic playing tokens, including the top hat and shoe. A wooden banker’s tray, die-cast tokens, and custom property deeds round out the set.

Industry observers note that scrabble Nordic takes a similarly considered approach. Its scorepad features graphics inspired by Scandinavian banknotes and folk art, while wooden letter tiles and racks bring warmth to the familiar game. The set also includes a microsuede tile bag, a pencil, and a sand timer with wooden end caps.

Photography courtesy of WS Game Company.

Recent findings suggest that the designers were careful to preserve the details that make Scrabble instantly recognizable, from the size and weight of the letter tiles to the small triangular markings along the edges of premium squares. Those markings help players identify bonus spaces even when tiles cover the board, preserving a small but vital functional detail of the original design.

Together, the two editions demonstrate how familiar games can be updated through materials, graphics, and playful details without losing the elements that make them enjoyable in the first place.

The collection builds on an idea WS Game Company has explored for years: Board games can be part of a home’s décor rather than hidden away between uses.

Photography courtesy of WS Game Company.

Its Vintage Bookshelf Collection takes a similar approach, packaging classic games in formats intended to blend into a bookshelf. The Nordic Collection extends that thinking through natural materials, a more sculptural presentation, and an emphasis on the physical experience of playing.

Industry observers note that “We’ve always believed that good design should have staying power,” Addis says. Rather than chasing fleeting trends, the company aims to create products that can evolve with people’s interiors and remain relevant as their lives change.

Industry observers note that as more daily activities migrate to screens, WS Game Company sees an opportunity to bring analog experiences back into everyday life. “Board games are a natural fit, bringing people together for shared experiences,” Addis says.

Photography courtesy of WS Game Manufacturer.

Industry observers note that the Nordic Collection makes a case for finding newly introduced possibilities in objects we already know. Monopoly and Scrabble don’t need to be reinvented to feel fresh. Sometimes, a thoughtful change in materials, a more intuitive construction, or a miniature forest of wooden houses is enough to make a familiar game worth leaving out long after everyone has gone home.

#233. Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions

📅 2026-08-26 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2982 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine

Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions

📅 2026-08-26 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meriem Benhabiles is a Designer specialising in User Experience, with over five years working in-house, agency-side, and independently.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In organisations today, data has never been more available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meriem Benhabiles is a Designer specialising in User Experience, with over five years working in-house, agency-side, and independently. Her background in … More about Meriem ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In organisations today, data has never been more available. Dashboards and performance decks exist for almost every function — sales, product, marketing, operations — and the tools to build them have never been more accessible. And yet, in weekly standups and quarterly reviews, the same thing happens constantly: someone shares the numbers, the room nods, and the meeting ends without a decision or clear direction.

When that happens, the data usually takes the blame. The numbers weren’t granular enough, the dataset wasn’t complete, we need more information before we can act. But the data is almost never the problem. The reality is that nobody designed it to deliver insights. The chart was built from what was available, not from the question that needed answering. The audience was assumed rather than understood, and what should actually change as a result of seeing this data — that question — was never asked at all.

According to recent reports, data visualisation and UX are solving the same underlying problem: both are trying to move the right information to the right person in a way that changes something. The vocabulary is different, but the underlying challenge is identical, and the moment you start treating them as complementary disciplines is the moment dashboards stop being a passive collection of charts and start doing something functional.

For designers who work with data, analysts who present to non-technical audiences, and marketers who need their numbers to do more than sit in a slide, this read is for you.

In 1973, the statistician Francis Anscombe (PDF) published a paper that made a quiet but clarifying point. He constructed four datasets that are statistically identical: same mean, same variance, same correlation coefficient, and same regression line. Run the numbers on any of them, and they are identical. Plot them, and they could not be more different.

Anscombe’s lesson to statisticians was about diagnosis: visualisation reveals the operational truth that raw numbers conceal.

Recent findings suggest that but visualisation isn’t just diagnostic; it is also communicative. The form you choose is where understanding either emerges or gets lost in the noise. Does your audience walk away with numbers, or with a story they’ll quote and talk about?

One of the most striking examples is Visual Capitalist’s History of Pandemics. Instead of burying the reader in a massive data table of casualty counts, it maps the death toll of major historical pandemics using a proportional bubble layout on a single timeline.

Before your brain reads a single number, your visual system grasps the sheer scale of the Black Death relative to everything else on the page. The right visualisation does not just plot the data but makes the story impossible to miss.

Edward Tufte codified a foundational principle for the craft with his data-ink ratio: every mark on a chart should serve the data, not decorate it. It remains a widely used framework in data visualisation, anchored in the assumption that clarity and visual hygiene are the goal.

For a chart in isolation, that holds. But a chart is never read in isolation: it’s read by a person, in a specific context, under specific pressure. Strip a chart down to its cleanest form, and you might be removing the exact layer of context a decision-maker needs. Simplicity isn’t the goal in itself; appropriate complexity is.

Data is a message, and the right amount of signal depends entirely on who’s receiving it.

Which leads to the core principle of data UX: roughly 80% of the work that determines whether a dashboard succeeds happens before you ever draw a chart.

That dependency is the thread the rest of this piece pulls on.

Sources indicate that the high-leverage 80% almost never happens on screen. It happens upstream: before a tool is opened, before a dataset is pulled, before a single design choice is made. It comes down to three questions, and once they become habitual, they change what you notice, what you ask, and what you push back on at the outset of every project.

Industry observers note that most data-heavy projects start backward: teams pull whatever metrics their internal analytics tools already track and build visualisations around them, while the question the data was supposed to answer either gets assumed or never gets asked. This happens simply because we anchor on the data in front of us as the boundary of what’s possible.

According to recent reports, defining a goal first sounds obvious, but in practice, it rarely happens with the necessary clarity. “Show me how the product is performing” is not a goal; “Identify which features drive retention among users who signed up in Q1” is, as it includes three things the first doesn’t: a metric, a population, and an implied action. That specificity is what converts an open-ended exploration into a constrained, answerable design problem. Which one you start from determines everything that follows: what you include, what comparisons matter, and what you leave out entirely.

Starting with available data produces a dashboard that answers no particular question, because it was never built for one — every number is present, none of them pointed anywhere. Starting with the operational question does the reverse: every element on the screen earns its place, because each one is there to help answer it.

Industry observers note that for example, consider a UX team trying to fix a leaky checkout flow for an e-commerce website. A data-first approach pulls everything available, from clicks to scroll depth and device types, yielding a massive dashboard that leaves everyone asking, “Okay, but what do we actually change?” A context-first approach starts with a constraint: “At which step of the checkout do users drop off?” By filtering out 90% of the noise, the team builds a simple funnel chart, instantly spots a bottleneck on the payment screen, and knows exactly what to redesign.

Designing for an audience comes down to two things: accountability and familiarity.

Familiarity is about data literacy. Do they read charts instinctively, or does a complex visualisation create friction? Handing a dense, multi-layered dashboard to a Head of Sales and a senior analyst is like giving the same map to someone who navigates by landmarks and someone who reads grid coordinates. The data is accurate, but it is only functional for one of them.

Industry observers note that accountability dictates how that complexity must be presented. A chart showing a 12% decline carries vastly different weight for the executive responsible for that number versus the analyst simply reporting it. Understanding your audience means grasping this relationship; data is never processed neutrally when your performance is on the line.

Together, familiarity and accountability decide one practical thing: how much you can put in front of someone.

In data visualisation, simplicity is not a fixed virtue — the right level of it is contingent on who is reading, and what they need to do.

According to recent reports, an analyst relies on a high-density environment to conduct diagnostic discovery. By isolating individual behaviour nodes and mapping out raw user flows, they interrogate the data at its atomic level to uncover the hidden insights and underperforming spend that will shape future campaigns.

Sources indicate that an executive, by contrast, requires a highly synthesised translation of that data to immediately identify what is driving commercial growth. Tailoring a dashboard to your audience means adjusting the density dial, delivering maximum signal with appropriate complexity for the specific brain in the room.

According to recent reports, most data projects operate on the comfortable assumption that if a chart is accurate and clear, the insight will take care of itself. In reality, information and insight are entirely different states. Information is what the data indicates, whereas insight is the specific decision, shift in understanding, or course correction someone makes as a result of seeing it. If the intended business change isn’t defined before the design begins, a dashboard will default to passive reporting rather than driving action.

Marketing and engineering teams experience the danger of this gap whenever a core business metric suddenly plummets.

A dashboard built for information simply sounds the alarm, showing a chart that tracks a sharp 15% drop in booking rates. Because the data lacks depth, leadership defaults to panic: they immediately call the UX design team, assuming the app is broken or the checkout flow is flawed. Because the data doesn’t pinpoint the core of the problem, it triggers a costly, misplaced fire drill.

It has been revealed that A dashboard built for insight isolates the variables required to make an informed decision. Instead of a single, flat booking metric, the visualisation maps the drop against traffic sources and campaign releases — instantly revealing that while app performance and core user conversion are perfectly stable, the sitewide rate was artificially diluted by a massive influx of low-intent click traffic from a newly scaled campaign. The team doesn’t waste time redesigning a functioning app; they get the exact insight needed to pause the underperforming marketing campaign and adjust their acquisition strategy.

Every visualisation implies a next step, even if that step is “nothing needs to change right now.” The question is whether the design makes that implication clear enough for the viewer to recognise it.

Industry observers note that my aha moment in data visualisation happened during a project for a client-facing B2B SaaS platform focused on enterprise talent management and competency tracking in Pegasystems skills. The platform captured a massive footprint of daily telemetry, and the brief arrived open-ended: “We have an immense archive of user activity, now we need to present it to enterprise teams.”.

We could very easily have charted everything that was captured, but we wouldn’t be doing end users any favours if they just ended up looking at a data graveyard. My responsibility immediately moved beyond pure interface craftsmanship; it became about architecting a highly practical tool for real people who would open this dashboard routinely and need it to tell them an honest, immediate story about their workflows.

Here is how the project actually went.

The client believed this massive pool of data could help their people perform better, and wanted an interface that finally enabled that growth. Translating that broad ambition into tangible visualisations required defining the practical mechanics of performance. What variables indicate advancement vs passive usage? What does “perform better” actually mean? How do you measure it?

It has been revealed that an obvious candidate was time spent by product. Every platform tracks it. It is easy to show, and it feels meaningful. But time spent is a proxy; it tells you someone was there, not whether they got anything out of it.

According to recent reports, the more meaningful signals were competency scores by area, certification completion rates, and historical performance trajectories. Integrating time-spent data alongside these performance metrics added a useful layer of interpretation, helping us surface which modules consumers were underutilising and whether that directly correlated with lagging scores. Time spent became a supporting signal in the larger story.

The second question was about the appropriate level of granularity. An identical metric carries completely different weight depending on who is looking at it. An individual contributor tracking their own completion rate needs to know if they are pacing correctly, whereas a manager reviewing a team aggregate needs to know precisely who requires immediate support. This distinction shaped every subsequent data-exposure and filtering decision. Defining that structural story early determined exactly what to show, and to whom.

It has been revealed that the most straightforward approach to this design would have been predictable: use the same charts, but offer an individual view and an aggregated team view. Far too many dashboards rely on this shortcut, subtly tweaking the scale of identical data visualisations and labelling it “personalisation.”.

It has been revealed that an authentic analysis of the audience reveals a much deeper rift. Frontline team leads and individual contributors required distinct narrative structures and design principles.

Having used e-learning platforms myself, I remember the frustration of opening a tool without a clear sense of my current standing, core strengths, or slipping metrics. That personal experience directly guided the individual contributor workspace; it needed to act as a highly tailored, self-directed mirror that was granular, honest, and personal.

Sources indicate that conversely, the manager’s interface had to bypass individual milestones initially to provide a macro pulse check on team vulnerabilities. It was designed around a different operational reality: how is the group progressing, and where are the consistent gaps? The view prioritised the aggregate picture first, while retaining an intuitive path to drill down into tactical day-to-day coordination when needed.

Our insight strategy was locked in during the early conceptual phase, long before wireframing a single chart. We intentionally abandoned the idea of building a dense, passive data log and focused on pacing the narrative arc.

For individual contributors, the core value was self-direction, ensuring they could glance at the interface on a Monday morning and immediately derive a clear priority list for the week ahead.

For managers, the goal was to fundamentally shift the timing of operational conversations, providing them with the necessary baseline to intervene before a skill gap evolved into a critical project failure. The visualisations needed to surface the exact moments when a human check-in would be useful, shifting their workflow from reactive post-mortems to proactive guidance.

According to recent reports, the comparison tool was the highlight nobody had asked for. A manager dashboard and an individual dashboard are easy to anticipate. What is harder to land is: what if a manager wants to compare two specific team members against the same metrics, side by side? That view came from a design assumption, and it turned out to be the feature that resonated most.

The decisions that mattered most in this project weren’t in the initial brief — capturing data they hadn’t thought to request, and structuring it to answer questions they had not previously known how to articulate, which is the core differentiator of a user-centric data strategy.

The choice of visualisation layout must follow the geometric nature of the data itself. For this project, the core design problem was enabling an individual user to answer a specific question at a single glance: across eight distinct competency areas, where are my relative strengths and gaps?

Industry observers note that to solve this, we mapped the data using a radar chart. By organising multiple variables across axes radiating from a central point using polar coordinates, the interface connects the data points to form a single, unified shape. An even, balanced polygon instantly signals well-rounded proficiency, while a sharply skewed shape draws the eye immediately to an outlier area.

While a traditional linear bar chart would have forced the viewer to scan eight individual bars and mentally calculate the variance, a concentric, radial layout segments the data layers to make progress tracking and skill gaps immediately readable. When all dimensions share an identical scale and scoring method, the radar chart is not an unconventional aesthetic choice — it is the most functional tool for multi-dimensional analysis.

It has been revealed that the colour system was the other decision made early, and I mean early. During the branding exercise, each of the three products was assigned a colour. That colour did not stay in the brand guidelines. It was built into the data model from the beginning, running consistently across every chart, every filter, every breakdown. By the time a user landed on the dashboard for the first time, the mental model was already in place. They had not been taught the language. They already knew it.

Sources indicate that the shift from passive information to active insight highlighted up first in how the dashboard was actually used. Following the deployment of the personalised dashboards and side-by-side team comparison tools, weekly active engagement on the platform’s analytics features rose noticeably, per internally reported figures. Managers were no longer opening the tool once a month to pull static reports. They were using it every Monday morning to actively plan their week.

Revenue and user growth also moved in the right direction over the following two quarters, though — as with most single-project outcomes — it’s hard to isolate the dashboard’s exact contribution from everything else that changed at the same time. The client reported churn across the platform falling to one of its lowest points on record. The clearest evidence of impact came from qualitative feedback. Managers reported that instead of using data to dissect a ‘bad’ month after the fact, the visualisations allowed them to instantly spot slipping performance and schedule a quick supportive catch-up before it turned into a real gap.

Recent findings suggest that data design reaches its full potential when visual presentation is treated as an upstream architectural choice rather than a downstream formatting step. Bringing structured UX thinking to data turns visualisations into active decision-making engines, ensuring every chart, report, and metric directly serves a human purpose:.

Sources indicate that the next time you are tasked with creating a data visualisation — whether it is an enterprise dashboard, an executive report, or a public-facing infographic — step away from the design canvas and BI tools. Focus your initial effort on the human decisions behind the screen. Only then will your data stop being a passive log of the past and start driving the direction of the future.

The Dinner Ladies

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Dinner Ladies needed a recipe for a rebrand that would not only pay respect to their unique origin story but bring their visual and verbal identity up to speed with their growth as Australia’s tastiest frozen meal service. We joined forces to cook them up a fresh look and feel that reflects their homely meals and anti-“mumsy” attitude, extending all the way from their website through to their packaging. Now whack the oven on, because Australia’s hottest frozen meal service has arrived.

Since it all began with two determined women in a Sydney-side backyard shed in 2007, The Dinner Ladies have been filling the freezers, bellies and hearts of thousands of busy Australian families with their ready-to-heat comfort meals. Born from a deep understanding of dinner time chaos, and the desire to bring some ease back into this routine, The Dinner Ladies’ commitment to delivering meals worthy of mum’s tick of approval remains unwavering.

Industry observers note that the market for pre-prepared meal delivery is an oversaturated landscape steeped in clichés and same-same messaging that claims to be the most healthy, convenient or delicious dinnertime solution. They not only lack a distinct personality but also relatability to their customer — time-poor people who just want simple, genuinely good, homemade meals that help take the pressure off when it’s needed most. This is where The Dinner Ladies shine. A flavour-stacked service that takes care of dinner, so you can focus on doing life.

The brand had become known and loved for their unexpected, no nonsense and slightly audacious approach. This was not only refreshingly real but a reflection of both their wholesome offering and the founding ladies. However, over seventeen years of brand iterations their look had become diluted, lost its attitudinal punch, and needed a significant serve of reinvigoration. Our vision was to bring back the best from their history and turn up the heat across the board to let the nation know they mean (meal delivery) business.

We fully immersed ourselves in The Dinner Ladies story, from taking a deep dive through past website designs and hand drawn logos on a napkin, to visiting the shed where it all began and the factory where it now thrives. This helped us draw out the strongest existing brand elements, like their early trad-tattoo-esque illustrations and counter-“mumsy” stereotype, and turn them into a modern evolution. Driven by “Food from the Heart,” each component of the visual identity communicates the brand essence and no-BS confidence of a service that truly helps take the stress out of dinnertime.

The first step was the refinement of the logo. By decoupling the heart and the script, we gave it flexibility, made it easier to read at every touchpoint and allowed it to scale as needed. The custom heart logo was designed by us and then, alongside the wordmark, handed to illustrator Jake Foreman to redraw and personalise with his iconic texture and gritty stipple.

The Dinner Ladies’ existing red already had distinct brand attribution in the category so we just refined it with a bright and modern twist. The secondary palette supports our hero red with a balance of warm, approachable and slightly retro hues. When united, the system unlocks a number of interesting and vibrant combinations that are particularly useful across hard-working digital applications.

In a recent development, we used the typeface Denim by Displaay Type Foundry to show off the brand’s confident personality yet retain practicality. Denim Wide’s used in headings and call-to-action applications to command attention, while its regular cut counterpart rounds out the system with a friendly, clean and legible option for subheadings and body copy. With its subtle details, the typeface can be an attention-grabbing hero element that showcases the bold tone of voice but also work alongside more expressive moments.

The tone of voice needed to capture the brand’s joyful, cheeky yet comforting personality, while steering clear of any patronising “mumsy” tropes and stereotypes. We worked with copywriter Cat Wall to develop a verbal identity that balanced the empathetic caregiver with the charmingly rebellious tone of the ladies themselves. In a category saturated with over-sincerity and fake friendliness, the tone offers a refreshing sprinkle of irreverence with a straight-forward, bull-free reflection of the audience and their needs.

The photography celebrates the authentic messiness of real life dinnertime. A reflection of the brand’s tell-it-like-it-is attitude, the shoot didn’t shy away from capturing raw moments — the remnants of a great dish alongside a fresh one being served or a bolognese-faced baby — mixed with the joy of sharing generous, mouth-watering food.

With Alana Dimou behind the lens, Jerrie-Joy Redman-Lloyd on styling, Oriana De Luca on wardrobe, Gavin Anesbury with a hair and makeup brush in hand, and Michaela Le on production, the brand came to life. Warm, natural lighting, combined with quirky styling choices, pops of colour or pattern and intentional (and encouraged) chaos set a homely and inviting scene with a pinch of rebellion.

Sources indicate that illustration has always been a major piece of The Dinner Ladies’ brand so we wanted to bring it across to the rebrand. The original illustrations’ punk and rough-around-the-edges flair drew us to references of traditional trad tattoos.

Collaborating further with illustrator Jake Foreman, we crafted a suite of illustrations that served as both personality-rich storytelling pieces and functional devices. While the small scenes and spots speak to specific offerings of the brand, the hero illustration speaks to the love behind every Dinner Ladies dish and the comforting shared experiences created around the table.

These illustrations are supported by our suite of type-furniture elements that not only support the main design elements but add character to any layout.

Sources indicate that as a product that’s often shoved into the freezer and then reached for in a rush, legibility and easy differentiation were priorities for designing the packaging. A simple colour-coded system helps to distinguish between protein groups at a glance, making it quick and effortless to find the crowd-pleasing meal that’s ready to save the day.

Industry observers note that the Dinner Ladies now have a brand that not only celebrates their seventeen year legacy but gives them the tools for future decades of success. The flexible design system and punchy tone of voice pays tribute to their tenacious past, the founding ladies behind the service and their wholesome mission put joy back into dinner time. Now The Dinner Ladies can stand loud and proud with a brand that reflects their readiness to dish up delicious dinners to an entire nation.

Photography courtesy of OKA.

Robotics startup OKA has released a lamp-shaped artificial intelligence robot designed to offer companionship by greeting people, dancing to music and playing nature sounds.

Mori by OKA (One Kind Artificat) is 26.4 centimetres tall, with a cloth-covered base and an illuminated, dome-shaped head that lifts to reveal cartoonish eyes that blink and swivel.

According to OKA, Mori “resembles a contemporary table lamp” and was designed to “help people feel calmer, more at ease, and more connected to the world around them”.

Industry observers note that “We wanted Mori to feel like a familiar object in the home rather than an unfamiliar machine,” OKA told Dezeen. “Many robots look technical, mechanical, or overly human, while a lamp is something people already live with comfortably.”.

The robot exists in two modes: a lamp setting, when it’s compact and at rest, and a responsive setting, when the head is lifted and tilted.

Powered by the start-up’s proprietary AI system, the robot’s responses include playing audio informed by rain and other nature sounds, changing the colour of its lamp top and performing nonverbal communication through multi-axis neck and body movement.

Customers tap the top of Mori’s head and it “retracts its face and becomes a quiet lamp”. As another part of its calming offerings, grabbing its base triggers a breathing exercise.

It also makes small sounds as part of these interactions.

Sources indicate that “Mori’s soft silhouette and tactile materials let it blend into domestic interiors,” noted OKA. “Its warmth, brightness, and subtle changes can suggest comfort, curiosity, or calm, which lets Mori express itself through illumination, sound, and movement instead of screens or conversation.”.

According to the company, Mori will remember occupants, routines, and interaction history and adjust its behaviour accordingly, such as using “judgment to decide when to proactively engage or remain quiet”.

The AI model is based on the concept of Attentive Intelligence, built upon research by OKA co-founder Weizhe Chen. Attentive Intelligence is an emerging framework within AI, wherein a model is proactive versus reactive to prompts.

“It reads the room before responding and weighs whether to join in, so sometimes a small nod is enough and sometimes it stays quiet,” said OKA.

According to recent reports, “Its responses are shaped by VIBE (Vitality, Interaction, Bonding, Emotion), an inner state that drifts with time and experience, so the same greeting can come out lively one day and gentle the next.”Mori comes in a variety of soft colourways and is rechargeable with a 2.5-hour battery life. However, OKA suggests keeping it plugged in.

It has been revealed that OKA was founded in 2024 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, by entrepreneur and designer Hua Wang and robotics researcher Weizhe Che. The firm is focused on creating robotic projects that “integrate seamlessly into human life rather than forcing human life to adapt to technology”.

Industry observers note that OKA plans to release five major “artifacts” or products in its lifetime, according to the team. The Mori robot is the first.

Mori joins a growing number of home robots released recently with “embodied AI” – or the act of inserting an AI model into a robotic body.

Other home robots include the Droxel “droid butler” and Neo, a humanoid robot dressed in a cloth bodysuit.

Photography courtesy of OKA.

Alpha Bank has unveiled a major transformation of its brand identity and retail branches, combining work by Pentagram and Dalziel & Pow.

Visiting a retail bank branch rarely tops anyoneâs weekend wishlist. Historically, retail banking has felt like visiting an administrative waiting room: grey acoustic tiles, harsh overhead fluorescent tubes, and pens tethered to counters by tiny bead chains. For Alpha Bank, a 147-year-old Greek financial institution with roots stretching back to 1879, modernizing that relationship required more than just slapping a fresh coat of blue paint over the ATM lobby.

To tackle the overhaul, Alpha Bank brought in Pentagram for the visual identity and Dalziel & Pow for the spatial retail experience. Pentagram designer Domenic Lippa looked back to the bankâs original 1972 emblem, which drew inspiration from the ancient silver stater of Aegina. Pentagram redrew the historic symbol, preserving the subtle asymmetry of the ancient coin while sharpening its central axis for digital screens. Backing up the refreshed mark is Alpha Sans, a clean custom typeface engineered in both Greek and Latin scripts, paired with a saturated revival of the institutionâs signature Alpha Blue.

Over in Athensâ Kolonaki district, Dalziel & Pow translated that graphic system into a pilot branch that feels remarkably welcoming. Light-toned timber, textured wall panelling, abundant greenery, and local Greek marble replace clinical barriers. Digital queue systems and self-service kiosks handle routine transactions, while acoustic felt panels and warm banquette seating create private consultation corners without closing off rooms. In the double-height atrium, a sculptural ceiling light abstracts the Aegina coin symbol, and the upper floor borrows cues from boutique hospitality for Alpha Gold clients.

With plans to roll out this modular blueprint across more than 240 branches across Greece alongside local architects A team, the project reveals what happens when graphic systems and interior architecture communicate from day one. It turns everyday banking into a comfortable, human space where people might actually linger over coffee.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The relationship between wood and ceramic remains central to the collection.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that delf began as a single bed. Danny Kaplan designed the Paravent Bed for his own home, basing its strong, paneled silhouette on the hinged screens of Jean-Michel Frank, before he and Vince Patti of Lesser Miracle saw the potential for a larger commercial collection. That collection launched in 2024. Following its commercial success, the two Newly introduced York–based designers have expanded it with Delf II, adding a desk, a coffee table, a console, and a nightstand that extend the series beyond the bedroom.

The relationship between wood and ceramic remains central to the collection. Each piece is crafted from white oak and accented with hand-built ceramic, the pairing that defined the original bed and inspired the collection’s name. Delf derives from delven, the Dutch verb meaning to mine or to dig, a reference to the channels carved into the wood and filled by hand with ceramic tile inlays.

Industry observers note that kaplan, a self-taught ceramicist who founded his studio in 2015, creates the tilework, drawing inspiration from the pottery of Vallauris, a region in southern France known for its ceramics. It is offered in the studio’s signature glazes: Stone, Anthracite, Terrasig, Ivy, Lapis, Agate, Bronze, and Chestnut, along with a new Navy. Around the tile, the oak takes modernist architectural forms softened by rounded edges and subtle curves.

According to recent reports, bringing the two materials together requires a carefully sequenced production process. The ceramic components are fired separately, then individually fitted into the hand-built wooden structures. The drawer hardware is first modeled in clay, then cast in brass and aluminum. A single piece in the collection takes weeks to produce.

As with the original collection, the design process begins with Kaplan’s hand sketches before moving through drawing, discussion, prototyping, and digital modeling between the two studios.

For Kaplan, the expansion was an opportunity to explore how the original design language could translate to different furniture forms. The new pieces allowed the pair to continue “developing that language while thinking about how the collection could live throughout an entire interior.”.

Patti sees the expansion as a natural evolution of their collaboration. The Brooklyn-based designer, whose practice draws on 1970s pulp fantasy, Timurid architecture, and the work of Frank Lloyd Wright, claims the new collection “builds on the same principles as the original pieces, but with greater confidence and complexity.”.

Leo Lei is the founder and editor of Leibal, a publication dedicated to minimalist design, architecture, and interiors. Through his writing and curatorial eye, he highlights thoughtful contemporary work from around the world.

PPAA creates twin houses in Mexico as an "argument for building less"

  • “Avándaro is a landscape that’s been quietly overbuilt for decades, so the first decision on Rejas was actually a renunciation,” Pablo Pérez Palacios, founder of Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados (PPAA), told Dezeen,.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Fabián Martínez.

Mexican architecture studio Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados has completed twin houses that combine concrete with glued-laminated timber in the forests of Valle de Bravo, Mexico.

The two houses – each measuring 500 square metres (5,382 square feet) – are collectively called Rejas and were designed for two brothers and their families, cohabitating on a 1.2-acre forested property in Avándaro, a couple of hours west of Mexico City.

“Avándaro is a landscape that’s been quietly overbuilt for decades, so the first decision on Rejas was actually a renunciation,” Pablo Pérez Palacios, founder of Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados (PPAA), told Dezeen,.

“Instead of designing a wall or a fence between the two brothers’ houses, we chose to regenerate the native forest that the site had partially lost, and let that stand as the boundary,” he said, explainging that decision set the tone for the rest of the project.

“The whole project is really an argument for building less, so the landscape has room to eventually reclaim the architecture.”.

The site, with its regenerated forest, is steeply sloped toward the Avándaro reservoir, allowing PPAA to partially submerge each house.

From the driveway, the houses appear as one-storey structures, but the lower levels emerge on the other side as the terrain descends.

To navigate this, the houses sit on bases of concrete and local stone that anchor them into the slope, while timber roofs top the upper levels and open the spaces to the surrounding trees.

The houses were designed to interact with the landscape, and have almost identical intends, though their place in the landscape differs.

Public spaces are on the upper level, with a kitchen, dining and living room in a glass box within the larger, rectangular platform.

A covered terrace comprises the remainder of the level with designated seating and outdoor cooking areas that are framed with planters.

Below, five bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms and a lounge area sit within the forest floor, cool and contained within the boxy volume.

The stepped arrangement of both floors, in proposal and section, also operates as a device for privacy between the two houses, PPAA explained.

Sources indicate that “The deliberate positioning of the openings eliminates any possibility of facing windows – no window in one house looks toward the other. Each dwelling establishes its own relationship with the natural surroundings as if the other did not exist.”.

The studio pulled the service areas for both houses into separate buildings placed along the edge of the property to free the centre of the plot for the houses and their relationships with the landscape.

Designed to patina with the landscape, the minimalist material palette relies on stone and concrete to give mass and solidity to the base and mass timber to be both the structure and spatial character of the upper level.

The pairing allows the materials to complement one another, juxtaposing lightness and weight.

“This tension between the stone base that anchors and the glulam roof that liberates is neither an aesthetic operation nor a reference to any vernacular tradition,” the studio said.

“It is a proposition about how to inhabit: what protects and what opens, what remains and what breathes, what belongs to the ground and what belongs to the air.”.

Long known for concrete construction like this subtractive house in Los Angeles, PPAA has been expanding recently into mass timber design with projects like a rotating cross-laminated timber pavilion in Mexico City and Mexico’s first “all-wood” mass timber structure in Querétaro.

Architecture: PPAADesign Team: Pablo Pérez Palacios, Emilio Calvo, Miguel Vargas, Jonathan Reséndiz, Adriana Hernández Interiors: Mariana Morales.

Photography by Fabián Martínez.

#223. Reviving an Enduring Emblem of Simplicity, Loll Designs Releases the Here and There Collection

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (630 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Design-milk

Reviving an Enduring Emblem of Simplicity, Loll Designs Releases the Here and There Collection

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the best designs almost always come out of necessity and quiet observation.
  • “Anyone that’s handy with a saw and some fasteners and lumber could easily build an Aldo bench,” claims Eric Swanson, president of Duluth-based outdoor furniture brand Loll Designs.
  • Sources indicate that this contemporary reinterpretation was twelve years in the making.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the best designs almost always come out of necessity and quiet observation. In the 1940s, legendary ecologist Aldo Leopold constructed a remarkably straightforward wooden bench so that he could sit outside his Wisconsin farmstead and contemplate nature’s primal force; the fundamental need for its conservation. The back-slanted seat was constructed from readily available dimensional lumber and almost immediately presented itself as an act of unpretentious, serendipitous genius: the quick assembly of a functional furnishing devised for a specific need but ultimately, one with universal potential. The particular brilliance of the design was its x-shaped self-bracing geometry, zero waste configuration, and uncomplicated assembly.

“Anyone that’s handy with a saw and some fasteners and lumber could easily build an Aldo bench,” claims Eric Swanson, president of Duluth-based outdoor furniture brand Loll Designs. “That’s the beauty of it.” The Minnesota manufacturer recently teamed up with Michigan industrial design studio Argenta Park to turn the foundational artifact into the Here and There Collection. Named for Leopold’s belief that our appreciation for the natural world should balance between what’s nearby and farther afield, the cohesive and complementary suite of furnishings includes a dining chair, dining table, and of course, a bench.

Photography courtesy of Loll Designs.

Sources indicate that this contemporary reinterpretation was twelve years in the making. For his outdoor wedding in 2014, Argenta Park designer Ricky Biddle was faced with the same practical challenge Leopold surmounted decades earlier: creating sturdy, durable, and comfortable outdoor seating. He didn’t want to rent generic, flimsy event furniture, so he spent his bachelor party assembling rudimentary Aldo benches. It was almost as if influential Italian designer Enzo Mari had sanctioned the task as one of his open-source “Autoprogettazione” self designs.

According to recent reports, the pieces have remained a fixture of Biddle and his family’s everyday life ever since. This permanence prompted him to reconsider how its raw genius might be retooled using advanced manufacturing, elevated ergonomics, and year-round durability. He brought the idea to Argenta Park founder Churu Yun and the Loll Designs engineering team.

Photography courtesy of Loll Designs.

Industry observers note that the best type of historical preservation is the kind that implements the latest technologies and refined strategies; doesn’t focus on creating replicas merely out of nostalgic reverence. “Not all historical designs lend themselves to being evolved into a modern-day furniture piece,” says Brian King, Loll Designs Brand and Marketing Director. “It’s more about being hyper selective in a design that has meaning, history, or a deep-rooted memory and identifying what’s most valuable.” Loll had done this many times before, most notably by bringing the ubiquitous Adirondack Chair up to contemporary standards.

While still carrying the original design’s understated silhouette, the re-edited and expanded collection carefully addressed the physical limitations of simple timber construction. Softly contoured surfaces replace flat planks, streamlined fastener assembly, and the use of 100% recyclable high-density polyethylene (HDPE)—available in Black, Charcoal Grey, Fog, and Sage—simplifies ongoing maintenance.

Photography courtesy of Loll Designs.

This calculus responds to changing demands: contemporary homeowners are increasingly looking for low-maintenance solutions that can withstand harsh seasonal shifts without sacrificing aesthetic refinement or tactile comfort. “With historical designs comes historical maintenance and poor ergonomics,” Swanson adds. “People want to enjoy their time outdoors sitting in their furniture more than working on it, which is why using alternative materials to traditional wood is a benefit; why a curved seat and backrest is so important; and why the right proportions—the height of the dining table—make all the difference.”.

Industry observers note that leopold is widely considered the founder of wildlife ecology and his bench stands testament to that; allowing people to enjoy nature for as long as they want. The latest Here and There Collection carries on that legacy.

The Death Of The Button: Why The Best Interface Is No Interface

📖 0% read
