  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, that contract is officially changing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, that contract is officially changing. Driven by advances in artificial intelligence and large language models, a new generation of web tools is pioneering a radical philosophy: Intent-Driven Design. Rather than expecting our users to learn complex menus and click through elaborate sales funnels, these platforms operate by capturing high-level human goals and silently executing the grunt work in the background.

This vision builds on long-standing HCI concepts like Golden Krishna’s “The Best Interface Is No Interface” and Don Norman’s principles of human-centered design.

The ultimate goal of modern web design is no longer to build prettier buttons or flashy animations; it is to eliminate the interface entirely.

Well, at least what we understand based on our current experience.

It is essential for UX designers to understand the changes we’re witnessing and even re-evaluate our role, shifting our focus from designing visible interfaces to guiding transparent, intent-driven AI experiences.

To understand where web design is going, we first have to look at the friction we have accepted as “normal” for decades.

Sources indicate that consider the traditional workflow of buying a flight online. The user experience is intentionally hyper-interactive:.

Recent findings suggest that this is a classic point-and-click UI paradigm. The computer acts as a passive container of data, and the human acts as the orchestrator, manually inputting parameters, interpreting raw outputs, and executing each micro-step along the way.

Recent findings suggest that intent-driven design flips this dynamic entirely. Instead of forcing you to navigate the mechanical steps of how to find a flight, the interface asks a simple question: What are you trying to accomplish?

When you express a goal, such as “Find me a non-stop flight to Chicago next weekend under $300 that arrives before 5 PM”, the software reads your intent, executes the multi-step search query behind the scenes, compares the options, and presents a single actionable resolution. The ten clicks dissolve into one clear intent outcome.

It has been revealed that this shift isn’t a theoretical vision of the distant future. Some of the world’s most accessible websites allow you to experience intent-capturing systems already.

Sources indicate that traditional search engines like Google were built as directories. You typed a keyword, and the interface rewarded you with ten blue links. The actual work of opening five tabs, skimming long articles, dodging ads, and manually assembling an answer was left to you. Although this is now changing, with AI content appearing first when you search on Google.

Perplexity AI allows anyone to perform instant intent-based searches. Instead of forcing you to click into multiple tabs, the interface synthesises the perfect result for your context.

According to recent reports, for years, creating a website meant using visual builders like Figma or drag-and-drop web editors. As designers, we spent hours manually drawing rectangles, picking hexadecimal colour codes, adjusting padding values, and sometimes writing CSS code.

Vercel v0 lets anyone test its generative interface builder right from the home page without signing in.

Sources indicate that many traditional productivity tools require you to manually construct task lists, drag items across Kanban boards, and assign micro-deadlines. Goblin.tools is a free, single-page suite of single-task AI tools designed specifically for neurodivergent owners or anyone feeling overwhelmed, requiring zero sign-ups or configuration.

According to recent reports, when you remove traditional menus, sidebars, and forms, how do you keep a website usable? Designers pioneering this space rely on three core pillars:.

In a recent development, an invisible interface doesn’t always wait for you to type a command — it leverages context to anticipate user needs. Guided by industry standards like Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines on Contextual & Ambient Design, modern systems read environmental metadata, such as device state, location, and past interaction patterns, to trigger proactive actions.

In traditional web design, every user sees the exact same layout. An e-commerce store reveals the same navigation bar whether you are a first-time visitor looking for customer support or a returning customer tracking a package.

In a recent development, as highlighted in the Nielsen Norman Group’s analysis on AI as a upcoming UX paradigm, computing is shifting from command-based interaction to outcome-specification. This enables Generative UI, where interfaces are rendered dynamically on the fly based on what you are trying to do in that exact moment. For example, platforms like Vercel v0 demonstrate how raw intent can instantly render functional code components without manual layout building. If you express a desire to compute complex financial data, the interface generates a dynamic calculator widget on demand, receding once your goal is completed.

Traditional interfaces are obsessed with prevention, constantly peppering people with confirmation pop-ups (“Are you sure you want to delete this file?”).

It has been revealed that intent-driven interfaces adapt Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics on User Control and Error Recovery by shifting the safety net from prevention to easy reversibility. Because autonomous agents take actions on your behalf, products prioritise frictionless rollback mechanisms. A prominent “Undo” button, simple revision prompts (“Make this summary shorter”), and transparent audit logs replace intrusive warning modals.

While removing interface friction is liberating, stripping away visual controls introduces significant product design challenges. When software acts on inferred intent rather than direct point-and-click commands, designers must navigate critical ethical and technical pitfalls.

It has been revealed that when a website makes decisions for you, it can swiftly feel patronising or invasive. As explored by the Stanford Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) Group, automation must maintain clear boundaries to prevent user frustration. Furthermore, ethical frameworks from the Center for Humane Technology emphasise that product designers must guard against manipulative defaults.

Designers must strike a delicate balance: automate routine execution, but explicitly prompt the user for high-stakes confirmations (such as financial transactions, publishing public content, or altering privacy settings).

In a traditional UI, if you get an unexpected result, you can usually diagnose the matter — perhaps you checked the wrong filter box or selected an incorrect date.

With an intent-driven interface, troubleshooting becomes harder. To address this “black box” challenge, the Google PAIR (People + AI Research) Guidebook advocates for transparent feedback loops. The system must explicitly state its interpretation (“Searching for non-stop flights to Chicago under $300…”) so consumers can calibrate trust and correct misinterpretations instantly.

As a UX designer, always being curious to understand how our design approach is changing in the world of AI, I find it essential that we re-evaluate the foundational elements of our craft.

Rather than designing static buttons and rigid forms, we need to learn to map and present dynamic, generative UI components that adapt on the fly to user intent.

By mastering these evolving patterns, like ambient feedback, inline prompts, and transparent AI status indicators, we can ensure that screenless, agent-driven tools remain intuitive, ethical, and deeply human-centered.

Industry observers note that for decades, the digital industry has evaluated software success through engagement metrics like time spent in app, click-through rates, and page views per session. Websites were deliberately engineered to maximise visual engagement and interaction volume.

The philosophy behind Golden Krishna’s seminal book The Best Interface Is No Interface, aligned with the broader Center for Humane Technology’s Time Well Spent movement, turns these metrics on their head. The ultimate test of a modern digital product is no longer how visually captivating its buttons are, but rather: How effectively did this software solve the problem and get out of the user’s way?,.

We are entering an era where web applications will no longer be measured by the beauty of their interfaces, but by their ability to render those complex interfaces completely obsolete. The future of the web isn’t more interaction — it is seamless, invisible completion.

#221. Philadelphia city council investigates sudden closure of oldest natural history research institution in the Americas

Philadelphia city council investigates sudden closure of oldest natural history research institution in the Americas

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Academy of Natural Sciences, a 198-year-old public museum in Philadelphia run by Drexel University, shuttered in September because of rising costs.
  • It has been revealed that while many of the Academy’s workers have been laid off, collection managers still on staff have faced an “astronomical increase” in emails and calls, notes Amber Redfield, a former geosciences collection manager and fossil preparator at the Academy who was recently laid off and is now volunteering there.
  • Isa Betancourt, a former curatorial assistant in the entomology department and an organiser with the Save the Academy coalition, says the number of curators has dropped from 11 to five.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Academy of Natural Sciences, a 198-year-old public museum in Philadelphia run by Drexel University, shuttered in September because of rising costs. The university’s president will now testify under subpoena before Philadelphia’s city council on 16 November, answering questions about the sudden closure and what will happen to the museum’s valuable collection of more than 19 million specimens.

It has been revealed that while many of the Academy’s workers have been laid off, collection managers still on staff have faced an “astronomical increase” in emails and calls, notes Amber Redfield, a former geosciences collection manager and fossil preparator at the Academy who was recently laid off and is now volunteering there. She says that people have been asking: “Is this safe?” “Can I see it?” “Can I book an appointment?”.

Isa Betancourt, a former curatorial assistant in the entomology department and an organiser with the Save the Academy coalition, says the number of curators has dropped from 11 to five. The invertebrate palaeontology collection manager recently left for a job at the American Museum of Natural History. “There is no blueprint to replace her," Betancourt tells The Art Newspaper. Endowed curator posts in entomology and palaeontology have gone unfilled for years, she adds.

Founded in 1812, the Academy describes itself as the oldest natural history research institution in the Americas. It opened its museum to the public in 1828 and, in 1868, put Hadrosaurus foulkii on view as the world’s first mounted dinosaur skeleton. Its millions of specimens include plants collected on the Lewis and Clark expedition, John James Audubon’s birds and Thomas Jefferson’s fossils.

The Academy became a Drexel affiliate in 2011, while retaining its status as a separate non-profit with its own board. Drexel recently told the city council it had “stepped in as a partner” that year, when the Academy “faced severe financial distress”.

The city council passed a resolution on 17 September to investigate the Academy’s closing. The resolution calls institutions like the Academy “part of the cultural fabric of the city” and says its shuttering would especially affect area residents “for whom the museum is a fixture of the neighbourhood”. An initial hearing took place on 26 October, which Drexel’s president did not attend.

At the hearing, representatives for Drexel cited the building's "substantial capital needs" and told the city council that public exhibitions need a newly introduced model, "almost certainly in a different location".

According to recent reports, sarah McAnulty, a squid biologist and Save the Academy organiser, states city council members asked Drexel representatives to check their numbers. "If all you need to keep the public museum open is a million dollars, what the hell are we doing here?" she says, describing the city council’s reaction.

The Academy’s Dinosaur Hall Photo: Ms3733, via Wikimedia Commons.

According to recent reports, staff learned of the Academy’s closure at a morning meeting on 1 September, Redfield states. Most staff were laid off by 1 November, and many people "found out they were let go in a report by The Philadelphia Inquirer", she adds.

Redfield says the museum drew more than 60,000 visitors in its final 12 days of public hours. "That's not enough time to shut down a lifetime of scientific and educational work," she adds. "I planned to retire at the Academy and don't have any backup looks." Now she is volunteering.

"Unfortunately, volunteer labour is essential to most natural history collections, but it’s not sustainable,” Betancourt says. “The fact that the volunteer manager was initially slated for termination and had to be reinstated shows Drexel has no idea how these collections function.".

Betancourt adds that the Academy's social media accounts have been inactive for two months and staff do not have access because Drexel controls them. The Academy's director of marketing and communications was let go with the closure. Betancourt says the university may not realise that communications and education staff connect the collections with the public and potential benefactors, "otherwise, the collections work in darkness”.

The William Penn Foundation has offered a year of funding to replace Drexel's subsidy for the museum. "The foundation has not received a response to our offer," a spokesperson told the Inquirer. Drexel later stated that it had not received a "formal proposal with a defined level of financial support".

In a recent development, betancourt claims Save the Academy wants Drexel to explain "why no capital campaign was undertaken" and "why the scientific community has been shut out of behind-the-scenes negotiations. The closed-door negotiations got us a closed museum. Natural history collections tied to a financially haemorrhaging university are not safe natural history collections.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Japanese office intended to evoke a tree canopy, and a revived US concert hall are among the interior design projects to win Best of Globe at this year’s Shaw Contract Design Awards.
  • The upgrade of an athletics clubhouse in the US, a legal workplace in the UK and a large three-story office in India also took the top prize in the annual award programme, now in its 21st year.
  • Held annually by flooring manufacturer Shaw Contract, the Shaw Contract Design Awards celebrate interior design projects that “spark creativity, connect communities and contribute to a better, more sustainable world”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Japanese office intended to evoke a tree canopy, and a revived US concert hall are among the interior design projects to win Best of Globe at this year’s Shaw Contract Design Awards.

The upgrade of an athletics clubhouse in the US, a legal workplace in the UK and a large three-story office in India also took the top prize in the annual award programme, now in its 21st year.

Held annually by flooring manufacturer Shaw Contract, the Shaw Contract Design Awards celebrate interior design projects that “spark creativity, connect communities and contribute to a better, more sustainable world”.

This year’s winning projects were selected from nearly 550 global submissions by an international jury of architects and designers, with interior design students also joining as part of Shaw’s commitment to supporting the next generation of design talent.

According to the jury, the 2026 winners were unified by “a clear design narrative, an understanding of local context, varied and inclusive user experiences, responsible material strategies and a meaningful relationship between design intent and completed space” – despite their varying scales and styles.

“Throughout the global judging session, the jury returned to a central question: whether each project’s stated intent was visible and understandable in the completed design,” explained Shaw Contract.

“The panel distinguished between attractive spaces and projects that used planning, materials, detail and experience to communicate a clear and consequential idea.”.

The St Louis Symphony Orchestra Powell Hall in the US, overhauled by Christner Architects, was one of the winners.

According to Shaw Contract, the jury selected it for its sensitive balance of old and upcoming elements, as well as the key social role it plays in the city, thanks to improved accessibility and audience facilities.

Also in the US is the winning Missouri Athletic Club project, completed by HOK. The scheme involved revamping an existing clubhouse to better suit the needs of its current members.

HOK’s design was commended for adding “a newly introduced layer to the club’s heritage rather than treating the past as a fixed visual theme”, according to the brand, introducing a contemporary layout and aesthetic.

The third winner was We Labo 25F, a small workspace in Japan that embodies the principles of biophilic design – the use of natural features such as plants to improve the wellbeing of building occupants.

Its architect, Okamura, was praised for incorporating greenery as more than just “a decorative layer” and creating an interior that mimics working beneath a tree canopy.

The office was also selected in recognition of its adaptable interiors and circular design features, including furniture made from tsunami debris.

We Labo 25F was one of three workplaces to win Best of Globe, alongside Diageo by M Moser Associates in India and DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects in the UK.

Diageo spans 7,700 square metres and accommodates 300 employees across each of its three floors, accommodating its owner’s expansion from Bengaluru to Gurugram.

Twice Shyâs packaging design for London soap atelier Tula Louise pairs translucent vellum wraps, metal clips, and 12 apothecary outlines.

Jowanda Daley-Thomas debuted Tula Louise in London during COVID while testing clays, charcoal, indigo, and turmeric, yet years of ad-hoc labels had pulled the brand in too many directions. Retailers couldnât tell what separated her bars from standard bath-aisle stock. Independent studio Twice Shy stepped in to reframe the label as a working soap atelier â splitting the catalog with Daley-Thomas into a repeatable Core Collection for shop reorders alongside experimental Studio Editions. Looking to old workshop, boutique, and apothecary tags, Co-founder Jeroen van den Bogaert and his team stripped away every ornament until only 12 double-lined black outlines remained.

Those empty frames donât sit passively around text; the shapes carry the identity on their own. One rule governs every pairing. Angular polygons always lock into soft curves so the geometry never turns harsh. An oval threaded through a sharp rectangle forms the primary logo, floating in crisp white over debossed bars soaking in a milky porcelain basin. Other combinations link up to four shapes horizontally or vertically to match an itemâs proportions, from an oval-diamond-square-diamond chain across an unpigmented card box to a brown glazed ceramic dish molded from an octagon and an oval. Set apart from that mark, Daniel Gremmeâs Memoir gives the custom-kerned TULA LOUISE wordmark curved notches, while Hanken Grotesk handles body copy across stone-toned boards pairing bars like TL-02 and TL-06 with #706C7F and #9C484C swatch cards.

According to recent reports, color belongs strictly to the soap. On single-bar packaging design like BARA, Daley-Thomas hand-cuts and folds translucent vellum pouches sealed along the top fold with twin metal closures. Speckled rose clay indicates right through the paper behind a bold octagon-and-circle outline on the front and a handwritten blue-ink Batch 2 mark on the back. In her London studio, she also presses the wordmark into every bar by hand with a custom acrylic stamp, leaving recessed letters that catch lather first and gently soften as the soap wears away.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ecuadorian studio Caá Porá Arquitectura has teamed up with US-based Jerome Haferd Studio and engineer Juan Sebastián Pérez for the Bombódromo performance centre in Carchi, Ecuador.
  • The building will feature a central venue that has massive bamboo support elements based on local drums.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ecuadorian studio Caá Porá Arquitectura has teamed up with US-based Jerome Haferd Studio and engineer Juan Sebastián Pérez for the Bombódromo performance centre in Carchi, Ecuador.

The building will feature a central venue that has massive bamboo support elements based on local drums.

The campus will include dozens of buildings centred around a massive auditorium in the province of Carchi, north of Quito, sited along the Chota River in an Andean valley.

Masterplanned by Caá Porá Arquitectura, the campus was designed for local government to celebrate Afro-Ecuadorian culture.

Based on this, the central performance centre has a design based on the bomba, a drum used by local people.

“The inspiration for a lot of the design language was kind of to bridge African and Andean kind of design languages and ancestral aesthetics,” Jerome Haferd told Dezeen.

“That is embodied in the bomba drum, which is a unique instrument that is made by the people in this region, who we worked with very closely to come up with the design concept for the master initiative.”.

“[The bomba] was adapted and generated out of materials local to this valley in Ecuador, and so it’s really a hybrid between the Andean mountains and Africa.”.

The main performance space, designed to hold more than 10,000, will have massive bundles of laminated bamboo supporting a roof system 30 metres in diameter.

These bundled columns have been designed to feature laminated bamboo and timber elements, reflecting the construction of the bomba drum and local construction methods more generally.

Acoustic fabric will hang from the wooden rafters of the semi-enclosed performance space.

A series of stone buildings will flank the main performance space, forming the back-of-house facilities.

An outdoor area will feature a tiered gathering space tucked into the low-lying trees around the river and provide the main viewing platforms for the performances.

As many as eight outbuildings will feature on the campus, including classrooms, a restaurant and artisan kiosks.

These structures will be built with metal roofs and rammed-earth walls, furthering the connection to local building techniques.

“The result is a radical, place-based reinterpretation of how a performing arts venue can respond to a unique cultural context while accommodating flexible uses,” noted the team, which worked with local group Fundación Casa Oshun for the community outreach.

The project is expected to break ground in 2027.

Recently, a team including SANAA, Caá Porá Arquitectura, Estudio A0 and Jerome Haferd Studio was selected to design the National Museum of Ecuador in Quito, after the original design was cancelled following community backlash.

#213. Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom

📅 2026-09-11 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2568 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine

Building A UX ROI Case That Survives The Boardroom

📅 2026-09-11 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alex Williams is a seasoned full-stack developer and the former owner of Hosting Data UK.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alex Williams is a seasoned full-stack developer and the former owner of Hosting Data UK. After graduating from the University of London with a Masters Degree … More about Alex ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sooner or later, a CFO looks at your wireframes and asks what any of it actually does for the bottom line. Storyboards don’t answer that question, and the era when a 5-minute pitch could answer it ended, unfortunately, a while ago.

These days, if you want to win budget, buy-in, and backing for UX, the design has to be provably good for the business, not only for the people using it.

And proving that takes more than taping a dollar sign to a redesign. You have to understand how your organization defines value in the first place, how it measures that value, and how a credible line gets drawn between a design initiative and an outcome leadership already cares about.

Industry observers note that rather than scatter tips, this article follows one worked example the whole way through. Meridian is a mid-size B2B SaaS tech giant, and it is entirely made up — that label matters, so it gets repeated where it counts. Its onboarding redesign carries the same figures from goal-setting through cost accounting, causal testing, and the final ROI number, because a framework only becomes tangible when the numbers connect. Every step is one you can rerun inside your own organization.

Companies now want clarity on what every dollar buys, and “delightful user experiences” stopped clearing that bar some time ago. I still remember a former colleague celebrating a $1 million redesign he’d gotten greenlit mostly on the strength of a couple of three.js tricks. Try that pitch in front of a finance team today and see how far the particles get you.

It has been revealed that executives don’t hate UX, they just hate vagueness. A pitch built on “users will find it easier” loses, every time, to the department promising 12% more sales in Q3. The difference is the one between a streamlined checkout flow that reduced cart abandonment with completed purchases up 22%, and the same work rewarded with “the QA testers like it.” One of those goes on your resume. The rest of this article is about earning the first version, with Meridian’s numbers doing the work.

It has been revealed that most writing about UX ROI makes a convenient assumption: that the organization already owns clean business goals and KPIs for you to hook your work onto. Real companies are messier than that. Plenty run on ambitions like “grow faster” or “improve the customer journey” that nobody ever broke into anything measurable, and an ROI case built on that ambiguity sounds impressive right up until somebody scrutinizes it.

So the first job is often to help the organization define what success even looks like. Interview stakeholders across departments — what does product consider a good quarter, where does customer success watch owners struggle, where do sales deals stall — and listen for the themes that keep resurfacing across conversations, because those recurring themes are the organization’s latent business objectives. A useful forcing function is the OKR model (Objectives and Key Results), which doesn’t tolerate vagueness.

At Meridian, the stated ambition was “improve the rate of upcoming owners’ adoption of the platform,” which you can neither design toward nor measure against. Interviews turned up the real shape of the problem. Trial users needed a median of 14 days to reach first value, most churned before getting there, and onboarding questions were burying the support queue. Out of that came an OKR with actual edges: reduce median time-to-first-value from 14 days to 7 with the use of a guided setup flow, and lift trial-to-paid conversion from 8% to 9.5%.

In a recent development, one warning about formalizing KPIs: Impose them from inside the UX team and leadership will suspect you’ve rigged the field in your own favor, so co-create them with whoever owns the outcome — though never at the price of accepting targets that set your team up for an uncomfortable situation. Meridian’s head of product agreed that setup-completion rate was a fair proxy for onboarding usability, and customer success signed off on time-to-first-value, a number already sitting on their own dashboard.

Recent findings suggest that ROI has a denominator, and the denominator is where most UX teams go wrong. You can’t calculate a return without strategic financial planning, yet cost usually gets counted as designer salaries or consulting hours and nothing else. A finance team will find the rest whether or not you counted it, so count it first.

Direct costs are the visible ones. Meridian’s redesign ran $45,000 in design and research labor plus another $8,000 in tooling and participant incentives. Licenses for Figma, UserTesting, Hotjar, analytics platforms, research incentive spend — all of it belongs in the total, and that’s before the inevitable instances of vendor lock-in every UX team eventually faces. Engineering sits in the same column, because a UX redesign doesn’t stop at the mockup. Building the guided setup took two frontend sprints plus a QA pass, $38,000 worth, and the project generated about $4,000 of coordination overhead along the way in latest syncs and shared dashboards.

Recent findings suggest that the line item nearly everyone misses, and the one worth stealing from this article if you steal nothing else, is stakeholder time. Workshops, design reviews, and feedback sessions all pull senior people away from their primary work. A VP of Product spending four hours a week in UX reviews is a VP not spending those hours on roadmap planning or partner negotiations. Log the attendance — who came, for how long, at what seniority — and price it at fully loaded cost, meaning salary plus benefits divided by productive hours. A quarter’s worth of workshops, reviews, and interviews at Meridian priced out at $22,000.

Add it all up: $45,000 in design labor, $8,000 in tooling, $38,000 in engineering, $22,000 in stakeholder time, $4,000 in coordination. The investment is $117,000. Saying that number out loud beats saying “we spent $45K on design,” precisely because it already includes everything a finance team would have dug up on its own.

Most UX ROI pitches die right here. Conversions rose after the redesign, sure — and the CFO wants to know how you ruled out the new pricing, the seasonal traffic bump, and the marketing campaign that shipped the same week. Without a convincing answer, your entire ROI story crumbles.

After all these years, the gold standard for proving causation is still A/B testing: run the old experience against the new one on an even traffic split until the sample means something.

It has been revealed that onboarding happens to suit a phased rollout, which is why Meridian could do this cleanly. For eight weeks, half of newly introduced trial signups received the redesigned guided setup while half stayed on the legacy flow. Control converted to paid at 8.0%. The variant came in at 9.4%. With roughly 6,100 trials inside the window, the difference was statistically significant, but a 1.4-point gap on a single test is still the kind of result that deserves a second look before anyone builds a budget on it, which is one reason the team held back on attribution below. Where a split isn’t feasible — a change too structural, a user base too small — fall back to a time series instead. Measure steadily for weeks before the change, implement, then keep measuring against the baseline you established.

Documenting whatever else happens around the same time as your UX change is the unglamorous half of causation.

A pricing-page test from Meridian’s marketing team overlapped weeks five through eight of the rollout. The UX team noted it, confirmed it hit both cohorts evenly, and still chose to attribute only 70% of the observed lift to the redesign in the final math. There is no formula that produces that number; treat it as an illustrative assumption for this example.

According to recent reports, the team asked how much of the lift could plausibly belong to the pricing test if it had helped one cohort slightly more than the other, settled on a ceiling of about a third, and rounded the redesign’s share down to 70%. Your figure will differ. What matters is that it is written down and argued for before the results arrive, not fitted to them afterwards. That restraint is worth money in a skeptical room. “We attribute roughly 70% of the lift to the onboarding change, with the remainder likely influenced by concurrent pricing work” survives cross-examination; claiming everything does not. Cohort analysis then backed the number up, since the lift held across acquisition channels and tenure bands, and at that point the skeptics had very little left to work with.

Leading and lagging indicators belong on the same slide, because each covers the other’s weakness. Meridian’s leading indicators moved first — setup completion climbed from 62% to 89%, median time-to-first-value dropped from 14 days to 6.5 — and the lagging trial-to-paid number followed. Mechanism first, business outcome second. Presented together, they form a causal chain that’s harder to poke holes in than either one alone.

Industry observers note that so what did Meridian actually earn? The tech giant sees about 40,000 trial signups a year. Lifting conversion from 8.0% to 9.4% adds roughly 560 paying customers annually, and at an average of $1,800 in annual recurring revenue per account, those customers represent about $1,008,000 in newly introduced ARR. Applying the conservative 70% attribution from the causal work trims the defensible figure to roughly $706,000.

Set that against the full $117,000 investment and the first-year ROI lands near 5:1, with payback arriving in roughly two months. There’s a second line, too. Onboarding-related support tickets dropped about 30%, some 3,600 fewer tickets a year, worth another $54,000 annually at $15 per resolved ticket. Keep it as its own line rather than folding it into one swollen headline number. The case reads as more honest that way and loses none of its force.

Three assumptions carry that result, and each belongs on the slide next to it. The 40,000 signups and the $1,800 average ARR are the prior year’s actuals held flat, so a growth or pricing change moves the outcome in either direction. The 70% attribution is the illustrative assumption from the causal work, not a measured quantity. And the two-month payback counts new ARR as it lands rather than revenue recognized net of churn, which flatters the timeline; on a net basis the payback stretches to roughly a quarter. State those three plainly and a finance team can adapt the example to its own numbers. Hide them and the whole thing starts to look like marketing math, however careful the experiment was.

What persuades in the final presentation is not sophistication. Open with the baseline: what stalled trials and support volume were already costing. Show the delta in terms leadership reads fluently, metrics like conversion rate uplift chief among them. A chart of setup completion climbing from 62% to 89% will beat a paragraph of UX jargon, and a translation like “each abandoned setup costs us 0.3 support tickets” beats the chart. Above all, keep every figure identical from the first slide to the last. A room full of finance people forgives many things, but never numbers that wobble between slides.

Budget decisions come out of coalitions. A CFO may hold the final say when adding AI to the checkout process, but marketing, product, and customer success all lean on that decision, and each means something different by “value.”.

A CFO hears cost, revenue, and risk. A CMO hears conversion and acquisition cost, since UX is a lever for increasing marketing ROI. Product counts support tickets; customer success thinks in retention. The underlying numbers never change; only the framing rotates, and a CFO wants a projection, not a moodboard. Meridian’s CFO slide read “the onboarding redesign protects roughly $706,000 in upcoming ARR a year against a $117,000 investment,” while the CMO version led with what a 9.4% trial conversion does to blended acquisition cost.

Some UX outcomes never translate cleanly into revenue, and pretending they do weakens the parts of your case that are solid.

Recent findings suggest that scores like Net Promoter Score (NPS), CSAT, and Customer Effort Score already sit inside most reporting cadences, which makes them cheap to borrow. Tie your work to their movement, and segment wherever the data allows.

According to recent reports, meridian could say that NPS among trial customers on the redesigned onboarding was 51 against 34 for the legacy flow, which lands far harder than any blended average. Verbatim feedback from surveys, support transcripts, and app store reviews adds the emotional weight the scores lack. Internal tools deserve the same discipline, since employee experience is increasingly recognized as a business driver — a dashboard redesign that hands account managers 45 minutes a day back is a productivity gain, a satisfaction gain, and a retention lever all in one.

Industry observers note that brand perception resists direct measurement but leaves tracks in repeat visits, organic referrals, and social sentiment. It carries extra weight in trust-sensitive industries like finance or healthcare, and it forms fast, given that UX design influences the first impressions of a whopping 94% of customers.

Sources indicate that whatever you collect, systematize the collecting. Run pre- and post-surveys with consistent question sets, use structured usability testing with task-based scoring, and put the qualitative right next to the quantitative when you present.

UX loses the budget battle unless it’s mapped to company-wide objectives, so phrase the proposal in the words of this year’s board presentation.

Nobody at Meridian pitched “simplify the onboarding UI”; the pitch was a redesigned trial experience worth 1.4 points of upgrade rate, roughly $1M in annual recurring revenue before attribution. Bring evidence in both registers, since that is what social proof is for: the case, clearly labeled, plus screenshots, impact graphs, and user quotes. Find internal allies who can repeat the ROI narrative in rooms you’ll never enter, and write the playbook down, because repeatable ROI is what earns recurring investment.

In a recent development, this topic has been explored extensively by researchers, practitioners, and consultancies. Here’s a curated set of resources worth studying if you want to build a stronger ROI practice around UX.

A seat at the table never comes from beauty or novelty. It comes from measurable, defensible impact, which means UX leaders have to trade the artist’s posture for the strategist’s. Speak in outcomes rather than outputs. Connect pixels to profit.

When someone challenges the numbers, don’t flinch. Show the controlled experiment, the cohort analysis, and the before-and-after metrics, every figure holding steady from the first slide to the last, the way Meridian’s did, with the customer quotes and the employee-satisfaction data sitting right beside the revenue impact. Prove the work does more than delight customers, and be ready to defend the ratio line by line. That’s when the CFO leans in, and that’s when design stops being optional.

Walnut-grain panels, floating shelves, glass display cabinets, and a console with drawers share a single aluminum frame in Canvas, the Arundel Collection’s wall system by Eureka Ergonomic. Designed as one piece, the system allows an entire wall to be specified at once, in a range of finishes and layouts suited to a living room, a study, a bedroom, or a home office.

Image courtesy of Eureka Ergonomic.

The idea grew from how founder and CEO Tom Hu regards the wall. “A residence is defined as much by its walls as by its furniture,” he claims. “Usually, though, paneling, shelves, display cabinets, storage, and lighting are specified separately and added to the wall one by one, and the wall becomes a place where many decisions meet but never quite agree.” Canvas brings them together from the start, in the same design language as the rest of Arundel.

Image courtesy of Eureka Ergonomic.

Industry observers note that panels come in layered or plain walnut grain or a pale oak grain, and the frame in matte black, espresso brown, graphite grey, or satin platinum. The display cabinets take one of four types of glass, among them clear and frosted, and the console top comes in two tones. “The structure stays exactly the same; the character changes completely,” Hu explains. “Walnut grain with a dark frame and grey glass makes a warm, low-lit library for the evening. Oak grain with a pale frame and clear glass opens the wall to daylight, closer to a gallery.”.

Image courtesy of Eureka Ergonomic.

Sources indicate that arrangement offers another layer of choice, with shelves, glass cabinets, shelf boxes, and closed storage composed around a television, set in rows for a library, or grouped in a study. According to Hu, “open shelving puts things on display, and more closed storage makes the wall calmer and more architectural.” He adds, “The richer the material palette becomes, the more disciplined the composition has to be.”.

LED lighting is set along the floating shelves and inside the glass cabinets, and in some configurations along the panel edges, with all wiring housed within the frame. “It decides how every surface is read, so it cannot be an afterthought,” Hu says of the light.

Image courtesy of Eureka Ergonomic.

Sources indicate that standard layouts measure between just under 10 and nearly 17 feet wide, and the system installs with no structural changes to the room. For spaces beyond those dimensions, Canvas can also be made fully custom. As Hu puts it, “Either way, the designer gets the built-in look without rebuilding the wall.”.

In a recent development, canvas can be seen at Eureka Ergonomic’s High Point showroom, IHFC D440. Designers can initiative a wall with the Eureka Ergonomic team at [email protected] or apply to the trade program.

#210. Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries

📅 2026-09-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2078 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine

Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries

📅 2026-09-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Industry observers note that to be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I Code. I Write. Meme Rules. Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot. In my spare time, I like to build products that would … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that to be completely honest with you, I missed the news when CSS Container Queries first shipped. And when I finally heard about it, my very first thought was, “Why exactly do I need this when media queries already exist?”.

In a recent development, I’m not proud of that reaction, knowing what I know now, but it was comforting to know that I wasn’t alone. In fact, there are legions of us out there.

What baffles me is that container queries aren’t a fresh feature, as it currently sits at around 94% browser support. And yet, very few people are actually using it. According to the State of CSS survey, 86% of developers are aware of container queries, but only 41.4% actually use them. Surveys can be biased and not completely representative of our entire field, but this one is certainly the best indicator we’ve got.

According to recent reports, kevin Powell also talked about this at SmashingConf Amsterdam 2026: Container Queries adoption has been terrible. And that is so strange to me, knowing that the ability for components to adapt to the size of their outer container has been at the top of so many CSS wishlists over the years.

I’m not particularly interested in how many people are using container queries as much as in how they are using them. I can’t account for everyone, but from what I’ve seen — including in my own early attempts — many of us are using them wrong.

The bottom line is that incorrect use comes down to the same impression I had when learning about them: they absolutely look just like media queries at first glance. And since they look similar, it’s easy to assume they serve similar purposes and work the same way.

Note: I should state up front that what I’m focusing on in this article is using container size queries, i.e., a responsive design technique for responding to the size of a particular container. There are also container style queries that respond to a container’s computed styles (and are experimental at the time of this writing). You can catch up on those in Juan Diego’s piece here on Smashing Magazine where he examines their possible use cases.

Recent findings suggest that the viewport is a proxy. It always has been. Media queries are what gave us the illusion that screen width alone is responsible for how responsive apps adapt to their environment.

Ask yourself this: When you write @media, what are you asking the browser?

I, like most developers, am asking the browser: How wide is the screen right now? That’s it.

Media queries answer that beautifully, but what happens when this .card component is placed in a grid cell that’s 300px wide on a 1920px desktop screen?

The media query doesn’t care; it does its job. The viewport is still 1920px, so min-width: 1024px fires and the matched query styles are applied, even though the card only has 300px of space to work with. Eventually, everything in the card deforms, overflows, or cramps up.

It’s common to think of responsive design purely as a system for updating complete page layouts, like going from two columns on a large screen to a single column on a small screen.

Recent findings suggest that container queries are smarter than that. They make responsive layouts more reliant on what’s happening inside a component rather than on the outer context that has no insight into a component’s contents. It is more like: “How much space is available for me in this specific spot, right now?”.

Here is the same card code example we looked at in the last section, but with a container query:.

Recent findings suggest that this changes everything. The card isn’t influenced by the viewport; its only concern is whether the .card component’s parent wrapper has at least 450px of inline (i.e., horizontal in a left-to-right writing mode) space. If that condition is true, the component goes horizontal; if not, it goes to its default block display.

See the Pen [Viewport vs Container [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73d-6f39-709f-8dae-037f6b588852) by Vayo.

A very interesting way to distinguish @media and @container queries is the layout type.

It has been revealed that media queries are for the “macro” layout; they look outward. Stuff like page structure, the header that spans the window, footers, main grid layout, system preferences (prefers-color-scheme), device capabilities (touch screens). You know, anything that is majorly true to the entire page structure.

It has been revealed that container queries, I’d say, are for “micro” layouts, i.e., most things that live inside the “macro” layout. We use them when any content needs to responsively fit whatever space it is allocated. Components that come to mind are things like cards, widgets, forms, navigation, and so on.

In other words, think “page layout” vs. “component layout”.

Recent findings suggest that an element shouldn’t magically become “tablet-sized” just because the width exceeds an abstract width threshold like 768px. Instead, it should switch layout when it has enough space to do so, whether that happens on a mobile viewport or inside a desktop sidebar.

Sources indicate that in case you’re still not convinced, did you know there are over 2,300 unique viewport sizes on the modern web? Do you think it is possible to account for all of them?

In a recent development, I’m not hating on media queries. It’s that in this era of responsiveness and component re-use, layout logic is closer to the container than the viewport. When we think in terms of containers and components, we’re effectively relying on the content to determine layout, not the viewport.

Responsive typography is a good example of something many of us have relied on media queries for. The fact that media queries come with their own CSS units — e.g., vw, vh, and so on — that are relative to the viewport size makes media queries look really good for adjusting font size based on the user’s screen size.

This works until that same component is moved into a different context, like a sidebar, where the viewport is completely irrelevant. Now, because we tied the responsiveness to the wrong reference point, the scaled typography can get too big or too small.

Container queries come with their very own units — cqi, cqw, cqb, among others — and we can take responsive components further by coupling those units with the CSS clamp() function, using it for fluid typography that scales with the component rather than the viewport:.

See the Pen [Fluid Typography [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73f-1a44-750c-8b40-9b0ab774d981) by Vayo.

With this in place, the entire code is self-contained to that element’s specific container.

Interestingly, container queries can, in a way, detect the state of a component’s internal layout. It’s not bulletproof, but it is also something media queries simply cannot do because they only observe the external browser window and are structurally blind to internal layout events like when, for example, flex items wrap onto a fresh line. Let’s poke at that.

Recent findings suggest that flexbox is superb at wrapping content (flex-wrap: wrap), allowing flex items to automatically wrap to new lines when the flex container runs out of space to fit them in a single row. But CSS by itself can’t tell when that wrap happens. There isn’t something like a :wrapped pseudo-class or a media query like @media (flex-wrapped: true) that would get us there.

Media queries only observe the browser window, as they can’t see internal changes. That is pretty much what flex wrapping is: a width state change on the item itself.

According to recent reports, for example, if you have a horizontal menu that is lined up with flexbox and you want the items to restyle themselves only when wrapped, you’d be in JavaScript territory, using ResizeObserver to get that information. However, when we nest container queries inside flex items, we can come up with a workaround to get what we need without JavaScript, thanks to this technique I learned from Kevin Powell. The core idea is to allow a flex item to flex-grow: 1 when we query the container’s inline size.

See the Pen [Fluid Typography [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a73f-1a44-750c-8b40-9b0ab774d981) by Vayo.

This works. As the parent size shrinks and the cards wrap to two lines, the card item expands, the container query fires, and applies the necessary styles.

See the Pen [Flex Wrap Detection Using Container Queries [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a0a752-150a-754e-a77a-07fe1b046658) by Vayo.

Container queries, like all things, come with some side effects or caveats you will want to watch for before reaching for them.

Container queries need something similar to a parent-child relationship to function as expected. Let’s say we have this markup:.

We can’t actually query the .card component to adjust the .card-content, like this:.

According to recent reports, this doesn’t work because a container cannot query itself. In that last example, we’re querying a card container and then attempting to adjust that container’s display based on its size. It’s an infinite loop.

Instead, we need an additional wrapper that makes the .card a descendant of the container:.

From there, we can query the .cards container and adjust the .card layout accordingly:.

In media queries, this doesn’t matter as @media does not care which element you style inside the block; its only concern is the viewport, which is always available. So you can just slap a condition on any element and call it a day.

This happens when querying the container’s size (i.e., its block, or vertical, size) instead of its inline-size:.

Why? Because the browser calculates the container’s dimensions without looking at its children. If we don’t give the .hero-banner an explicit height (or min-height or aspect-ratio), the browser sets a height of 0px.

For that reason, it’s often better to query a container by its inline-size instead. That is, unless you genuinely need to query the container’s block size.

Media queries aren’t affected by this, as they treat height the same way they treat @media (min-height: ...) does, i.e., ask the viewport and move on.

Another container query limitation: we can’t query against a custom property value:.

This is because custom properties depend on values that cascade down the DOM tree. There’s the possibility that a container query that relies on a custom property can change that same custom property. And it can promptly get complicated:.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t think any project should wholesale use @container instead of @media. Media queries still play an vital role in responsive layouts. It’s about understanding the separation of concerns.

In a recent development, I tend to reach for container queries when a component is used in more than one layout context. For example, a .card element could live in a full-width grid or a narrower sidebar. If that’s the case, then we’ll want the component’s content to determine when it adjusts rather than a media query that looks at the outer viewport.

Similarly, I reach for media queries when a component solely exists at the page level. This would be something like a main navigation that always sits at the top of the page. It is directly influenced by the viewport’s size, meaning that the viewport is a reliable reference for when the navigation needs to adjust. Again, it’s all about “macro” layout versus “micro” layouts.

Here’s a diagram for how I reason about which type of query to use:.

According to recent reports, at the end of the day, the core reason why container queries look incredibly similar to media queries is simply familiarity. They’re not exactly “latest”, but they are way less understood and adopted than media queries. But media queries have plenty of their own limitations; otherwise, we wouldn’t need container queries to fill those gaps.

What we have is a more effective feature for detecting when a specific component’s context changes and a means for adjusting styles based on its content, as it should be when that component can exist in multiple contexts.

Renders by Counterspace.

South African architect Sumayya Vally is designing a permanent home for the Elie Khouri Art Foundation (EKAF), which will be located within a renovated villa in Dubai.

Set to be built in the Jumeirah 1 development in Dubai, the foundation’s home will be located in a former villa, which will be dramatically overhauled by Vally – principal of architecture studio Counterspace.

Industry observers note that “I think of buildings as having many lives,” stated Vally. “At EKAF, we begin with a house that has already held a world within it. Its doors, cornices, balustrades, and particular ways of receiving people and separating rooms contain the traces of another life,” she continued.

“I am interested in what happens when we take these intimate geometries and give them a new public scale: when the architecture of a room becomes the architecture of a city-facing facade, and the memory of a house becomes the beginnings of an institution.”.

Although few details of the design have been revealed, a render shows what appears to be a three-storey building with a light pink textured facade.

Lines across the facade appear to suggest fragments of the previous building, with recognisable shapes including doorways visible. Geometric holes punched in the facade will reveal activities taking place inside.

In a recent development, EKAF was established by Lebanese-French businessman Elie Khouri and its permanent home is planned to open in 2028. The foundation will contain gallery space to show its permanent collection and will also include space for temporary exhibits.

“I hope that artists, designers, researchers and makers from the region will bring other imaginations into the work, and that the institution will continue to acquire forms and meanings we cannot yet anticipate,” added Vally.

Designer of the Serpentine Pavilion in 2021, Vally was named emerging architect of the year at Dezeen Awards in 2023 and one of Time magazine’s 100 leaders of the future in 2021.

Tech Report: WHEN

📅 16 Dec 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Identitydesigned

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information.
  • The conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown.
  • Traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information. They came to us to conceive a brand that could balance credibility and compassion in equal measure. One that felt just as comfortable in a trusted doctor’s office as the shiny shelves of a global beauty store.

The conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown. But with all that focus on the fear-inducing countdown, there’s not a lot of helpful talk — about how fertility works, the proactive steps we can take to improve it, or why the biological clock is an outdated trope. That’s where WHEN comes in — a fertility medtech company on a mission to ensure no one with ovaries is left wondering about them.

Traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise. But this narrow focus has resulted in a category that feels overly clinical and sometimes cold, losing sight of the real people at the heart of it all. We saw an opportunity to create something that balanced the two — trust and credibility, with warmth and humanity. A direct-to-consumer lifestyle brand built on deep medical experience that felt equally at home in a retail environment.

Fertility is, understandably, incredibly personal and seldom discussed. To get to the heart of the glitch, our friends at VML conducted a series of focus groups, one-on-one interviews and stakeholder research. Because in failing to talk about it, we’re failing to give people the information they need at the right time. People are proactive about pap smears, mammograms, skin checks, sexual health tests—all considered lead indicators that look ahead to impact the future. But fertility is measured as a lag indicator, only measured once it’s more difficult to affect the outcome.

Without jumping through costly medical hoops, there is no accessible way for people to know what’s happening inside their very own bodies without a referral. The medical industry is not set up to provide this kind of information proactively, which can make people feel blocked. And when it comes to fertility, information is power.

Recent findings suggest that given WHEN is the first of its kind in Australia, care needed to be taken to communicate the importance and impact of its service. Credible medical expertise was a leading reason to believe. But we also knew people needed to hear the real stories behind the brand to build trust in something so latest. Striking the balance was critical.

According to recent reports, the result is a visual and verbal system that blends emotion with science, expression with information. Designed to showcase fertility stories, expert advice and the endless questions we ask ourselves, the brand moves seamlessly from packaging to print, retail stores to social media.

Sources indicate that the WHEN wordmark sits at the heart of the visual identity. Clear and confident, it anchors the brand as a dependable figure in the health and medical space. Paired with an organic cell shape that reacts to the world around it, the wordmark and logoform are a perfect foil to the other. Together, they represent standing strong amid the ever-changing nature of life.

According to recent reports, WHEN’s typeface is ABC Diatype. It’s used for everything — from wordmark to body copy. Chosen for its modernity and scientific edge, it brings calm and clarity to everything we say. Paired with a colour palette of lemon and neutrals, the identity feels light and warm against an industry so often cold and clinical.

An crucial first touchpoint was the at-home testing kit — the Egg Count Check. The kit is split into three sections: Prepare, Collect, and Send. We designed the packaging experience to follow the same logical structure, ensuring the steps were simple to follow and easy to use.

It has been revealed that inspired by the sleek aesthetic of our favourite tech brands, the kit’s box takes a rigid form with special attention paid to premium print finishes. We also created a custom instruction booklet to guide the user through the process, designed and illustrated in-house.

Recent findings suggest that our primary photography style uses intimate portraits and close crops to focus on the subject’s internal thoughts and feelings. We aim to capture moments that feel like a natural extension of everyday life, empowering and relatable in their familiarity. As a secondary style, we splice natural textures and fluid forms with our portraits, like fragments of memory telling the story of a person’s inner world.

Industry observers note that to further enhance this sense of intimacy, a series of icons were developed to capture the different states of mind one might feel around this sensitive and personal topic. Following the same visual language as the logo, these icons add flexibility and expression to the brand, especially when used with the intimate portraiture.

The brand name itself is a question — when? But it’s also a statement of intent. We worked with copywriter Amy Scott to develop a verbal concept exploring the idea of an inner monologue, giving voice to the questions we ask ourselves but perhaps never verbalise. The brand speaks as an empathetic expert, both insightful and inclusive. By creating space for open conversation and asking the questions people ask themselves, we show no matter where they’re at in their fertility journey, they’re not alone.

WHEN doesn’t only set to change fertility testing, but to also facilitate an aspirational platform that aims to drive community and empowering conversation around fertility. The brand was crafted to grow into a multidimensional platform for fertility information access and support. We helped design the first step of this journey through WHEN Matters — a curated blog for sharing real fertility stories and credible medical expertise to ensure no one with ovaries was left feeling alone on their journey.

Breaking: 25 Years of Bilibo: The Toy That Lets Imagination Lead

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that with two round eyes and a curving grin, Bilibo looks like a character waiting for its story to begin.
  • To mark the milestone, Moluk, the Zurich-based toy company Hochstrasser runs with his sister Doris, an architect, is introducing Bilibo Midi, a smaller shell for toddlers, and Bilibo Dots, a set of colorful counters that translate the original’s open-ended approach into a fresh form.
  • Both additions build on the premise that has carried Bilibo into homes, classrooms, and museum collections around the world—and continues to anchor Moluk’s entire catalog: offer a pared-back object and leave the rest to the imagination.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that with two round eyes and a curving grin, Bilibo looks like a character waiting for its story to begin. Designed by Swiss designer Alex Hochstrasser, the sculptural shell is an open-ended toy that can become anything from a seat or boat to a helmet or drum. Twenty-five years after its 2001 debut, the toy remains remarkably unchanged, a testament to the enduring appeal of a design that leaves almost everything to the imagination.

To mark the milestone, Moluk, the Zurich-based toy company Hochstrasser runs with his sister Doris, an architect, is introducing Bilibo Midi, a smaller shell for toddlers, and Bilibo Dots, a set of colorful counters that translate the original’s open-ended approach into a fresh form.

Both additions build on the premise that has carried Bilibo into homes, classrooms, and museum collections around the world—and continues to anchor Moluk’s entire catalog: offer a pared-back object and leave the rest to the imagination.

Sources indicate that hochstrasser’s starting point for Bilibo was what he saw on store shelves at the turn of the millennium. “I was struck by how rigidly most mainstream toys were categorized by age and gender, giving them an expiration date long before they wore out,” he claims. “There was also a flood of licensed toys, with the story already written. I wanted to create something more universal and inclusive that could grow with children and leave them in charge of the story.”.

In a recent development, alex Hochstrasser’s sketches for the first Bilibo. Illustration courtesy of Moluk.

Sources indicate that firsthand observation of play and repeated rounds of testing shaped the toy, along with input from child-development experts. “The final step in the design belongs to the children,” Hochstrasser explains. “They become the co-inventors, deciding what the object is and what it can do.”.

According to recent reports, early studies drew on archetypal forms like eggs and turtle shells. “What interested me was how a hollow hemisphere’s behavior changed simply by turning it over,” Hochstrasser explains. “Resting on its rim, it was stable, a hill to climb or a shelter for things underneath. On its rounded base, it became dynamic, a vessel that could rock and spin.”.

The shell’s threefold symmetry allows two identical pieces to lock together into a cheerful sphere. The two openings read as eyes, lending the object personality and a sense of direction—but they also work as peepholes, anchor points for a pull rope, and spouts for pouring water.

“Each detail had to contribute to both its character and its possibilities for play,” he claims. “I wanted the form to feel friendly and familiar, yet odd enough to make children curious.”.

Recent findings suggest that bilibo appeared in ‘Century of the Child’ at MoMA in 2012. Photography courtesy of Moluk.

In a recent development, the deceptively simple design soon attracted attention beyond the toy industry, earning a Design Distinction in I.D. Magazine’s 2002 Annual Design Review, an honor the first Apple iPod also received that year. Bilibo went on to appear in MoMA’s Century of the Child: Growing by Design, 1900–2000 in 2012 and enter the permanent museum collections in Zurich, Brussels, and Paris.

Recent findings suggest that bilibo Midi brings a lighter, more compact shell to younger children, with room for a 2- or 3-year-old to sit and spin. It’s also easy to carry, even when filled with sand or water.

Industry observers note that bilibo Midi toys as stepping stones. Photography courtesy of Moluk.

According to recent reports, “A modest change in size can make a significant difference to how independently children use an object,” Hochstrasser notes. “When we tested Midi, it was striking how naturally toddlers picked the shells up or used them as stepping stones—no help needed.”.

Alongside the smaller shell, Moluk introduced Bilibo Dots, a set of 36 counters, each carrying the original’s curved profile and two eyes in miniature. They can be sorted, counted, threaded, or tossed inside the original Bilibo shell to rattle around.

Bilibo Dots. Photography courtesy of Moluk.

“I see all MOLUK toys as a family of building blocks for play, designed to work together so each new addition opens up possibilities for the others,” Hochstrasser says. “Put a handful of Dots in a Midi, and it’s a treasure chest.”.

The Classic Bilibo also comes in four special-edition colors for 2026–2027: amber, emerald, graphite, and coral. Aside from fresh colors and a 2021 retooling that made it lighter and stronger, the original has retained its form for a quarter century. Children who grew up with Bilibo are now watching a new generation discover it.

“Longevity depends on both the toy surviving and children continuing to find latest uses for it,” he says. “Bilibo has no batteries to replace, no screen to update, and no mechanism to break. It’s a simple but distinctive shape that changes character depending on how you position or look at it. It invites rough-and-tumble physical play—rocking, balancing, spinning—and can just as easily become a drum, a boat, or a cradle in a child’s imagination. The object stays the same, but the play it enables keeps changing as the child grows.”.

Hayley Arsenault is a writer and editor covering architecture, interiors, and design. Based in Upcoming York, she covers materials and manufacturing in the built environment.

Breaking: Five little-known stage designs from the archives of Zaha Hadid

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Luke Hayes unless stated otherwise.
  • The unsung set designs of Zaha Hadid take centre stage in the latest exhibition curated by her foundation in London.
  • Named Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance, the exhibition is the Zaha Hadid Foundation‘s first collection-based show dedicated to the architect’s portfolio of stage and set designs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Luke Hayes unless stated otherwise.

The unsung set designs of Zaha Hadid take centre stage in the latest exhibition curated by her foundation in London. In this roundup, we spotlight five standout objects that were uncovered from her archives for the show.

Named Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance, the exhibition is the Zaha Hadid Foundation‘s first collection-based show dedicated to the architect’s portfolio of stage and set designs.

It coincides with the reopening of the foundation’s home in Hadid’s former office – a former Victorian schoolhouse at 10 Bowling Green Lane in Clerkenwell, following a refurbishment by Studio KA coinciding with the 10th anniversary of Hadid’s passing.

The exhibition was curated by the foundation’s senior researcher Catherine Howe and design historian Libby Sellers as guest curator, and contains five projects illustrated through a mix of archival models, drawings, video footage and even costume.

Together, these offer insight into the evolution of Hadid’s signature complex geometries and digital design techniques, through the lens of sets for dance, opera and pop music.

According to curator Howe, the exhibition exemplifies how Hadid “didn’t want to be fixed” in her work, and how “she wanted to work across so many media”.

Howe added that the exhibition came about serendipitously, after the foundation had kept discovering records of these unsung projects while unpacking boxes.

According to recent reports, “We open a lot of boxes,” she told Dezeen during a tour of the exhibition. “Sometimes it’s fortuitous, or it’s that there’s a massive box and we need to move it, and we kept noticing all these amazing projects that hadn’t really been talked about.”.

“Of course, everyone talks about her incredible buildings, but I think the interdisciplinarity of some of these projects was just being forgotten about, and we said ‘we need to do something on performance’.”.

The foundation’s chairman, Rana Hadid, who is also the niece of Hadid, told Dezeen the reopening of the foundation was a “very emotional” moment for her, but suggested the exhibition only marks the beginning of discovering treasures in the foundation’s archive, which is estimated to contain 300,000 items.

“[Hadid’s] archive is so extraordinary, it’s limitless paintings, drawings, sketchbooks, digital material, personal material, it goes way beyond architecture,” Rana Hadid explained.

“It’s really about studying the process of her thinking, and using all that to help younger generations learn more about the process, the experimentation, the way you can start an idea and move forward with it, use technologies to be able to build it.”.

The Zaha Hadid Foundation is an independent charity founded by Hadid in 2013. The Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance exhibition is on until 27 March 2027.

The foundation’s reopening programme also includes a video artwork by artist LionHeart and a timeline visualisation of Hadid’s life by data journalist Mona Chalabi.

Read on for five stand-out exhibits from the Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance exhibition.

Hadid created this model for her design for the staging of Mozart’s Così fan tutte opera, presented at Frank Gehry’s Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles in 2014.

Her dynamic stage design featured a spiralling white platform, engineered with sections that could rise and fall to help echo the shifting relationships of performers in the opera.

It had a curvature that mirrors many of her buildings, including the iconic Heydar Aliyev Centre in Baku, completed two years prior.

Another model featured in the exhibition is one Hadid created when designing the set for the Pet Shop Boys’ Nightlife World Tour, which took place between 1999 and 2000.

It has been revealed that the design comprised an interconnected, reconfigurable system of ramps that could be tailored to suit different venues while maintaining the overall aesthetic. It also incorporated projection surfaces, transforming the stage into a multimedia environment.

According to the foundation, it was Hadid’s “first commission for a major pop concert”.

This collection of digital drawings depicts the stage design that Hadid created for the Metapolis Ballet in 1999, and embodies the abstract design language for which the architect was best known.

Sources indicate that these ultimately became a trio of lightweight bridge structures that were moved, reconfigured and even worn by dancers across the stage. It is exhibited alongside a costume, which Hadid also designed for the ballet.

This trio of models were developed by Hadid for her pavilion at an event in Groningen called What a Wonderful World! Music Videos in Architecture in 1990.

It responded to a brief that asked for explorations into how the cultural phenomenon of music videos could be translated from screen to public space.

Hadid’s final design featured an uncharacteristically bright colour palette and a grid-like structure with shifting floors and angular walkways, and proposed “how architecture could shape the experience of viewing itself”, the foundation said.

The final pavilion was exhibited alongside contributions by her fellow ‘deconstructivist’ architects, including Rem Koolhaas, Bernard Tschumi, Peter Eisenman, and Coop Himmelb(l)au.

This abstract sketch of an unnamed architectural project, originally developed by Hadid for Hamburg, later formed the basis of a dance performance called d1 by British choreographer Rosemary Butcher.

The project, which was Hadid’s first dedicated to performance, saw the sketch transformed into a monochromatic network of lines on a floor, across which dancers moved as though “navigating a cityscape”.

In a recent development, zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance takes place from 3 November 2026 to Saturday 27 March 2027. For more events in architecture and design, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

#201. Neri&Hu Reinterprets Cape Town’s Maritime Heritage for Edition
