Neri&Hu Reinterprets Cape Town’s Maritime Heritage for Edition

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, located on Quay 7 at the V&A Waterfront in Cape Town, South Africa, the Cape Town Edition Hotel turns heritage into a destination that feels contemporary yet unmistakably local.
  • Part of a global portfolio of hotels, The Cape Town Edition revolves around The Drum—a soaring cylindrical space open to the elements.
  • For Lyndon Neri, co-founder of Neri&Hu, The Drum began with a conversation about how to connect and distinguish the hotel’s hospitality and residential spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, located on Quay 7 at the V&A Waterfront in Cape Town, South Africa, the Cape Town Edition Hotel turns heritage into a destination that feels contemporary yet unmistakably local. Designed by Neri&Hu in partnership with local architects and professional firms, the hotel draws inspiration from the site’s industrial maritime character while embracing the city’s evolving cultural landscape. Although the original warehouse was too unstable to preserve, its footprint and construction logic informed the fresh building, which references the long, narrow forms and pitched roofs of the surrounding industrial structures.

Part of a global portfolio of hotels, The Cape Town Edition revolves around The Drum—a soaring cylindrical space open to the elements. The harbor, Table Mountain, the Atlantic, and the waterfront below are all visible from the 360-degree outdoor viewing platform. Guests, visitors, and locals alike can ascend the spiral staircase to discover Cape Town from a bird’s-eye view.

For Lyndon Neri, co-founder of Neri&Hu, The Drum began with a conversation about how to connect and distinguish the hotel’s hospitality and residential spaces. “The route is both architectural and civic,” he claims. “It turns circulation into an experience of the landscape and gives the project a public dimension beyond accommodation.”.

Grounded in its landscape, the Cape Town Edition is crafted with a deep appreciation for materiality. Local sourcing was central to the hotel’s sustainability strategy, informing not only the selection of building materials but also the curation of the furniture, art, and objects throughout the space.

Metalwork and joinery were supplied by local manufacturers, while the joinery draws inspiration from 19th-century travel trunks. Custom furnishings manufactured locally and rugs woven by KwaZulu-Natal-based Shuttleworth Weaving layer exceptional craftsmanship into the interiors, where warm finishes are complemented by expansive window frames that capture sweeping views.

Industry observers note that more than 6 million bricks, supplied by a family-owned Western Cape manufacturer and laid by hand, create shifting patterns across the façade, giving the building texture and rhythm. Their warm sand tones complement the natural hues of the surrounding landscape, providing a striking backdrop against the cooler blues of the sea beyond.

It has been revealed that “Our interest was never in an architecture that competes with this landscape, nor one that simply defers to it,” Neri indicates. “Instead, we asked how the building might register those forces: how brick, light, and the deliberate framing of views could create a sequence of spaces at once bound to the Waterfront and unmistakably of Cape Town.”.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the hotel, art serves a purpose beyond decoration, reflecting Africa’s creative landscape and connecting guests to the people and traditions that shape the destination. Design Network Africa sourced objects from makers across the continent, including Zulu ukhamba vessels and mouth-blown recycled glass from Eswatini. Cape Town gallery Southern Guild curated the art collection, which includes black-and-white portraits by Zanele Muholi, Usha Seejarim’s artwork Fading Dish Cloth, and smoke-fired ceramics by Chuma Maweni, which lend a sculptural presence to the lobby and dining spaces.

A 240-square-meter Penthouse and a 112-square-meter Harbor Suite crown the hotel, each offering ample living spaces and panoramic views. The Cape Town Edition comprises 142 guestrooms and suites that balance elevated comfort with residential appeal. Below sea level, the spa features a sauna, steam room, infrared beds, and aromatherapy. A daily program of sound baths, yoga classes, and movement sessions enhances the experience, with additional opportunities to unwind beside the heated rooftop pool and sundeck.

Sources indicate that the Punch Room draws on the centuries-old tradition of communal punch drinking, a ritual carried along trade routes that once passed through the Cape. Velvet banquettes, wood paneling, and atmospheric lighting create an opulent retreat that offers a modern interpretation of the region’s rich cultural and culinary heritage.

The end goal? For guests and visitors to leave with a lasting sense of Cape Town, shaped by the connections between the hotel’s interiors and the surrounding landscape. For Neri, the intention was “for the building to reflect not only the visual character of Cape Town, but also its material culture and craftsmanship.”.

Malia Agostinelli is a writer and editor blending design and the built environment with the art of storytelling. Rarely found without a pen in hand, she also enjoys exploring latest countries, taking yoga classes, and gathering inspiration for her Substack, Collected Elsewhere.

Japanese tech giant Not a Hotel‘s in-house architecture team has turned a 1967 warehouse into a workspace divided by glass partitions and filled with design classics, including an entire Jean Prouvé house.

The former logistics warehouse has a brutalist design and spacious interior with seven-metre-tall ceilings.

To create zones that could house different departments for the Not a Hotel (Nota) company, which is known for its striking hotel designs, the architects added three-metre-high glass partitions that divide the floor proposal into three rows.

These were then divided into multiple smaller rooms that have different functions.

While creating the new interior, the in-house team, called Not a Hotel Architects, decided to keep the building’s existing structure and make it a defining feature of the design.

“The project embraced the raw, brutalist beauty of the existing structure – retaining its steel frame and exposed concrete surfaces,” Not a Hotel architect Kei Shiho told Dezeen.

The building will function as the office and headquarters for Not a Hotel, as well as a location that could be used by the owners of its Nigo House – a hotel built into a cliff overlooking Tokyo Bay and designed by artist Nigo.

“We wanted the Nota office to not just be a place for our employees but two other things: a foundational base for the brand’s vision and identity, as well as a place to host the Nigo Lounge for owners of The Nigo House,” Shiho stated.

As a result, the office features a mix of both unusual Nigo designs and design classics, with the large spaces enabling the architects to play around with the interior.

“The high ceilings created a great canvas to experiment with interior design, including exhibiting a bit of Nigo’s rare goods collection in USM Haller boxes up to the ceiling as well as installing the Jean Prouvé demountable house,” Shiho remarked.

Sources indicate that in the Harumi Lounge, a 15-metre-long table with a decorative wooden tabletop sits underneath the seven-metre-tall ceiling. Translucent curtains can be closed on both sides to create a calmer environment and shield it from the workplaces next door.

An original demountable house by architect Prouvé has its own room and can be used for work or meetings.

“Its inclusion serves as a daily reminder and educational tool for the architectural team regarding material longevity and functional beauty,” Shiho explained.

The Nigo Lounge, which is near the office entrance, features three walls clad with 352 USM Haller cabinets filled with design and art pieces.

Another room holds Nota’s library of physical architecture samples inside 96 custom Globe-Trotter trunks, which function as a materials library that is searchable via QR codes.

The design pieces on display in the headquarters were chosen as a callback to things that inspired the launch of the manufacturer, which has a strong design focus.

“Our founder Shinji Hamauzu was a vintage furniture collector, and he started Not a Hotel with the idea that he wanted to build properties that could be a place to exhibit masterpieces of design,” Shiho said.

“So the main showpieces in the office are all things related to our brand and our creative community, as well as our inspirations: many pieces by the late designer Virgil Abloh, vintage furniture from Prouvé, Perriand, and Jeanneret.”.

The project has been shortlisted in the large workplace interiors category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Not a Hotel recently released designs for a giant Poké Ball guest room and is working with Nigo and Pharrell on a upcoming district in Tokyo.

Photography by Not a Hotel.

#196. Comment | Is art market regulation too much of a ‘good thing’?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (675 w)

Comment | Is art market regulation too much of a ‘good thing’?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that anyone who says the art market is unregulated probably has not spent much time in an auction house compliance department.
  • Sources indicate that in the European Union (EU) and UK, this includes regulation around money-laundering, data protection, imports and exports, artist resale rights, a growing economic sanctions regime, endangered species, firearms and complex tax reporting.
  • None of these areas of control seem objectionable at first glance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that anyone who says the art market is unregulated probably has not spent much time in an auction house compliance department. At the major houses, such departments might consist of half a dozen full-time personnel tasked with ensuring that the business can digest what has become an expanding layer cake of government regulation in the art sector.

Sources indicate that in the European Union (EU) and UK, this includes regulation around money-laundering, data protection, imports and exports, artist resale rights, a growing economic sanctions regime, endangered species, firearms and complex tax reporting. The UK has additional obligations around ivory and issuing annual “modern slavery” statements.

None of these areas of control seem objectionable at first glance. But a careful observer must consider two things. Does the imposition of regulation achieve the intended goal? And, if it does, does it need to apply across the board, both up and down the market, to all participants?

Industry observers note that in 2015, the British Art Market Federation undertook an analysis that listed 167 laws and regulations impacting the UK art market. The organisation’s current chair, Tom Christopherson, tells me that the impact of laws and regulations has increased considerably since then. Sophisticated players, with their compliance teams and in-house lawyers, may be able to spot trends, change course and avoid falling foul of the many rules. But what about the small fish?

Consider anti-money laundering regulations, which were extended to the art market by the EU and the UK in 2020. Absolutely nobody wants ill-gotten gains to proliferate in the art market. But despite negative stereotypes and hearsay around “dodgy dealings”, I have yet to find convincing evidence of money laundering in the European art market that could have justified such an expansive regime.

In the UK, data from HMRC (the official tax, payments, and customs authority) highlights that more than 200 art market participants have been fined for violating the rules from the date enforcement began in 2022 to September 2025. None of these infractions involved the actual laundering of money, merely the failure to register with HMRC or to report material changes. (One gallery failed on additional grounds relating to risk assessments, due diligence and staff training.) Many of those fined are small operations, such as a toy soldier shop in London that featured in a recent Financial Times story on this topic.

Recent findings suggest that with registration and reporting obligations, the onus falls on market participants. The scope of an offence can extend well beyond laundering itself. With the art market now a “regulated sector”, failure to report suspicions around, for instance, activities that could conceivably be connected to the funding of terrorism is now a criminal offence. An east London art dealer was caught under this new “failure to report” offence in 2023 and sentenced to two-and-a-half years behind bars.

Industry observers note that another area involves sanctions, far less simple than checking customer names against a list of oligarchs. The Russia sanctions list continues to grow by the month; in the UK, it consists of nearly 2,000 individuals and 1,000 companies—with additional lists for countries including Belarus, Iran and Libya—often with a multitude of transliterated names.

Also in the UK, an offence exists that goes beyond dealing with listed sanctioned individuals to exporting or “making available” luxury goods (including art) to anyone “connected with Russia”. This offence was used recently to charge the gallery Hauser & Wirth, along with its shipping company. Judge Tony Baumgartner of Southwark Crown Court dismissed the case in July, having found that the prosecution had failed to make a case that the individual to whom the work had been shipped was indeed “connected with Russia”, as he was no longer ordinarily residing in that country.

Recent findings suggest that we all understand the benefit of regulation when it comes to saving lives, protecting the environment and smothering criminality in high-risk markets. But whether every piece of regulation is justified for the art world remains to be seen—or, rather, proven.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Design-milk

Latest Update: ROOM’s Designers on Design Series Returns with A Story of Hospitality and Human Connection

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that who understands the struggles and successes of a designer better than another designer?
  • According to recent reports, “When we launched ROOM’s Designers on Design series, the idea was simple: create a space for designers to have the kinds of conversations that don’t always happen in the day-to-day,” states Elyse Heckman, SVP, Brand & Communications at ROOM.
  • Industry observers note that hospitality legend Anda Andrei of Anda Andrei Design and award-winning designer Matthew Goodrich of Goodrich design studio sit down for a discussion in the most recent installation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that who understands the struggles and successes of a designer better than another designer? That’s the core concept behind ROOM’s Designers on Design video series, which pairs leading designers together for open conversation on the future of architecture, design, and human connection.

According to recent reports, “When we launched ROOM’s Designers on Design series, the idea was simple: create a space for designers to have the kinds of conversations that don’t always happen in the day-to-day,” states Elyse Heckman, SVP, Brand & Communications at ROOM. “No interviewer, no moderator, no prescribed talking points. Just two creative minds coming together to exchange ideas, challenge perspectives, and explore what moves the industry forward.”.

Industry observers note that hospitality legend Anda Andrei of Anda Andrei Design and award-winning designer Matthew Goodrich of Goodrich design studio sit down for a discussion in the most recent installation. Unlike earlier episodes of this series, Andrei and Goodrich know each other outside of the studio—and have for years. Goodrich attributes his love of hospitality design to Andrei’s hotels, while Andrei has had a front-row seat to the evolution of Goodrich’s career. (Plus, their work shares a certain symbiosis: Andrei’s recent renovation of the Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris aligns with Goodrich’s past in museum exhibition design.).

Recent findings suggest that “For this episode, we wanted to take a slightly different approach to our previous pairings,” notes Heckman. “Rather than bringing together designers who may be meeting for the first time, we were drawn to the idea of connecting two individuals who already share a history and familiarity with each other’s work. We loved the opportunity to explore how those relationships shape our perspectives, influence our creative instincts and ultimately help us grow as designers.”.

Photography by Eric Vitale, courtesy of ROOM.

Tapping into the spirit of authentic exchange that ROOM set out to foster, the duo’s conversation begins with their first (almost) meeting. In 2003, Goodrich was helping his partner, Barnes Foundation Executive Director Thomas Collins, open Zaha Hadid’s Contemporary Arts Center in Cincinnati when he heard that Andrei would be there in 20 minutes. “I looked to Thom, and I stated, ‘You’ve got to go home, take a shower, and put on a suit. This is a big deal,’” Goodrich shares.

In a recent development, however, the pair didn’t officially meet until years later—after Andrei had left the Ian Schrager Tech giant, starting her own firm at 59 years old. “You came very highly recommended, and I wanted to hire you,” she indicates. “But then I asked you a crucial question: ‘Have you ever opened a hotel before?’” “And I had to say no,” Goodrich adds.

Designing a hotel is no easy feat, which Goodrich learned when opening his first hotel, Arlo SoHo, in 2016. He shared how the final month before opening was chaos. With nearly 40 years shaping hospitality projects, Andrei knows this reality well—but emphasizes that it’s even more painful when operations start changing after the design is finished. Like living organisms, hospitality projects evolve with the staff, owners, and guests over the years.

In a recent development, still, the pair agree that all these problems and pain points provide valuable lessons. “Understanding how operations affect the success of restaurants and of hotels is foundational for making great designs,” Goodrich indicates.

Photography by Eric Vitale, courtesy of ROOM.

Sources indicate that on the topic of design inspiration, Andrei believe the best hotels have a story. Much like an elevator pitch, she believes projects should have a one-sentence design concept. For example, at the Delano Miami Beach Hotel, which she created in collaboration with Philippe Starck, the one-liner was: “a Greek fisherman that finds a diamond in the sea.” Goodrich agrees with the sentiment of this design tool: “If you have that short phrase, if you can go back to the essence of what your concept is, things fall into place.”.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the episode, there is a sense of mutual respect and deep appreciation for the other’s work. Goodrich calls Andrei a superhero collaborator, while Andrei compliments Goodrich’s work (and name). Both value collaboration, imagination, and challenging work. Heckman sees the pair’s connection as proof of the series’ larger purpose: “It’s a wonderful example of how seemingly different creative paths can intersect, and how the work we encounter early in our careers can continue to influence us in unexpected ways.”.

Industry observers note that “When you started your firm, we had some empty desks in my office and we shared offices. And who knew that nine and a half years later, we would be sitting here and talking about how amazing you did,” Andrei states with a laugh.

Industry observers note that this is what ROOM’s Designers on Design series does so well: It brings design to the human level. From the ideas and experiences that shape the work to the friends, colleagues, and mentors who leave a lasting impact, each episode looks at the people behind the portfolio.

“What makes this episode especially compelling is that the conversation extends beyond design itself,” shares Heckman. “It gets to the heart of how we become the designers we are — the people who influence us, the experiences that shape our creative instincts, and the ways inspiration gets passed from one generation to the next. In that sense, it embodies exactly what we hoped the series would become: a platform for authentic exchange, unexpected perspectives and the stories behind the work.”.

And who knows? The series might even inspire newly introduced work of its own. “I want to do a project together,” Andrei says. Goodrich answers: “I know, me too. That’s my dream.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, naming is hard. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it. That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables.

In a recent development, sometimes, the names we choose are too generic, so it’s difficult to understand what exactly is meant. And sometimes they are too specific, leaving little room for flexibility and reuse. How do we choose the right names? And which naming conventions work best? Let’s take a closer look.

If you’re looking for some inspiration for naming HTML classes, CSS properties, or JavaScript functions, Classnames is a wonderful resource jam-packed with ideas that get you thinking outside the box.

It has been revealed that the site provides thematically grouped lists of words perfect for naming. You’ll find terms to describe different kinds of behavior, likeness between things, order, grouping, and association, but also themed collections of words that wouldn’t instantly come to one’s mind when it comes to code, among them words from nature, art, theater, music, architecture, fashion, and publishing.

How would you choose the right name for a given color? Fortunately, David Aerne maintains a tremendous repository of color names, right now with 30355 unique color names, sourced from various references and 1000s of user contributions.

Of course, the repository comes with a color picker and name search and plenty of other color pickers as well. Tremendous work, which is also a fantastic reference to keep nearby.

Industry observers note that what makes a good name? Javier Cuello summarized a set of naming best practices that help you name your layers, groups, and components in a consistent and scalable way.

As Javier points out, a good name has a logical structure, is short, meaningful, known by everyone, and not related to visual properties. He shares do’s and don’ts to illustrate how to achieve that and also takes a closer look at all the fine little details you need to consider when naming sizes, colors, groups, layers, and components.

It has been revealed that how to build a flexible design token taxonomy that works across different products? That was the challenge that the team at Intuit faced. The parent organization of products such as Mailchimp, QuickBooks, TurboTax, and Mint developed a flexible token system that goes beyond the brand theme to serve as the foundational system for a wide array of products.

It has been revealed that nate Baldwin wrote a case study in which he shares valuable insights into the making of Intuit’s design token taxonomy. It dives deeper into the pain points of the old taxonomy system, the criteria they defined for the fresh system, and how it was created. Lots of takeaways for building your own robust and flexible token taxonomy are guaranteed.

According to recent reports, looking at what other people call similar things is a great way to start when you’re struggling with naming. And what better source could there be than other design systems? Before you end up in the design system rabbit hole, Iain Bean did the research for you and created the Component Gallery.

It’s a collection that includes plenty of examples for more than 50 UI components — from accordion to visually hidden — and also lists other names that the UI components go by. A fantastic resource, and not only with regard to naming.

Features often have low adoption due to poor discoverability. Feature adoption needs time — first the feature must be discovered, then understood, then tried, learned, and eventually built into existing workflow. Erin Gannon has written a helpful practical guide on how to make sure all of it happens.

Good names are driven by user needs and problems. They should signal the value or outcome of a feature (the job-to-be-done), and — most importantly! — tap into the user’s own language. So ask people to explain a feature in their own words and then use the words they use.

It has been revealed that A wonderful example of naming guidelines for a complex multi-brand, multi-themed design system comes from the Vodafone UK Design System team. Their Variables Taxonomy Map breaks down the anatomy and categorization of a design token into a well-orchestrated system of collections.

In a recent development, the map illustrates four collections required to support the system and connections between tokens — from brand and primitives to semantics and pages. It builds on top of Nathan Curtis’ work on naming design tokens and enables everyone to gather insight about where a token is used and what it represents, just from its name.

If you want to explore more approaches to naming design tokens, I’ve put together a list of useful Figma kits and resources that are worth checking out.

Romina Kavcic created a helpful little tool for naming design tokens — from learning how they work and how to name them well to configuring your own naming structure with components, categories, states, and roles.

If you are looking for the right name for your product or service, Onym is a fantastic open-source repository that organizes tools and resources for finding names for brainstorming, vetting, guides, sprints, etymologies — all the way to cautionary tales and agencies that name things, as well as useful books to take a look at.

A quick-reference list of tools and guides for naming just about… well, anything, in one place:.

According to recent reports, the right name is the one that’s well-understood and used by the team and users. So much time is wasted speaking about the very same thing but in different dialects — the designer’s dialect, the developer’s dialect, the product manager’s dialect, and the user’s dialect. That’s what often causes frustration and confusion.

So if you see low adoption, it might be merely because of the name. And pay attention to potential naming conflicts and put them in a backlog of things to address later. It’s one of those fine little details that can reduce frustration and confusion and help teams work together better.

Public toilets in Paris by Chartier-Corbasson "elevate the ordinary"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Romain Meffre & Yves Marchand.
  • French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes has transformed a neglected underground passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens in Paris into a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel.
  • The project forms part of the ongoing OnE masterplan, a competition-winning scheme to develop the public spaces and gardens around the Eiffel Tower that was awarded to Paris-based Chartier-Corbasson Architectes and London studio Gustafson Porter + Bowman in 2019.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Romain Meffre & Yves Marchand.

French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes has transformed a neglected underground passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens in Paris into a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel.

The project forms part of the ongoing OnE masterplan, a competition-winning scheme to develop the public spaces and gardens around the Eiffel Tower that was awarded to Paris-based Chartier-Corbasson Architectes and London studio Gustafson Porter + Bowman in 2019.

The public toilets occupy a tunnel through the Trocadero Gardens that was originally designed for the 1937 Universal Exposition by Roger Lardat, framed by distinctive openings in bush-hammered concrete and lined by flint walls that were etched with graffiti by US soldiers at the end of the second world war.

The tunnel had long been closed to the public, used instead as a storage area for the city’s cleaning services. For its renovation, which has been shortlisted in the Heritage project category of Dezeen Awards 2026, Chartier-Corbasson Architectes looked to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a new purpose.

“Far from being a mere functional adaptation, the project, entirely off-site, transforms a closed, neglected, and invisible space into a high-value, integrated, and dignified public amenity situated in a busy urban environment,” explained the studio.

“By restoring meaning and form to a previously purely utilitarian space, this project demonstrates that architecture can elevate even the most ordinary uses, while having a significant impact on the city, its customers, and its collective memory.”.

The distinctive pink-toned bush-hammered entrances at either end of the tunnel have been carefully restored, and now frame a series of fresh Corten steel gates that incorporate sculptural seating elements at either end.

The original domed skylights that illuminate these entrance spaces have been updated with custom-made glass blocks, while below, their form is mirrored in a series of circular stainless-steel sinks.

The majority of the toilets occupy a row of stainless-steel cubicles inserted between the flint-lined walls of the central passage, creating a two-way route with doors that open on alternating sides.

As much as possible, the existing structure was adapted with minimal intervention, demonstrated by a series of cubicles that have been tucked into a series of curved niches at one of the tunnel’s entrances and simply fronted with stainless-steel doors.

“The direct reuse of the underground space, without expansion or alteration, demonstrates a restrained and intelligent approach to urban transformation,” said the studio.

“The intervention focuses on a clear material contrast: the systematic use of stainless steel highlights the original flint walls and concrete, further enhanced by strategic artificial lighting,” it added.

As part of the project, Chartier-Corbasson Architectes introduced natural ventilation into the subterranean spaces and also created new stainless-steel gutters to help manage water infiltration from above.

Given its setting in a high-traffic public park, the newly introduced elements were predominantly constructed off-site to minimise disruption and on-site waste.

Other projects that have recently sought to elevate public toilet design include a toilet block in London by Studio Weave, which is clad in contrasting panels of stone salvaged from a demolished office building, and the 17 Tokyo Toilets designed by famous architects.

Photography by Romain Meffre & Yves Marchand.

Inside the Craft of the Nubank Brand Refresh by Koto

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Koto's Nubank brand refresh turns a 140-million-customer bank into one flexible system: purple, modular, and unmistakably Nu.
  • Nubank started in Brazil with a simple idea, that banking did not need to be so complicated.
  • According to recent reports, the type does the heavy lifting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Koto's Nubank brand refresh turns a 140-million-customer bank into one flexible system: purple, modular, and unmistakably Nu.

Nubank started in Brazil with a simple idea, that banking did not need to be so complicated. It now serves more than 140 million people across Brazil, Mexico and Colombia. Koto kept the logo and wordmark, refined the signature purple inside a wider palette, and built a system of color, modules and layers that stretches across new markets.

According to recent reports, the type does the heavy lifting. Nu Sans Display and Nu Sans Text are Nubank's first proprietary typefaces, drawn to hold up as poster-scale headlines and app labels alike. Display runs huge and loose across the ads, white on purple, the small purple nu square sitting inside the copy like punctuation.

The grid is a set of simple rules. Color, modules and layers combine and recombine, so the same ingredients build a billboard, a card or a phone screen. Photo strips stagger across the purple field, and motion extends the same logic, from bold brand moments to animated illustrations in the app.

It has been revealed that the physical pieces carry the same discipline. The purple Mastercard keeps its clean face, chip and wordmark, and the welcome card pairs it with illustrated green hills and blue sky under "Hello Alex!" The card is the product, and Koto photographs it that way, on a restaurant table among receipts.

According to recent reports, digital is where the system works hardest. Koto rebuilt nu.com to hold products, languages and regulations behind one effortless front, with a bright purple hero, a row of photography and a giant lavender "That's Nu." The app follows the same order, a piggy bank banner, deposit and send buttons, balances split between spending and savings.

Two libraries give the system range. The global photography library, more than 50 photos and films, shows real relationships and unguarded moments of joy, people out in the world instead of models selling a bank. Beside it sits a hand-painted illustration library, drawn to move as well as stand still, from the welcome art's green hills to the rider on a purple card.

The refresh took the stage in Miami, at Nu Stadium, on September 10, 2026, as Nubank started operations in the United States and introduced Nu Global, a multi-currency account for global lives. Koto shaped the moment from screen to stage, with launch films and the founder's keynote.

It has been revealed that the sub-brands stretch the system without breaking it. Croma turns more expressive and colorful, with a gold card and a Portuguese voice that talks about progress rewarded. Ultravioleta goes richer and more refined, deep purple packaging with gold lettering and debossed type, premium without old codes of exclusivity.
